My friend once helped me with homework and now expects me to help him cheat. Being grateful does not mean I must do wrong; I can repay him in honest ways.
I find a hundred-rupee note in the corridor, and my heart races with ideas of what I could buy. Wanting is natural; a wise choice is handing it to a teacher or asking whose it is.
I think of the child who lost the note and how worried he might be. Imagining someone else's feelings makes returning it feel simple and warm, not like a loss.
Friends say, finders keepers, let's buy chips. I feel torn between fitting in and doing right. I can decline politely, and often a friend quietly feels relieved that someone said it.
The shopkeeper gives me extra change by mistake. Nobody will know, but I would. Returning it feels awkward for a moment and then makes me feel light and trusted.
My parent hears that I returned a wallet and hugs me. I feel proud, but I should do the right thing even when nobody praises me, because honesty is for me first.
The child whose money I returned smiles and says thank you. It feels good, but I must not expect a reward each time. Doing right is its own quiet reward.
At the temple, mosque, church or gurudwara, everyone sings together and I feel part of something bigger. Belonging is precious; I can also ask why we do things, not just copy.
My grandmother teaches me a prayer and her eyes shine. I feel loved and rooted. I take it in with respect and can still ask questions later; good elders welcome them.
I listen to the religious teacher's stories and believe them fully. Trust is natural at this age; over time I learn to notice whether teachings promote kindness and never fear, cruelty or secrecy.
I thank God for my family and food before eating. The feeling is warm and simple. Gratitude can also become action, like sharing my food with someone who has less.
I prayed hard and my wish did not come true, and now I wonder whether anyone hears. Doubt is honest. I can talk to a trusted elder about it instead of hiding it or feeling wicked.
Diwali, Eid, Christmas or Baisakhi means sweets, new clothes and guests, and I am bubbling. Joy is good; a mature child also remembers those who cannot celebrate and shares a little.
At the gathering I am told I cannot join because of who I am. It hurts and confuses me. It is not my fault; I can tell a trusted adult and know that real faith does not shut a child out.
My friend fasts, wears a cross, or eats different food, and I want to know why. Asking kindly and listening shows respect, and I learn that different ways can each be sincere.
My friend invites me to his festival and explains each thing patiently. I feel welcome. I can join with respect, without needing to agree or feeling that my own faith is threatened.
I laugh at a classmate's prayers or clothes because others do. It feels like fitting in, but it hurts someone. Standing quietly aside or changing the subject is braver.
Classmates mock my prayer or dress. I feel ashamed of who I am. There is nothing wrong with my faith; I can tell a teacher and lean on friends and family who love me.
An elder says people of that faith are bad. I feel confused because my friend seems good. I can hold on to my own experience and ask questions, without being rude to the elder.
When someone insults my friend's religion, I speak up even though it is uncomfortable. Friendship shows in defending someone's dignity, not in staying silent.
I stand tall for the anthem and feel goosebumps on Republic Day. Pride in the country feels warm; a wise child also learns that love for one's land includes caring for all its people.
We stand for the anthem because the teacher says so and I do it without thinking. Over time I learn it is a way of showing respect, not just a rule to fear.
I giggle during the anthem because friends do. It is easy to copy others; I learn that respect for shared symbols matters to many, and that I can save jokes for another time.
I hear a story of a soldier or freedom fighter and feel awed at their courage. Admiration can inspire me to serve in my own small ways, like honesty and helping the community.
A classmate of another region or faith says he too loves the country. I see that loving one's land is not owned by any one group, and I welcome him as a fellow citizen.
I hear elders argue angrily about the country and leaders. It confuses me. I can listen, ask calm questions, and understand that respect for the nation does not mean everyone must think alike.
I see someone litter near the flag or a monument and feel uneasy. Civic respect means caring for shared places too; I can pick it up or gently remind someone.
I receive weekly pocket money and feel grown up. Gratitude means remembering it comes from my parents' hard work, and thoughtful spending shows I value it.
I see a toy and spend my whole allowance in a minute, then feel regret. This is how children learn; waiting a day before buying teaches me to tell wanting from needing.
I saved for months and bought a cricket bat with my own money. The pride is deep. Saving teaches patience and shows me that effort builds what I want.
My friend gets much more pocket money and buys many things. I feel a pang. It helps to remember that families differ, and to value what I have instead of comparing.
A friend keeps borrowing money and never returns it, saying we are best friends. I feel used but scared to say so. I can politely refuse and talk to a parent if it keeps happening.
I share my pocket money to buy my little sister a gift. The joy of giving feels bigger than buying for myself. Generosity is good when it comes freely, not from being pressured.
My parents let me keep a small savings box and do not check every rupee. I feel trusted and try to earn it. Trust grows when I report honestly, even about mistakes.
A player in my online game is kind and helps me win, and I feel close to him. Game friends can be fun, but I keep private details to myself and let my parents know who I play with.
Someone in the game shouts insults at me. My face gets hot and I want to hit back. Muting, blocking and telling a parent is smarter than trading insults, which only feeds it.
A player offers free gems if I share my password or address. It feels like a lucky offer, but it is a warning sign. I refuse and tell a trusted adult right away.
My friend and I are fiercely competing for game ranks. Rivalry is exciting, but if I cannot stand losing or start sulking, I should take a break and remember he matters more than the score.
I keep thinking about the game while at school and get upset when I must stop. This is a sign to loosen my grip. I can agree with my parents on time limits and balance it with outdoor play.
My parent says switch off now and I shout that I am at a key part. Anger comes from being interrupted; agreeing beforehand to finish the round, then stopping, keeps peace.
The game keeps offering purchases to look cool or win. It is designed to tempt me. I can ask a parent before spending, and remember that real friends do not care about my skins.
A stranger in the game asks if I am okay after I lose badly. It feels nice, but kindness online still needs care; I stay friendly and never share private information.
A person messages me and seems interesting, and I want to reply. Curiosity is natural, but I check with a parent before chatting, and I never share my school, address or photos.
A stranger says I am so mature and special and asks me to keep our chats secret. Flattery plus secrecy is a red flag. I stop replying and tell a parent or teacher, and I have done nothing wrong.
A stranger says he knows where I live and I freeze. It is right to be scared. I save the messages, do not answer and immediately tell a trusted adult; help is available.
I chatted with someone I should not have and I am afraid to tell my parents. Shame keeps children silent; telling them early is the bravest and safest step, and they are on my side.
My friend is secretly chatting with a stranger who asks for photos. Being loyal means telling a trusted adult, even if she gets angry, because her safety matters more than the secret.
A classmate posts a mean message about me in a group chat. I feel hurt and exposed. I can save the proof, avoid replying in anger and tell a parent or teacher; it is not my fault.
I ask an AI assistant many questions and love how it answers instantly. It helps me learn, and I can also double-check with books and teachers because it can be wrong.
I ask the AI to do my homework and feel relieved. But if it does my thinking, I learn nothing and cannot answer in class. I can use it to explain things, then try the work myself.
I believe everything the AI says because it sounds confident. A wise child learns that fluent answers can still be mistaken, and checks important facts.
When I feel lonely, the AI chatbot is easy to talk to and never gets tired. That comfort is fine sometimes, but I also need real friends and family; I can tell a trusted person how I feel.
My teacher asks if I used an AI for my project. I feel tempted to say no. Honestly saying how I used it, and what I did myself, keeps trust and lets her guide me.
My parent worries about me chatting with AI and asks to see. I feel watched, but sharing openly helps them trust me. I can explain what I use it for and agree on some rules.
The AI writes a poem in seconds and I think it is magic. Wonder is lovely; I also remember it is a tool made by people, and my own imagination is what makes stories mine.
An ad shows a cool toy and I suddenly need it. Ads are made to create wanting. I can pause and ask myself if I still want it tomorrow, or if it was just the ad.
A cartoon or celebrity says this snack makes you strong, and I believe it. I learn that ads sell things, so I can ask a parent whether it really is good for me.
All my friends have the new branded shoes and I feel left out. Wanting to fit in is human. I can ask myself whether friendship depends on shoes, and talk to my parents honestly.
I beg my parents for something I saw in an ad and they refuse. I feel angry and it seems unfair. Understanding their limits and offering to save for it myself shows growing maturity.
I love watching a YouTuber who seems to have a perfect life. Admiration can inspire me, but I remember that videos are edited and nobody's real life is only fun.
My parent buys me something after I waited patiently. It feels extra special. Learning to wait makes me value things and understand the effort behind them.
My parent takes my tablet and I feel furious and cheated. Underneath, I am upset at losing something fun. Negotiating a fixed schedule is better than sneaking screens.
My mother says I look tired and stares at my screen habit. She is worried, not being mean. Listening to her and setting a limit together shows I can take care of myself.
When I am bored I grab the phone and scroll. Boredom is where new ideas begin; sometimes I can try drawing, playing outside or reading instead.
My brother and I fight over the TV remote. Taking turns with a timer, or asking a parent to decide, is fairer than shouting or grabbing.
My friends only want to play online now and I feel lonely if I do not join. I can invite them to play outside, and notice how I feel after long screen time.
I watched something I knew I should not, and I feel embarrassed. Curiosity is normal; telling a trusted adult helps me understand what I saw and feel safe again, without being punished for asking.
My grandfather says we children never talk to him because of phones. I feel guilty. Putting the phone away for a story-time chat gives us both something we need.
My dog has died and I cannot stop crying. The hole in my chest is real grief. Crying, talking and making a small memory box are healthy ways to say goodbye.
My father hugs me and says it is okay to cry. I feel less alone. I learn that being sad is normal and that sharing it makes the load lighter.
A friend says, it is only a dog, get a new one. It stings because my pet was family. I can tell him gently that I need time, and turn to people who understand.
I think I could have done something to save my pet. Children often blame themselves, but this is not my fault. Talking to an adult helps me see that I loved my pet well.
My little brother is also crying about the pet, and I want to look after him. Comforting someone else helps me feel my own sorrow and makes us closer.
My grandmother died and the house feels empty. I miss her stories and her hands. Grief comes in waves; letting myself cry and remember her is a way of loving her still.
I see my parent crying for the first time. It is frightening, but it shows that adults also feel deeply. I can hug them and say I am sad too.
Relatives gather for prayers and rituals after the death. The songs and food give me a sense of belonging. Whatever our beliefs, rituals help families carry sorrow together.
I do not understand where my grandfather has gone and adults give different answers. It is okay to ask questions and to hear that people have different beliefs and that nobody knows everything.
I feel nothing after the funeral and worry there is something wrong with me. Children grieve in different ways, sometimes later. I can tell a trusted adult and play or cry when I feel it.
A friend sits quietly beside me and does not say much. That quiet company helps more than advice. I learn that just being present is a strong way to care.
I see a classmate in torn shoes and feel sorry. Feeling for him is kind, but pity can turn into looking down. I can be a friend, share and treat him as an equal.
A classmate has a big house and gadgets, and I feel small. Envy is normal; I try to see my own gifts, and remember that wealth does not make anyone better or happier.
A rich classmate brags and calls my things cheap. I feel ashamed. His words show his insecurity, not my worth; I can walk away and stay close to kinder friends.
I cannot afford the class trip and feel embarrassed. It is not my shame to carry. I can talk privately to a teacher, who may find quiet help, and my worth does not depend on money.
The maid or driver at home is treated as lesser by some visitors. Respect means greeting them, saying thank you and remembering they too are somebody's parents.
I see a child begging at a signal and feel a tug in my heart. Wanting to help is good. I can ask my parents about safe ways, like giving food or supporting an organisation.
A richer friend shares his tiffin and does not make a show of it. I feel grateful and a bit awkward. I can accept warmly and share something of my own in return.
A classmate is called names for his caste, religion or accent, and I see it. It is not right, and I can feel angry. I can sit with him, and tell a teacher if it continues.
An older relative talks badly about a group and my family nods along. I feel uneasy. I can quietly hold my own view and later ask a trusted elder why they think so.
I am told girls should not play cricket or boys should not cry. I feel it is unfair. I can keep doing what I love, find friends who accept me and ask why that rule exists.
I see the cook being made to drink from a separate glass. I feel confused and sad. Asking my parents about fairness and treating everyone the same is a start.
Friends want to exclude a child because he is different. I feel afraid to disagree. Staying friendly with him, even quietly, can help him and shows courage.
A teacher treats all children equally regardless of background, and I notice. It makes me feel safe, and teaches me that fairness is a choice adults make.
I laughed at a joke about someone's caste or religion and later feel bad. That feeling is my conscience. I can apologise and avoid such jokes next time.
I watch rain or a big tree and feel amazed. Wonder makes me want to protect nature, and simple things like planting a sapling connect me to it.
I see a stray dog thirsty in the heat and put out water. Small kindness to animals grows my heart, and I learn to be careful and tell an adult first.
We waste water and burn plastic at home, and I feel uneasy. I can suggest small changes politely, like a bucket for washing, without shaming my parents.
Classmates laugh when I pick up litter. I feel embarrassed but I believe it matters. Doing the right thing even when laughed at shows quiet strength, and others may follow.
I hear about climate change and become anxious about the future. That is understandable. I can talk to an adult and focus on small steps that are within my control.
I learn how a farmer grows my food and how a sweeper keeps streets clean. Respect for those who work with their hands makes me waste less and thank them.
I am scared of a big dog or a snake. Fear keeps me safe; I keep distance, ask adults and learn about animals so I do not react with cruelty.
I failed and I feel like the whole class knows I am stupid. Shame makes me hide, but a failed test is information about what to practise, not a label on me.
My parent shouts about my failure and I go quiet. I feel small. I can wait until things cool, then say I want to improve and ask for help with a plan.
My teacher stays back to explain what I got wrong. I feel cared for. Accepting help is not weakness, and it shows that someone believes I can improve.
A classmate laughs at my marks. It hurts, but I know one score does not define me. I can answer calmly or walk away, and remember that he too has weak spots.
My friend says he also struggled and offers to study together. I feel less alone. Shared effort turns a failure into a team problem with a solution.
After failing, I decide to practise the hard chapter every day. Growth starts when I look at mistakes without hating myself, and celebrate small improvements.
I am scared of the dark and imagine things in the corner. Fear is real even if the danger is not. Talking about it and having a small light helps, and it fades with time.
My mother sits beside me after a nightmare and says I am safe. Her calm makes my heart slow down. I learn that fear shared becomes smaller.
A friend laughs that I am a scaredy-cat. It stings. Being afraid does not mean I am weak; I can say everyone is afraid of something, and choose friends who do not tease.
I did something scary, like a swim or a stage show, and felt proud afterwards. Facing small fears builds trust in myself, and I do not need to prove bravery by risking safety.
An older child threatens me and I am terrified. It is right to feel scared. I do not have to face it alone; telling a teacher or parent is smart, not shameful.
I spilled ink on a friend's book and feel my face burn. Shame says I am bad, while guilt says I did a bad thing. I can apologise and offer to fix it.
The whole class laughs when I stammer or fall on stage. I want to disappear. Most of them forget soon; a friend who stands by me matters more than the laughter.
My mother forgives me quickly when I confess a mistake. I feel a weight lift. Being forgiven teaches me that a mistake can be mended and does not end love.
The teacher scolds me sharply for a slip. I feel ashamed and defensive. Listening to what I can learn, without deciding I am useless, helps me grow.
I broke something at home and hid the pieces. The secret feels heavy. Telling the truth, even late, usually brings relief and shows my parents I can be trusted.
A classmate draws or sings beautifully and I am amazed. Admiring others opens my heart, and I can ask how she practises instead of thinking I could never do it.
Everyone praises my classmate's talent and I feel invisible. Envy shows me what I care about. I can work on my own strengths instead of running down hers.
My parents say, look at your cousin, he is so good. I feel crushed. I can say that I am trying in my own way and ask them to notice what I do well.
I won a prize for my talent and love the applause. Pride is healthy; I stay humble by thanking those who taught me and helping others who are learning.
My friend goes cold after I win a contest. I feel confused and guilty for winning. I can stay kind, give him space and remind him that his friendship matters to me.
I believe I am not good at anything special. At this age, talents unfold slowly; trying different things and enjoying them is more valuable than being the best.
My teacher notices a small skill in me that I never saw. I feel seen and surprised. One honest encouragement can open a path, and I can keep practising.
A classmate teases me about my weight, height or skin colour. It cuts deeply. Their words reflect their unkindness, not my worth; I can tell a trusted adult and seek kind friends.
I look in the mirror and dislike how I look. Many children feel this. I can focus on what my body can do, like run and play, and talk to an adult I trust about how I feel.
Films and ads show only fair, slim, perfect people. I begin to feel I am not good enough. I remember that images are edited and that real people come in every shape and shade.
My parent says I am beautiful just as I am, though I do not believe it. Even so, it plants a seed. Being loved unconditionally helps me build a steady view of myself.
A friend does not care how I look and only wants to play. I feel relaxed with him. Friends like this remind me that worth is in who I am, not how I appear.
I feel strong and happy after winning a race. Feeling proud of my body for what it can do is healthy, and I can respect other bodies that are different from mine.
Nobody is watching and I could take an extra sweet or skip my chore. Doing right anyway builds a self I can trust, and that inner steadiness is worth more than getting away with it.
The teacher leaves the room and the answer key lies open. My heart beats fast. Deciding beforehand not to look, and walking away, helps more than fighting the urge in the moment.
My parents leave me at home alone and trust me to follow their rules. I feel grown up. Keeping their trust when unobserved makes them give me more freedom.
I told a small lie and nobody knows, yet I feel uneasy. Small lies grow bigger if I keep them. Fixing it by telling the truth helps my conscience and my relationships.
A friend dares me to do something naughty while adults are away. I fear looking like a coward. I can say no with a smile or a joke, and true friends will not mind.
In a village honesty shop, people pay by leaving money in a box. I feel the weight of being trusted. Being trusted is a gift that I honour by paying the full amount.
I see a policeman in uniform and feel respect and slight fear. Police exist to keep people safe; I can learn that I may ask them for help if I am lost or in trouble.
My friends tell scary stories about police and I get nervous. I can ask parents what police really do, and learn that a good officer helps children.
I learn to stop at red lights and cross at zebra crossings. Rules keep everyone safe, and I remind adults politely if they break them.
An adult in authority is rude or unfair to my family. I feel angry and powerless. I remember that power does not make someone right, and rely on my parents to handle it safely.
The guard at our building greets everyone each morning. I greet him back and learn his name. Respecting everyone, whatever their job, is part of being a good citizen.
An adult tells me to keep a secret or do something that feels wrong. I feel torn because I must obey elders. I can say no, leave, and tell a trusted adult; safety comes first.

I feel treated like a small child and stew in silent anger. Wise: say calmly what the rule costs me and offer a trial of trust. Immature: sulking, slamming doors, or punishing them by dropping my studies.

I start thinking my parents are backward and clueless, so their words stop counting. Wise: separate their fear from their outdated methods and still hear the concern. Immature: sneering and treating them as fools.

I am the parent's fear made visible: they picture accidents, bad company, gossip. A teen in this spot should see that rules often come from love plus anxiety, and ask what exactly they fear so it can be addressed.
I follow a rule I dislike because they have earned my trust before, and I say my disagreement openly. Wise: comply, then negotiate for later. Risk: swallowing every wish just to avoid conflict.
I fake tears, praise, or emotional blackmail to get a yes. It works sometimes and leaves me feeling slippery. Wise: notice the habit and make an honest case instead, since trust is what buys freedom.

As the parent I clamp down after seeing my teen change, and I feel shut out. A teen can help by sharing plans and whereabouts freely, which lowers the parent's need to control and grows real autonomy.
As the teen whose phone is monitored, I feel watched. Wise: ask for a clear reason and a path to more trust, and share enough openly that constant checking is not needed. Harmful: secret accounts.

When told to be like the topper cousin, I feel small and defective, as if love depends on marks. Wise: name the hurt to a trusted adult, keep my own goals. Harmful: believing the comparison as truth about my worth.

I resent my parent and quietly dislike the cousin who did nothing wrong. Wise: tell the parent how comparison lands and ask for support with my own targets. Immature: sabotaging my work to prove them wrong.

I am compared aloud at family gatherings and feel judged in front of everyone. It is not my fault, and their pride and anxiety are the source. Wise: ask privately to stop and show effort on my own terms.

As a parent I compare my child because I fear they will fall behind and I feel my own regrets. Wise: notice that comparison motivates rarely, and praise real effort. Harmful: making love feel conditional.
I am the cousin held up as ideal and feel awkward, unable to share my own struggles. Wise: stay kind, admit I have difficulties too, and refuse to gloat. Harmful: enjoying the pedestal.

I stop reacting to comparisons and go numb, telling myself I do not care. Wise: check whether I truly stopped caring or just stopped feeling; then have one honest talk. Harmful: turning off effort altogether.
I mourn the family I thought I had and feel it as my loss too. Wise: let myself cry, keep routines, and talk to a friend or counsellor. Harmful: pretending I am fine to protect everyone.

I blame one parent and cannot sit in the same room with them. Wise: recognise that anger covers sadness and that adult relationships are more complicated than I see. Harmful: cutting one parent off entirely.
I secretly wonder if my fights or grades caused the split. Wise: hear from the parents plainly that it was not my fault and keep loving both. Harmful: trying to fix them by behaving perfectly.
A parent uses me as messenger or spy, or badmouths the other to win my side. It is not my job or fault. Wise: kindly refuse to carry messages and tell a trusted adult if the pressure continues.
I feel torn, afraid that loving one parent betrays the other. Wise: say I love both and will not choose. Harmful: siding with the louder parent or hiding affection from the other to keep peace.
After time I see both parents as flawed humans who do better apart, and I take care of my own life. Wise: stay open to visits and honest with them. Risk: forcing calm before I have grieved.
Absorbed in their own pain, my parent forgets my meals, exams, or feelings. It is not because I am unlovable. Wise: ask for what I need clearly and lean on a grandparent, teacher, or relative.
A grandparent steps in with food, listening, and stability while my parents break apart. I feel safe but sometimes disloyal. Wise: accept the care with gratitude and keep including both parents.
I watch my brother or sister get gifts, trust, or praise I never get and feel invisible. Wise: tell a parent what I notice without attacking the sibling. Immature: making the sibling pay.
I keep a running tally of unfairness against my parent and stop confiding. Wise: raise it directly, using specific examples, and check whether I am also reading too much into small things.
I am the favourite and feel warm but uneasy, aware my sibling suffers. Wise: not to exploit it, to share credit, and to stay kind to my sibling. Harmful: enjoying the status or acting entitled.
Being treated as the golden child, I feel guilty when my sibling is snubbed. Wise: gently include them and refuse to compete for the parent's approval. It is not my fault, but my behaviour matters.
My sibling hates me for being preferred and says cruel things. Wise: see the pain underneath, avoid retaliating, and ask parents to fix their behaviour. Harmful: rubbing it in.

I bond with the less favoured sibling against unfair treatment and we protect each other. Wise: lean on that closeness while staying respectful. Harmful: turning it into a permanent war against parents.
As the parent I favour the child who is like me and never notice the other shrinking. Wise: for a teen, understand this is usually blindness and not hatred, and tell them plainly what I need.

We fight over the phone, room, and parental attention, each keeping score. Wise: agree on clear shared rules and ask a parent to referee once. Immature: tattling, hiding things, and escalating each round.
I fight with my younger sibling yet turn fierce when outsiders tease them. Wise: this loyalty is real; show it more kindly at home too. Harmful: bossing them and calling it protection.
I think my sibling is stupid or lazy and say it so. Wise: notice contempt shuts down closeness and ask what I envy or fear. Harmful: cruelty in front of others.
My younger sibling follows me everywhere and copies me, and I am annoyed and secretly flattered. Wise: give some time and boundaries, remembering I am their model. Harmful: mocking their need.

An elder sibling paid for my coaching or covered for me, and I feel thankful yet pressured. Wise: thank them in words and actions and do not let debt become silence. Harmful: pretending it was nothing.
My sibling is jealous of my grades or friends and needles me. Wise: stay kind, share what I can, and avoid boasting. Harmful: pushing back with put-downs.

I told my best friend something private and it spread. I feel sick and exposed. It is not my fault for trusting. Wise: confront calmly, reassess what to share with them, and tell a trusted adult if it hurts badly.
I leaked a friend's secret out of excitement and now I cannot face them. Wise: apologise plainly with no excuse, accept their anger, and give distance. Harmful: denying it or blaming them.
I imagine exposing their secrets in return. Wise: feel the rage, tell it to someone safe, and choose not to do it since revenge makes me the second betrayer. Harmful: acting on it.
They deny leaking and say I am overreacting or imagining it. Wise: trust my own memory, keep details, and step back. This is not my fault. Harmful: doubting myself until I apologise.
After a sincere apology I decide to trust them slowly with small things. Wise: watch consistent behaviour over words. Harmful: pretending nothing happened or demanding total forgiveness at once.
I pass on a secret because others want news and I want to belong. It gives a thrill and then guilt. Wise: recognise gossip as buying status with someone else's pain, and stop.
Losing my picture of them as perfectly loyal is worse than the leak. Wise: mourn it, then see people as flawed and choose closer friends carefully. Harmful: deciding nobody can be trusted.
I badly want to sit with the popular group and change my behaviour to fit. Wise: notice that belonging bought with self-erasure is fragile, and look for people who like the real me.
They go silent when I approach and laugh over inside jokes. It hurts and is more about their insecurity than my worth. Wise: leave with dignity, find other groups, and tell someone I trust.
I sneer at the popular group as shallow to protect myself. Wise: see the hurt behind the armour and avoid becoming the same kind of exclusion machine. Harmful: bitter gossip about them.
The leader grants and withdraws warmth to keep me anxious and obedient. Wise: notice the pattern, refuse tests of loyalty, and build friendships that are steady and kind.
I decide who is in and out and enjoy how others watch me. Underneath I fear losing my place. Wise: use influence to include people. Harmful: cruelty that keeps me on top.
I watch the group freeze someone out and stay silent, feeling ashamed. Wise: quietly befriend the excluded person or speak up in a small way. Harmful: joining in to stay safe.
After weeks of feeling on the edge, I am invited in and feel relief mixed with wariness. Wise: enjoy it without dropping older friends or my values.

I see my crush as flawless and hang on every word. It feels wonderful and blinds me. Wise: enjoy the feeling, remember they are an ordinary person, and keep my own life going. Harmful: rebuilding myself for them.

I check their profile constantly and cannot focus. Wise: recognise the loop as a mind-hunger, limit checking, talk to a friend, and channel energy elsewhere. Harmful: monitoring or turning up uninvited.

Someone clearly worships me from afar and I feel flattered and uneasy. Wise: be kind and clear that I am just a person, and set boundaries if the attention crowds me. Harmful: using it to feel powerful.
They said no or did not feel the same. It stings badly. Wise: accept it without pressing, grieve with friends, and let it teach me. Harmful: pestering, spreading rumours, or calling them cruel.
Someone likes me and I do not feel the same. Wise: say a kind, clear no with no mixed signals, keep their dignity, and do not mock them. Harmful: leading them on for attention.

I freeze near my crush and imagine all the ways I might embarrass myself. Wise: start with friendly ordinary talk and accept that awkwardness is normal. Harmful: hiding for years or sending a dramatic message.
I feel a strong pull toward someone and am unsure what it means or whether it fits my family's expectations. Wise: take my time, talk to someone I trust, and be honest without rushing to a label.
My friend started liking someone I like, and rivalry creeps in. Wise: speak honestly early and value the friendship above the crush. Harmful: secretly undermining them.
They demand my passwords, tell me what to wear, and get angry when I see friends. It is control and not proof of love. Wise: name it, keep friends close, and tell a trusted adult.
When I resist, they say I am selfish or that they will fall apart. I feel responsible for their feelings. Wise: care without giving in, and get help from a counsellor or elder if it continues.
I tiptoe around their mood, dreading explosions. It is not my fault. Wise: this is a warning sign; talk to a parent, teacher, or helpline and plan a safe way out.
I feel I will die without them and need constant reassurance and check-ins. Wise: see this as anxiety and not love, seek support, and build my own interests. Harmful: monitoring or controlling them.
I like them and we both can say no, keep friends, and enjoy the time. Wise: keep communicating openly and treat consent as always on. It grows because neither owns the other.
They press me to do something I am not ready for, saying everyone does. Wise: no is enough and a person who respects me accepts it. Harmful: giving in to keep them.
I catch myself using silent treatment or guilt to get my way. Wise: notice the pattern, apologise, and ask directly instead. Harmful: excusing it as passion.
After a breakup I feel hollow and replay it constantly. Wise: let it hurt, keep sleep and food routine, lean on friends, and give it time. Harmful: pinging them repeatedly or numbing with screens.
I am furious and want them to feel it. Wise: write it out, exercise, tell a friend, and do not post or send messages. Harmful: leaking their photos, spreading stories, or stalking their accounts.
I was dumped and feel worthless. It says nothing about my value. Wise: sit with it, stay in touch with friends, and avoid begging. Harmful: bargaining or turning it into self-hatred.
I ended it and feel awful for the pain I caused. Wise: be honest and respectful, avoid mixed messages, and give them space. Harmful: ending it by ghosting.
My ex keeps texting and turning up, saying I owe them another chance. Wise: give one clear final no, block if needed, tell parents or school, and refuse to feel guilty. It is not my fault.
Months later I let go of the anger, not because they deserved it but because I am tired of carrying it. Wise: this frees me without reopening the door.

Our private messages or photos were shared to shame me. This is a serious violation and not my fault. Wise: save evidence, tell a trusted adult, report to school or police cyber cell, and seek support.

A close friend stopped replying with no reason and I replay everything I said. Wise: send one honest message, then accept the silence and stop chasing. Harmful: blaming myself or messaging fifty times.
We talked daily and then they vanished. It feels like erasure. Wise: recognise it reflects their avoidance, not my worth; grieve, and ask friends for company. Harmful: fake accounts to check on them.
I stopped answering because I did not know how to say I wanted distance. Wise: a short honest message is kinder than silence. Harmful: hiding until they give up.
I am furious at being dropped and rehearse cutting replies. Wise: let the anger cool, decide whether the friendship is worth one calm message, and keep my dignity.
My friend moved on to new people and treats me as background. I am hurt but see that friendships shift with time. Wise: name it once, then invest in new and reciprocal bonds.
They reply only when it suits them and I keep waiting. Wise: say what I need; if it does not change, step back. Harmful: lowering my standards and calling it patience.
A group chat turns against me and screenshots circulate. I feel exposed and panicked. It is not my fault. Wise: do not reply in anger, save evidence, mute, and tell a trusted adult or school.
I join in mocking someone because everyone is laughing and I fear being next. Wise: notice how easily I slide into cruelty and stop or send the person a kind private message.
A friend said something harsh in the group and I want to blast them back. Wise: pause, take it to a private chat, and say what hurt. Harmful: public retaliation that everyone screenshots.
As admin I can remove people and enjoy that control. Wise: use it fairly and never exclude to humiliate. Harmful: kicking people out to please the loud ones.
I watch a classmate get torn apart in the chat and say nothing. I feel guilty and scared. Wise: one supportive private message or a report to a teacher helps more than staying quiet.

A false rumour about me spreads. My instinct is to explode or vanish. Wise: stay calm, tell parents or a teacher, correct it once with facts, and lean on real friends. Harmful: spreading counter-rumours.
I dread the corridor and lie about being sick. This is not my fault and bullying is never something to earn or endure. Wise: tell a trusted adult, note dates, and stay near supportive people.

I hate the person who torments me and picture hurting them. Wise: feel that anger as a sign of harm done, share it with someone safe, and seek adult intervention. Harmful: retaliating, which can put me at risk.
I bully others because it feels strong, often hiding my own hurt at home. Wise: notice what I am covering and ask a counsellor or teacher for help. Harmful: cruelty for laughs.
I look down on someone weaker and see them as fair game. Wise: challenge that story; it is a fear of being weak myself. Harmful: turning contempt into a public habit.
I saw it and did nothing and now feel ashamed. Wise: check on the target privately, report to a teacher, and refuse to laugh. Small acts matter.
I stand up for someone being bullied. Wise: stay calm, stand beside them, get an adult early, and avoid violence. Harmful: heroic fights that make things worse.
A bully treats me as a sidekick and rewards me for joining. I feel safe and sick. Wise: step away at some risk and stop taking part; being safe should not depend on hurting others.
A teacher notices and steps in. I feel relieved and embarrassed. Wise: accept help, give details, and understand that speaking up is not snitching. Harmful: denying it out of fear.
After the bully apologises I feel mixed: relief, doubt, anger. Wise: accept the apology without forgetting, keep boundaries, and take time. Forgiving is not the same as trusting again.
I feel the teacher targets me and I stop trying in their class. Wise: gather examples, ask for a private talk, and keep working since marks are mine. Harmful: cheating or sulking.
A teacher believes in me and I work hard to earn their respect. Wise: use their belief while building my own drive. Risk: crushing dependence on their approval.
I develop feelings for a teacher and find them thrilling. Wise: this is common and passes, keep it private, and choose peers for romance. Harmful: pursuing them or writing dramatic notes.
I am the teacher's pet and classmates tease me. Wise: stay humble, help others, and avoid smug behaviour. Harmful: using the favour to belittle peers.
A teacher insults me in front of the class. I feel shame and rage. Wise: keep composure, speak to a parent or another trusted teacher, and report if it repeats. It is not my worth.
I am scared of a strict teacher and freeze in their class. Wise: prepare a little more, ask one question a week to break the ice, and separate strictness from cruelty.
Years later I see that the hard teacher pushed me well. Wise: thank them. Harmful: assuming that harshness is always good just because it worked once.
A teacher humiliates me before the class. I burn with shame. Wise: it reflects on their conduct, not my worth; tell a parent or a coordinator and keep a written record.
I choose to report unfair treatment through the proper route, believing the school can fix it. Wise: be factual, bring a friend or parent, and give it time. Harmful: posting it online first.
A strict teacher is unfair sometimes yet also taught me a lot. I feel respect and resentment together. Wise: hold both truths and speak to the unfair part specifically.
A teacher threatens failing marks if I object. Wise: keep records, tell a parent, and use the school's grievance process; being afraid to speak is not weakness.
Months later the teacher admits an error in my marks. I feel vindicated and tempted to gloat. Wise: accept it graciously, and keep the lesson about how to raise concerns.
I follow my coach's every word and want their approval above all. Wise: learn from them and keep my own judgement, and notice when they cross a line. Harmful: silence about mistreatment.
A coach yells and shames players to win. I feel dread. Wise: distinguish tough training from abuse; talk to parents or a school official if it becomes humiliation or touching feels wrong.
A senior or mentor uses my work or time for their own gain while promising opportunities. Wise: notice the imbalance, ask clear questions, and seek other mentors. Harmful: hoping praise will come.
A mentor gave time without asking anything back. Wise: thank them and pass it on later. Harmful: idealising them so much that I cannot disagree.
I resent the coach who benches me and think they prefer others. Wise: ask what to improve and keep training. Harmful: quitting angrily or talking behind their back.
A younger student idolises me and copies everything I do. Wise: be a good example, admit my flaws, and encourage them to think for themselves. Harmful: enjoying the worship.
Friends push me to try something risky like smoking, vaping, or skipping class, calling me boring. Wise: say a light, steady no, and leave if needed. Real friends do not cost me my safety.
I go along because I fear being laughed at or left out. Wise: admit to myself the fear is real, find one ally who will say no with me, and practise a short reply.
I look down on friends who follow rules and call them babies. Wise: see the same insecurity in myself and respect different choices. Harmful: forcing others to join my risks.
I cover for a friend's rule-breaking because loyalty matters. Wise: be loyal to their wellbeing, not to the risky act; tell an adult if they could be hurt.
I refuse pressure and someone follows me. Wise: stay friendly and never preach. Harmful: sneering at those who cave.
An online contact flatters me, asks for secrets or photos, or says to keep it from parents. Wise: stop, do not send anything, block, and tell a trusted adult right away. It is not my fault.

My parent is unwell or money is tight and I worry constantly, hearing whispers. Wise: ask what is happening, take small helpful jobs, and still keep studying and friends. Harmful: silently carrying adult burdens.

I hide our situation from friends and refuse invitations I cannot afford. Wise: speak to one trusted friend, avoid pretending, and know that money does not measure me. Harmful: lying or stealing to keep up.
I resent that my parent's illness limits my life and then hate myself for it. Wise: mixed feelings are normal; say them to a counsellor or relative. Harmful: acting them out on the parent.
I see my parent's sacrifices and feel gratitude and pressure to succeed. Wise: say thanks and take on fair responsibility. Harmful: believing I must give up my own dreams to repay them.
My parent leans on me emotionally, sharing worries meant for adults. I feel proud and burdened. Wise: support them yet ask that adults handle adult matters.
Friends pity my situation and offer help. It is kind and stings my pride. Wise: accept what feels fair without shame and say when I do not want pity. Harmful: rejecting kindness.
A friend's family is struggling and I want to help. Wise: offer time, notes, and company without making them a charity case. Harmful: gossiping about their problems.
I am popular and sense envy behind compliments. Wise: stay kind and honest, do not assume all attention is friendship, and keep close a few real friends. Harmful: cruelty to stay on top.
Younger students idolise me. It feels good, but it distorts my view of myself. Wise: stay humble and remember I am mid-growth like them. Harmful: needing the audience.
I am an outcast and eat lunch alone. The ache is real. Wise: look for one interest group or activity, start small conversations, and tell an adult if it persists. Harmful: assuming I am unlovable.
I am mocked as weird or poor or fat. It is unfair and not my fault. Wise: protect my self-respect, find spaces where I fit, and report harassment. Harmful: believing their story.
I envy popular classmates and study their lives online. Wise: notice curated images hide worries and focus on building my own strengths. Harmful: tearing them down to feel better.
I am proud to be different and refuse to fit in. Wise: enjoy it while remaining open to others. Harmful: using superiority as armour against connection.
I use charm and gossip to climb the social ladder. It works, and I feel hollow. Wise: recognise the cost to trust and choose honest ways to belong.
I idolise a popular senior and copy their style and speech. Wise: borrow what inspires me while building my own voice. Harmful: dropping old friends or my values to earn their notice.
I know my friend copied on an exam and feel torn between loyalty and honesty. Wise: urge them privately to come clean and do not join in. Harmful: silent complicity.
I report cheating and feel like a traitor, then friends turn on me. Wise: acting on principle can cost belonging; accept it with steadiness and seek supportive people.
Classmates ask me to share my answers and call me selfish if I refuse. Wise: refuse kindly, offer to study together, and accept some anger. Harmful: giving in to be liked.
A friend confides they cheated and asks me to keep it secret. Wise: listen without judging, say I cannot approve, and encourage them to fix it. Harmful: acting as their alibi.
A teacher asks who cheated. Wise: weigh fairness to honest students against loyalty, and speak to the teacher privately when needed. Harmful: gossiping about it or lying outright.
A rival got the captain spot or top rank I wanted and I feel it in my stomach. Wise: admit the envy, study what they did well, and keep working. Harmful: sabotage or spreading doubts.
I cannot stand even hearing their name. Wise: see how my hate is tying my energy to them and shift my focus to my own goals. Harmful: plotting to hurt their reputation.
We compete fiercely yet admire each other's work. Wise: let rivalry push both of us. Harmful: denying the friendship for fear of looking soft.
My rival boasts about beating me. Wise: stay composed, congratulate briefly, and use the sting as fuel. Harmful: returning insults or hiding for days.
I won and now a former friend turns cold. Wise: stay gracious, share credit, and reach out once. Harmful: flaunting the win or pretending I did not care.
A rival spreads doubts about me to teachers and friends. Wise: keep my record clean, calmly correct facts to adults, and avoid retaliation.
A rival sneers that I only got in through favour. It stings, especially if I fear it is true. Wise: let my work answer, ask a mentor for honest feedback, and avoid feeding the argument.
I accept the engineering or medicine path my family wants, partly from love and partly from fear. Wise: ask myself what I truly want and talk openly. Harmful: silent resentment for years.
I insist on my own path in arts or sport and feel guilt and defiance together. Wise: show a plan, some proof of effort, and a fallback. Harmful: shouting matches or lying about my studies.
My parent brags about my future to relatives and I feel a weight to perform. Wise: enjoy the belief and say honestly when it is too heavy. Harmful: hiding failing marks.
My parent has given up much for my schooling and reminds me of it. I feel indebted and trapped. Wise: honour the sacrifice with effort and honesty, not with my whole life plan.
My parent is disappointed by my result. I feel like I failed them. Wise: own the result, ask for help, and separate the mark from my worth. Harmful: hiding the report card.

A friend confides something painful. I feel honoured and scared. Wise: listen, do not joke, keep it private, and encourage them to tell a trusted adult. Harmful: promising total secrecy when they may be in danger.
I fear a friend is in real danger, such as self-neglect or unsafe home. Wise: breaking a secret to a trusted adult can be love, and tell the friend I am doing so. Harmful: carrying it alone.
I keep prying into a friend's private matters because I want to be in the know. Wise: let them share at their own pace. Harmful: pressuring them or sharing what I learn.
A friend leans on me at all hours and I am worn out. Wise: care, set limits, and encourage other support like family or a counsellor. Harmful: quietly resenting them.
I keep a friend's harmless secret through teasing and pressure. Wise: loyalty here is a strength; still check that the secret is not hurting them.

A younger friend tells me I am their hero and shares everything. I feel proud and pressured. Wise: stay honest about my flaws and point them to other supports. Harmful: leaning into control because they listen.
I say no to a hug, a photo, or a dare and feel awkward. Wise: a clear no needs no reason, and a good friend accepts it. Harmful: apologising for my boundary.
My crush says they are not comfortable with something. Wise: stop at once, thank them for honesty, and do not pout. Harmful: pushing, teasing, or sulking to get my way.
An older teen flatters me and pressures me for things I am unsure about. It is not my fault. Wise: no is enough; leave, tell a trusted adult, and know that real affection waits.
Friends demand that I share private photos or tease me for not dating. Wise: my body and messages are mine; do not send them, and tell an adult if anyone threatens to spread them.
I dread the result because my parents have staked their hopes and savings on it. Wise: tell them plainly how much I can carry. Harmful: hiding a bad mock score until it explodes.
I am being measured by marks, and it feels like love is conditional. Wise: hear the fear behind their push and say what helps, like a plan or a calm evening. Harmful: shutting down.
A classmate tops every test and I feel small and bitter. Wise: study their method and accept that ranks are one narrow measure. Harmful: spreading rumours or hiding notes.
Friends grow cold after I score well. Wise: stay warm, share notes, do not flaunt marks, and accept some distance may pass. Harmful: shrinking my effort to be liked.
One low result makes me feel I am worthless and have shamed my family. Wise: separate the paper from my worth, list what went wrong, and ask a teacher for a recovery plan.
A coaching centre ranks students in batches and makes the low-ranked feel lesser to sell fear. Wise: notice the business model, keep my own pace, and talk to a trusted adult if I am crumbling.
My friend has stopped eating and sleeping before boards. Wise: sit with them, offer a break, and tell a parent or counsellor if they sound hopeless. Harmful: joking or ignoring it.
After a bad paper I speak to myself as I would to a friend and plan the next one. It does not lower standards; it lets me keep working. Harmful: punishing myself as motivation.
A teacher stays after class to explain what I missed. I feel thankful and a little embarrassed to need help. Wise: say thanks and use the time well; asking is strength.
I want arts or design but my family expects science and engineering. Wise: research real paths, show numbers, ask for a trial period. Harmful: sulking or secret rebellion.

My stream is being decided for me because of prestige or a relative's success. Wise: stay respectful, bring a counsellor or elder as a bridge, and ask for reasons. It is not disobedience to have a mind.
I know my parents sacrifice for my future and feel both indebted and trapped. Wise: honour their effort while telling them my honest interests. Gratitude does not need to erase my choices.
Everyone in my group is picking the same stream, and I follow to stay together. Wise: notice friendships change anyway and choose for myself. Harmful: regret blamed on them later.
I do not know what I want and the deadline makes me panic. Wise: try small experiments, talk to people in real jobs, and accept that the first choice can be revised.
An older cousin who works in the field tells me honestly the good and bad of a career. I trust the honesty more than the glamour. Wise: hear more than one voice before deciding.
At family gatherings I am compared with a cousin who got into a top college. I feel small and angry. Wise: smile, answer briefly, and avoid making my path a contest.
I have a bold goal like the civil services or sport and I feel both fire and dread. Wise: build daily habits, keep a backup plan, and count effort rather than only outcome.
An admissions agent promises guaranteed jobs and pushes me to pay a deposit today. Wise: pause, verify with others, and never rush money decisions under pressure.
A police officer stops me and my heart races. Wise: stay calm, be polite, keep hands visible, give my name, ask if I am free to go, and call a parent. Harmful: running or arguing.
I have seen bad police behaviour and I now see every uniform as a threat. Wise: stay careful without hating everyone, and know that many officers do their duty properly.
An officer shouts and threatens me for being out late with friends. Wise: stay respectful, do not sign or confess anything, and ask for a parent or lawyer. Being scared is normal, not guilt.
An officer helps me after a lost phone or accident. I feel grateful and see that authority can protect. Wise: cooperate and thank them; holding both trust and scrutiny is fine.
I notice that officers treat rich kids gently and poorer boys roughly. I feel anger and helplessness. Wise: record what happened, seek an adult or legal aid, and channel anger into knowing my rights.
A friend brags about talking back to police. I feel the pull to copy. Wise: courage is knowing when to stay calm; a video for likes can cost me my safety.
My parent is frightened after I was questioned and turns strict. Wise: listen to the fear, share the full story, and agree on safe habits like sharing locations.
I lose belief in some rituals, yet I still sit beside my grandmother at prayer because I love her. Wise: honour the person while being honest inside. Harmful: mocking her faith.
The temple, mosque, church or gurdwara gives me friends and a sense of home. I value belonging, and I also ask questions. Wise: keep both without fearing either.
When I ask a doubtful question, elders call me disrespectful and shun me. It hurts deeply. Wise: seek an open-minded elder or friend, and not treat one group as the whole faith.
After a loss I am angry at God for not preventing it. Wise: anger is a form of relationship or a form of asking; it can be spoken aloud or written, and believers and non-believers both feel it.
I tell my parents I no longer believe as they do. Wise: choose a calm time, say I still respect them, and do not demand immediate acceptance. Harmful: attacking their beliefs.
My parents fear I am leaving the faith and lose their way of passing on their traditions. Wise: hear their fear, remain part of family events I can join honestly, and let time work.
I feel I do not believe in any god and feel lonely about it. Wise: find people, books and values I can rely on. Non-belief can also carry deep ethics and awe.
My friend follows a different religion, and we ask each other real questions. Wise: listen to learn, not to win. Curiosity and kindness matter more than converting.
A charismatic speaker online makes life feel clear and meaningful, and I watch every video. Wise: enjoy what helps, but compare it with other sources and note what it asks of me.
I start believing this preacher has all the answers and see others as lost. Harmful: a single voice takes over my thinking. Wise: stay curious, keep diverse friends, and check claims.
A preacher uses guilt, fear and us-versus-them to make me donate or cut off family. Recognise it: real guidance does not demand secrecy, money or isolation. Talk to a trusted adult.
I argue with my parent about a preacher they trust and I doubt. Wise: ask what they find helpful, share specific concerns, and avoid ridiculing them.
I discover that the preacher I admired lives against his own words and earns from followers. I feel foolish and angry. Wise: keep the teachings that were true, and not blame myself for hope.
A friend is pulled into an extreme online group and changes. Wise: stay their friend, ask questions with warmth, avoid mocking, and involve a trusted adult if they are cut off or at risk.
Their community welcomes me warmly when I feel unseen at home. The warmth is real, yet warmth alone is not proof of truth. Wise: also build offline friendships.
Someone mocks the leader or cause I support and I flare up. Wise: pause, ask what they mean, and separate a person from their view. Harmful: insulting or trolling.
I start to see the other side as stupid or evil. It feels good and makes me lonely. Wise: notice the stereotype, meet one real person from that side, and hold my view with humility.
I am abused online for my opinion or my religion. Wise: do not reply in kind, block, save proof, tell a trusted adult, and remember that disagreement is not permission for cruelty.
At dinner my uncle and I clash over politics. Wise: listen for his worry, keep facts calm, and leave respectfully if it turns heated. A relationship matters more than winning.
A close friend backs the opposite party. Wise: talk about values behind the views, agree not to convert each other, and not let it break the friendship.
Memes and videos push me to hate a group and share outrage. Recognise it: content built to anger me is often built for profit or power. Pause and verify before sharing.
I hold views that don't fit either side and feel pressured to pick. Wise: it is fine to say I'm still learning. Reading widely is stronger than joining a team early.
I feel the pull of a cause like the environment, farmers or exam fairness, and want to act. Wise: learn the facts, choose peaceful and lawful ways, and tell a trusted adult where I will be.
Friends push me to join a rally or share something fierce that I don't fully understand. Wise: understand before acting; belonging is not a reason to do what I don't believe.
An organiser uses students as a crowd or shield and offers little safety. Recognise it: wise leaders protect the young, and I can leave when it feels unsafe.
I'm afraid of consequences like police action or school punishment. Wise: know my rights, keep to peaceful means, and remember that fear is honest data, not cowardice.
My parents forbid me to join a protest because they fear for me. Wise: hear them, offer safer ways to contribute like writing or fundraising, and show I take risks seriously.
I pour everything into the cause and feel guilty about resting. Wise: causes need people who last; rest and studies are part of long-term commitment.
Peers challenge my activism as pointless. Wise: answer with facts and patience, accept that change is slow, and act where I can make a real difference.
I follow a rich influencer and feel my own life is dull. Wise: remember the feed is edited and paid; take inspiration for skills, not for comparing lifestyles.
I feel close to a star as though they know me and cry at their news. Wise: enjoy the comfort while remembering they do not know me; keep real friendships alive.
A fan writes to me as if we are best friends. As a public figure I must keep kindness and boundaries. Wise: appreciate warmth, not feed dependency.
When my idol is criticised I defend them fiercely, even when the criticism is fair. Wise: loyalty to a person should not switch off my own judgment.
Fans of rival stars abuse each other online and I join in. Wise: notice how it feels good to belong and hurts real people; step out when it turns cruel.
A creator sells expensive courses or betting apps to young fans. Recognise it: trust built on likes can be monetised. Check claims and never spend what isn't mine.
I admire an athlete for the years of discipline behind the success. Wise: copy the habits, not the image; use admiration as fuel for my own work.
A charismatic leader's speech thrills me. Wise: enjoy the inspiration, then ask what they actually do, who benefits and what they hide.
I see friends' holidays, looks and parties and feel left out. Wise: remember they post highlights; limit scrolling time, and message a friend instead.
I keep posting for likes and feel low when they are few. Wise: notice the loop, post for reasons that are mine, and mute accounts that make me feel less.
The feed keeps serving more of what upsets or hooks me, and hours vanish. Recognise it: apps are designed for attention. Wise: set limits, curate follows, and step away.
I check my phone every few minutes so as not to miss anything. Wise: notice the anxious pull, turn off notifications, and meet friends offline.
A friend keeps flashing new things and grades. I sense they compare to feel better than me. Wise: stay warm, avoid competing, and stay grounded in my own values.
Filters and edits make my real face look wrong. Wise: notice that the images are engineered, follow real people, and spend time on what my body can do, not only how it looks.
I can't stop scrolling late at night and I am tired and irritable. Wise: charge the phone outside the room, plan an alternative, and talk to someone if I feel unable to change.
A post of mine goes viral and I feel a rush. Wise: enjoy it lightly, and do not tie my worth to numbers that will drop.
I ask an AI to explain a topic and to check my homework. Wise: use it as a helper, verify facts, and do my own thinking so I actually learn.
I start telling the chatbot everything and prefer it to people because it never judges. Wise: it can support me, but real friends and adults are needed; tell someone when I feel low.
The chatbot answers confidently but is wrong or invents sources. Recognise it: AI can sound sure and be mistaken. Wise: cross-check with books, teachers or reliable sites.
I am tempted to have AI write my assignment. Wise: notice the short-term relief and the long-term loss of skill; use it to explain and practise, and follow school rules.
A chat companion app feels like a friend or romantic partner. Wise: enjoy it as a tool, remember it's designed to keep me engaged, and keep real relationships alive.
I am about to paste my photo, address or family details into a chatbot. Wise: treat it like a public space; never share private identity information.
My parents worry that AI will take my future or ruin my mind. Wise: show them what I use it for, agree on limits, and talk about skills that stay valuable.
A teacher suspects my work was AI-written when it was mostly mine. Wise: calmly show drafts and notes, and be honest about any help I used.
A stranger online calls me mature and special and asks me to keep our chats secret. Recognise it: secrecy and flattery are grooming warning signs. Tell a trusted adult; it is not my fault.

Someone threatens to share my photos unless I send more. Do not comply or pay; stop replying, save evidence, tell an adult and report to cybercrime helplines. It is a crime, and the shame belongs to them.
A message promises a prize, a job or easy money if I pay a small fee or share an OTP. Recognise it: real offers do not ask for money or codes. Do not share OTPs; tell a parent.
I feel lonely and a stranger is kind to me. Wise: warmth is welcome, yet a friend who asks for secrecy, photos or money is unsafe. Keep chats open to a trusted adult.
I suspect a friend is being groomed online. Wise: don't shame them, listen, help them save evidence, and bring in a trusted adult or helpline. Their safety matters more than promises of secrecy.
I want to meet an online friend in person. Wise: stay cautious, tell a parent, meet only in a public place with an adult, and step back if they push secrecy.
After a scam I feel afraid to tell my parents. Wise: tell them early; most parents prefer the truth to hidden harm, and quick action can limit the damage.
In games, older users offer gifts and free items for friendship. Wise: notice why an adult is giving gifts to a teen and never accept things that come with secrecy.
Classmates post memes or edited photos to mock me. I feel hurt and exposed. Wise: don't retaliate, save screenshots, block, report, and tell a trusted adult; it is not my fault.
An anonymous account sends nasty messages and I obsess over who it is. Wise: preserve evidence, report to platform and school, and don't let guessing consume me.
I am removed from a group chat and left out of the plans. Wise: I feel rejected, and I can seek other friends and speak to an adult if it turns into sustained targeting.
I want to hit back with something equally cruel. Wise: the impulse is human, but revenge often makes things worse; choose evidence and reporting.
I dread going to school because of what's online. Wise: fear is a signal, not weakness; tell a parent or counsellor, and request the school to act.
I saw the mocking post, and did nothing, and I feel guilty. Wise: guilt can prompt me to check on the target, report the post and refuse to share it.
I joined a joke that got out of hand and hurt someone. Wise: own it, delete, apologise plainly and repair. Harmful: excuses like it was just a joke.
A friend stands by me while others mock. I feel deeply grateful. Wise: tell them so, and support them when they need me.
At a party, friends offer cigarettes, vape or alcohol and say don't be boring. Wise: a simple no with a joke or an exit works; real friends respect it.
I am curious about trying something because everyone talks about it. Wise: notice I am reacting to curiosity and image; learn real effects, especially on a developing brain, and choose knowing.
An older boy offers free vapes, pills or sweets to draw me into his circle or to sell for him. Recognise it: it's a hook. Refuse, leave, and tell a trusted adult.
I want to use something to ease stress or sadness. Wise: understand that relief now can deepen the problem; talk to someone and find safer coping like sport, music or a counsellor.
A friend is using regularly and getting worse. Wise: express care without lecturing, encourage help, and tell a trusted adult when their safety is at risk.
My parent says I can call anytime if I am in an unsafe situation, no questions asked that night. Wise: use that offer; safety first, talking later.
I tried something once and feel horribly guilty. Wise: one mistake does not define me; learn from it, be honest with a trusted adult and set clear limits.
I hate how my body looks after comments from others and pictures online. Wise: notice the standard I am measuring against is edited; focus on health, strength and what my body does for me.
Classmates joke about my weight, skin or height. Wise: it says more about them; ignore, avoid feeding it, and tell a teacher if repeated. Self-worth is not up for vote.
I follow fitness and beauty influencers and feel I must change. Wise: check who benefits when I feel inadequate; choose accounts based on evidence and wellbeing.
I count calories and check mirrors all day and feel out of control around food. Wise: this is a sign to speak to a trusted adult or doctor early; asking for help is strength.
My parent comments on my weight or complexion, meaning well. It stings. Wise: say how it feels, ask for kinder words, and focus on health habits together.
A friend says I look fine but also talks honestly about her own insecurities. I feel less alone. Wise: share and support without attaching worth to appearance.
On a bad body day I treat myself as I would a friend and move on with my plans. Wise: neutral is enough; I don't have to love every part daily.
I compare my puberty and looks with others who change earlier or later. Wise: bodies develop at different speeds; patience and care matter more than racing.
I want to fit in so much that I change how I talk and dress. Wise: adapt lightly, but keep my core; friends who need me to hide aren't yet home.
I am unsure about who I am, including my feelings about attraction, and feel afraid. Wise: no need to label quickly; find safe people and reliable information.
A friend trusts me with a private truth about who they are. Wise: listen, keep the confidence, and don't out them; simply being a safe person matters most.
My family reacts harshly to who I am. I feel heartbreak. Wise: find safe supporters like a counsellor, teacher or helpline, take time, and stay safe; their reaction is not my worth.
Classmates tease me for my accent, name or manner. Wise: I need not shrink; tell a teacher if it continues and find people who value me as I am.
A teacher or club welcomes me without judgment. I feel deep relief. Wise: hold onto these anchors and pay the kindness forward.
I feel proud of where I come from, my language and culture. Wise: pride can live alongside curiosity for other people and needn't require putting anyone else down.
I meet a classmate whose life is very different from mine. Wise: ask respectfully, listen more than assume, and let differences teach me.
A classmate makes remarks about my caste, religion, region or family income. I feel small and angry. Wise: it is their bias, not my truth; tell a teacher and stay with friends who respect me.
A school rule or official treats my group unfairly. Wise: document facts, ask allies, and use formal complaint routes. Righteous anger is useful when channelled.
I notice I hold stereotypes I absorbed at home about another group. Wise: name it, meet real people, and unlearn gradually without self-hate.
A friend faces a bigoted remark and I hesitate to speak. Wise: a small stand like saying that isn't okay, or checking on them later, can matter greatly.
Relatives look down on my friend from another community. Wise: respectfully disagree, don't drop the friend, and accept that changing elders takes time.
I moved to a new city and am teased for my language and food. Wise: keep my roots, learn the local ways gradually, and find one or two allies.
I look down on classmates who are poorer or on scholarships. Wise: notice how privilege shapes me and treat people by who they are.
I am ashamed of my parents' job or our home when friends visit. Wise: the shame is learned; dignity of work is real, and true friends care about me, not the house.
I overhear my parents fight about debts and fees. I feel scared and guilty for costing money. Wise: ask what is happening, offer help within my role, and remember I am a child, not the fixer.
My parent hides the money problem to protect me. I sense it anyway. Wise: say kindly that I can handle honesty, and adjust my asks without blaming them.
Friends have new phones and trips while I can't. I feel bitter. Wise: acknowledge the feeling, focus on what I have, and avoid pretending or borrowing to keep up.
I consider working part-time or dropping studies to help. Wise: discuss with family and a teacher; look for scholarships and small safe earning, keeping education first.
A classmate teases me about my second-hand books or uniform. Wise: dignity does not depend on brands; reply calmly, tell a teacher if persistent.
Ads promise quick money through betting, trading apps or fake jobs. Recognise it: get-rich-quick offers target teens and families in need. Ask an adult and never send money.
A relative pays my fees and reminds us of it. I feel gratitude and humiliation. Wise: thank them sincerely, plan to give back one day, and gently ask my parents to set boundaries.
Money stress fuels my drive to succeed. Wise: use it, and don't let it push me into hating my family or myself for being poor.
My grandparent has died and I feel numb, then suddenly weep. Wise: grief comes in waves; talk about them, join family rituals, and let myself feel without rushing.
A classmate has died in an accident. I feel shaken and fear my own mortality. Wise: seek company, talk to a counsellor if it lingers, and honour them with small acts.
My parent is so lost in mourning that they seem absent. I feel doubly alone. Wise: name my own need, reach for another trusted adult, and remember their absence is grief, not lack of love.
My pet has died and people say it's just an animal. It hurts as real. Wise: love is real whichever the object; mark the loss with a small ritual.
After the death I am angry with God or the universe. Wise: anger is part of grief and can be voiced; some find comfort in faith and some in people, and both are fine.
A friend sits with me without giving advice. It helps more than anything. Wise: I can say what I need, whether space, company or distraction.
I feel guilty for not saying goodbye or for a quarrel before the loss. Wise: guilt is a form of love; forgive myself and write the unsaid words in a letter.
Classmates go on as normal and say nothing about my loss. Wise: people often don't know what to say; tell one or two what would help.
I fail in front of everyone like a missed goal or a stage freeze, and they laugh. Wise: shame fades faster than I expect; laugh at it if I can, and try again.
I replay the failure at night and cringe. Wise: tell a friend, since sharing shrinks it; treat the memory as data and not as a verdict.
A friend says I still respect you and sits by me after I lost. I feel relief. Wise: accept comfort, and later do the same for them.
My coach or teacher looks disappointed after my result. Wise: ask what I can learn, avoid taking their frown as total rejection.
After failing I restart with a smaller plan. Wise: progress follows practice and correction; famous people fail often too, quietly.
A rival gloats over my failure. Wise: don't stoop to their level; their need to gloat says more about them; work on beating my own past score.
I refuse to try things I might fail at. Wise: fear of failure limits me more than failure does; start with low-stakes attempts.
My parent comforts me instead of scolding after a failure. I feel safe. Wise: share honestly what happened and plan the next step together.
I see a friend cheating or bullying and feel torn between loyalty and right. Wise: talk to the friend first if safe; if harm continues, tell a trusted adult. Real loyalty isn't silence about harm.
After I reported a wrong, friends call me a snitch and freeze me out. Wise: hurt is real; distinguish telling to protect from telling to punish, and find allies.
I report to a teacher I trust that someone is being harassed. Wise: give facts, ask for confidentiality, and follow up; don't take the law into my own hands.
I reported, but the school ignored it or exposed me. I feel betrayed. Wise: document, escalate to the principal, board, parents or helpline, and keep myself safe.
I am afraid the bully will retaliate if I speak. Wise: fear is reasonable; use anonymous reporting routes, stay in groups, and let adults handle the danger.
I speak up in class against a joke that humiliates a classmate. Wise: courage can be quiet and calm; small stands change what is normal.
The student I defended thanks me quietly. Wise: accept it and know that seeing someone often matters more than any speech.
I stayed quiet earlier and someone got hurt. Wise: guilt shows conscience; act now, apologise to the person, and speak sooner next time.
After a mistake I call myself stupid and useless. Wise: notice the cruel voice, and ask what I would tell a friend; harsh self-attack rarely produces change.
I acknowledge the mistake, feel the sting, and treat myself kindly enough to fix it. Wise: kindness and high standards work together.
A friend says everyone messes up and stays with me. I feel a weight lift. Wise: let their view soften mine, and offer the same to others.
My parent is upset with me after a serious mistake. I feel worthless. Wise: separate my act from my self; apologise, repair, and ask for a chance to earn trust.
Everything feels pointless and I hate myself for days. Wise: tell a trusted adult or counsellor now; help exists and these feelings can change. If unsafe, reach a helpline immediately.
I punish myself for anything short of perfect. Wise: aim for improvement, not perfection; small good enough steps build confidence.
A mentor tells me they made worse mistakes at my age. I feel hope. Wise: seek people who share their honest stories.

Heart races and you idealise them from small signs. Wise: let it stay a feeling, get to know the real person over time, and ask directly instead of decoding every text. Immature: building a whole future from one smile.
Being liked by someone you barely know feels flattering and awkward. Wise: be kind and clear early if you do not feel the same. Immature: staying vague for the attention, or mocking them to friends.

You want to speak but freeze, imagining humiliation. Wise: accept a no would hurt but not define you, and ask simply once. Immature: hinting endlessly or using friends as messengers to avoid all risk.
Someone says they do not feel the same and it stings. Wise: give a gracious no, without lying about reasons or leaving hope. Harmful: leading them on because you enjoy being wanted.
You were turned down and feel small. Wise: let yourself grieve, stop chasing, and take distance without blaming them. Immature: repeated messages, sulking, or telling everyone they led you on.

Thoughts loop on them, you check their profile and mood constantly. Wise: notice it is fantasy feeding on uncertainty, widen your life, talk to a friend. Harmful: tracking their movements or turning up uninvited.
