Someone's attention feels intense and unwanted, and you feel uneasy. Wise: say a clear no once, stop replying, keep records, and tell a friend or hostel warden if it continues. It is not your fault.

Long-distance or online crush seems perfect because you see only highlights. Wise: notice the gap between image and person and meet in ordinary settings. Immature: dropping the real person when they show flaws.

You realise a close friend has become more than a friend and fear ruining it. Wise: weigh honesty against the friendship, tell them without pressure, and accept either answer. Immature: hiding it while resenting them.

Subtype: Crush × Caste, religion or family barrier [Actor]
Human Learning & Development: You like someone your family may not accept. Wise: think seriously about what you both really want and how you will handle family, rather than assuming love alone will win. Immature: secrecy that ends in a sudden crisis.

You choose one person and its meaning goes beyond feelings. Wise: love shows in reliability, honest talk and making room for their growth. Immature: treating commitment as ownership or a performance for social media.
You feel chosen and valued, which is both warm and a little scary. Wise: receive it with honesty about your own limits and keep your own friendships. Immature: taking the devotion for granted.

You choose to believe them without proof at every moment. Wise: trust builds through small kept promises and is not blind; you can still notice red flags. Immature: testing them constantly to feel safe.

You lean on them for mood, decisions and identity, and feel lost alone. Wise: keep your own friends, work and goals so love is a choice, not a need. Immature: making them responsible for your whole happiness.
Your partner needs you constantly and it feels heavy. Wise: give care but name the limit kindly and encourage their other supports. Harmful: feeling guilty into giving up your own life.
You want a partner who is equal, not a fantasy or servant. Wise: share decisions, listen to their ambitions, and split effort fairly. Immature: expecting them to follow your career or adjust always.
You notice what they do quietly, like showing up in a hard week. Wise: say thanks specifically and reciprocate. Immature: keeping a score of favours and sulking when they are not repaid.
You feel anxious they will leave, so you clutch or please too much. Wise: name the fear, work on your own worth, and talk openly. Immature: checking phones or picking fights to test them.

Different cities, time zones and studies make you feel forgotten. Wise: agree on realistic contact, share your inner life, and plan visits. Immature: demanding constant replies or reading silence as betrayal.

Subtype: Partner × Pressure to define the relationship [Receiver]
Human Learning & Development: They ask where this is going and you feel cornered. Wise: be honest about what you know and do not know, and avoid stringing them along. Immature: dodging, or saying yes to avoid a scene.

Goals and values start to diverge and you feel guilty. Wise: talk honestly early, and consider that ending kindly can be more respectful than staying out of guilt. Immature: quiet withdrawal until they give up.
One of you pays more, and unspoken expectations build. Wise: talk openly about money, do not buy love or obligation, and respect each other's budget. Immature: keeping quiet then resenting them.

Subtype: Partner × Public display and social media [Actor]
Human Learning & Development: You want the relationship seen and validated online. Wise: notice whether the posting reflects closeness or replaces it. Immature: comparing your love with others' filtered posts.

Marriage suddenly becomes real, with two families involved. Wise: be sure you both share values on work, parents and kids before rushing. Immature: agreeing to please everyone and postponing the hard questions.

You feel a hot pang when they laugh with someone else. Wise: name the insecurity behind it and share it as your feeling, not an accusation. Immature: interrogating, demanding passwords or forbidding friends.
They get upset about your friends and you feel watched. Wise: reassure once and hold the line that trust is not shown by surrendering your freedom. Harmful: hiding people to keep the peace.
You want them only yours and feel entitled to know everything. Wise: see this as fear, not love, and see them as a separate person. Harmful: controlling clothes, contacts or location.
Their control is framed as love, and you slowly shrink your world. Wise: recognise the pattern, talk to a trusted friend or counsellor, and do not accept it as normal. It is not your fault.

Your partner's promotion or rank makes you feel smaller though you love them. Wise: admit the envy privately, celebrate anyway, and work on your own path. Immature: undermining or mocking their achievement.
Your good news is met with coldness or jokes. Wise: notice it, talk kindly, and keep sharing wins with people who cheer. Harmful: hiding your success to protect their ego.
A late reply, a like or a new friend sets off doubts. Wise: separate evidence from anxiety and ask calmly instead of spying. Harmful: checking their phone or messages secretly.
You are accused of things you did not do. Wise: stay calm, state facts, and see whether the accusations ever end. Constant unfounded suspicion is a warning sign, not proof of your guilt.
Their exes bother you more than they should. Wise: accept the past is not a threat and talk about the fear itself. Immature: interrogating details or bringing it up as a weapon in arguments.

Seeing your ex with someone new stings hard. Wise: let the pain pass, mute or unfollow, and remember their happiness is not a verdict on you. Immature: comparing, contacting the new partner or posting to provoke.
Partner's close friend of the other gender makes you uneasy. Wise: get to know them and share the feeling without ordering a distance. Immature: ultimatums that force them to choose.

Discovering a partner was unfaithful brings shock, shame, rage and doubt about yourself. Wise: take time before decisions, lean on friends, and remember their choice was theirs. Harmful: revenge or blaming yourself.

You cross a line and feel thrill, then guilt and dread. Wise: admit the reason honestly, end the deception, and accept consequences. Immature: blaming the partner, lying more, or wanting forgiveness on demand.
You wonder if you can trust again. Wise: forgiveness is not forced or instant; it needs honesty, time and changed behaviour, and walking away is also valid. Immature: forgiving to avoid loneliness.

You are eaten by guilt and want to confess just to feel lighter. Wise: consider what confession actually serves and be ready for the fallout. Immature: turning your guilt into their burden to comfort you.
Their behaviour changes and you doubt yourself. Wise: trust your observation, ask directly, and avoid spying. Harmful: excusing every sign because you cannot bear the answer.

Subtype: Friend who cheats × Complicity and dilemma [Receiver]
Human Learning & Development: You know your friend's partner is being cheated on. Wise: think carefully, encourage the friend to be honest, and avoid gossip. Immature: telling the whole group or pretending nothing is wrong.

Subtype: Third person × Being the other person [Actor]
Human Learning & Development: You are drawn to someone already committed. Wise: see the risk of hurting others and yourself, and step back. Immature: believing you are special and the rules do not apply.

Subtype: Third person × Being the other person [Receiver]
Human Learning & Development: You learn the person you love was hiding a partner. Wise: feel the anger, end contact, and see you were also deceived. Harmful: fighting the other partner instead of facing the liar.
You share deeper feelings with someone else than with your partner. Wise: notice what is missing at home and talk about it, or end it honestly. Immature: calling it just friendship while hiding it.

Subtype: Partner × Being tempted but staying faithful [Actor]
Human Learning & Development: Attraction to someone else arises even though you are committed. Wise: attraction is human; you choose limits and do not feed it. Immature: guilt spirals or acting because you are bored.
Friends and social media take sides after the discovery. Wise: keep your private pain private, avoid exposing them online, and seek a few trusted listeners. Harmful: humiliating them publicly.
They end it and you feel worthless and confused. Wise: grieve openly, lean on friends, stop searching for a perfect reason. Immature: begging, threatening or seeking revenge.
You decide to end it and feel relief mixed with guilt. Wise: tell them honestly and face to face, without cruelty or false hope. Immature: ghosting or blaming them to feel justified.
Every place reminds you of them and you cry without warning. Wise: this is real grief, so sleep, eat, move and talk. Immature: numbing with distractions or rushing into a rebound.
You want to text them at night. Wise: decide about contact consciously, mute if needed, and let time do its work. Immature: testing if they still care or using friends to keep tabs.
You try friendship but one of you still hopes. Wise: honestly ask whether it hurts more than helps and give it distance first. Immature: staying close to keep a door open.
You replay how they wronged you and feel bitter. Wise: allow anger as information, then let it go for your own peace. Harmful: spreading their private matters or turning friends against them.
An ex keeps contacting you after you said no. Wise: say a clear final no, block, save evidence, and tell family, friends or authorities. It is not your fault and safety comes first.

You cannot stop watching their life and feel unable to move on. Wise: recognise this as pain, not love, and seek support such as a friend or counsellor. Harmful: showing up, monitoring or threatening.

Subtype: Ex-partner × Sharing private images or messages [Receiver]
Human Learning & Development: Fear that an ex will leak private material. Wise: it is a crime and not your shame, so keep evidence and report to the cyber cell or a trusted adult. Harmful: bearing it alone.
Parents learn of the relationship and the breakup and judge you. Wise: seek compassion, tell only what you choose, and see this as learning, not disgrace. Immature: lying deeper or shutting down.
You bump into your ex at a friend's gathering. Wise: be polite, brief and calm; you owe neither a scene nor a friendship. Immature: performing happiness or sniping.
Months later you can think of them without hurt. Wise: take lessons about your patterns and needs, without rewriting the past as all bad or all good. Immature: swearing off love.
You want closeness and must ask and listen, not assume. Wise: consent is clear, freely given and can change; a hesitation or silence is not a yes. Harmful: pressure, guilt or persistence.
They say if you loved them you would. Wise: you decide your pace; someone who respects you accepts a no. Harmful: giving in out of fear of losing them. Talk to a trusted friend if pressure continues.

You feel unsure about physical closeness or sharing photos. Wise: say what you are comfortable with plainly, and expect it to be respected. Immature: hoping they will guess or saying yes to avoid awkwardness.
You are told no or not yet and feel hurt. Wise: say thank you for the honesty, step back, and do not sulk or bargain. Harmful: punishing them with coldness or threats.
Friends tease you for being inexperienced. Wise: your timeline is yours, and real friends do not need you to prove anything. Immature: acting to fit in and regretting it.
In a party setting, judgement blurs. Wise: look out for each other, never take advantage of someone impaired, and leave with friends. Harmful: assuming compliance when someone cannot clearly agree.
You are asked for private photos. Wise: once sent, control is gone; you can refuse without guilt. Harmful: sending under pressure or threats. If threatened, tell an adult and report.
Someone in a bus, hostel or online will not stop. Wise: say a firm no, move away, report to authorities, warden or campus committee. It is never your fault.

Subtype: Friend × Learning that a friend crossed a boundary [Receiver]
Human Learning & Development: A friend confides someone forced them. Wise: listen, believe, do not blame, and help them find safe support. Harmful: gossip, doubting them or urging them to stay silent for reputation.

Subtype: Partner × Being accused of crossing a line [Actor]
Human Learning & Development: Someone says you made them uncomfortable and you feel defensive. Wise: listen without arguing, apologise sincerely, and change. Immature: insisting your intent was innocent.
You want to discuss what each of you wants without embarrassment. Wise: speak plainly and respectfully, and accept differences. Immature: expecting them to read your mind.

Different cities or colleges mean less contact and you feel a quiet loss. Wise: accept friendships change, reach out without keeping score, and let some stay smaller. Immature: sulking or cutting them off first.
A friend is pulling back and you wonder what you did. Wise: ask once, kindly, and accept if they need space. Harmful: guilt trips or demanding equal effort.
Your best friend has a new group or partner. Wise: admit the hurt to yourself, say it plainly, and let them grow. Immature: sabotaging the new bond.
You stand by a friend even when it costs you. Wise: loyalty includes honesty and not covering harmful behaviour. Immature: defending them blindly against every criticism.
A friend stands up for you in a hard moment. Wise: feel grateful and return it in your own way. Immature: treating it as an entitlement or forgetting.
Among many friends you feel unseen. Wise: share something real with one person rather than performing in the group. Immature: withdrawing without telling anyone.

Subtype: Friend × Being the one who always reaches out [Actor]
Human Learning & Development: You do all the calling and planning. Wise: try stepping back once to see the truth, then decide what the friendship deserves. Immature: silent resentment or dramatic ultimatums.

Subtype: Friend × Old friend and new self [Actor]
Human Learning & Development: You have grown but your school friend is same as before. Wise: honour the shared history while accepting less in common. Immature: looking down on them or hiding your new life.
Two friends fight and both want you on their side. Wise: refuse to carry tales, stay kind to both, and keep your own view. Immature: agreeing with whoever is present.
A friend asks for a loan again. Wise: help within your means as a gift, be honest about your limit, and do not lend what strains you. Harmful: silent resentment or lying that you have none.

Subtype: Friend × Asking a friend for money [Actor]
Human Learning & Development: You are short and need to borrow. Wise: ask clearly, say when you will repay, and repay. Immature: avoiding them or letting the debt sour the friendship.
Your secret spread and you feel exposed and furious. Wise: confront them privately, decide what trust is left, and be more careful. Immature: leaking their secrets in return.
You shared a friend's confidence, maybe for attention. Wise: own it quickly, apologise without excuses, and accept their distance. Immature: minimising or blaming their reaction.
You choose whether to forgive a friend who hurt you. Wise: forgiving can be for your peace, even if trust is not fully restored. Immature: pretending nothing happened.
You see photos of a gathering you were not invited to. Wise: feel the sting, ask directly if it matters, and remember it may not be malice. Immature: assuming the worst or retaliating.

Subtype: Friend × Taking sides in a conflict [Actor]
Human Learning & Development: You are pressed to choose. Wise: state what you think is right without hurting either. Immature: gossiping to both to be liked.

Subtype: Friend × Being used for notes, money or contacts [Receiver]
Human Learning & Development: You realise a friend only calls when they need something. Wise: help when you want, and set limits without bitterness. Harmful: giving more to buy affection.
You look down on someone in your circle for their background or English. Wise: see how the contempt hides insecurity and treat them as an equal. Harmful: mockery that isolates them.
Friends tease you constantly for accent, clothes or being from a small town. Wise: tell them it hurts; if it continues, find kinder people. It is not your fault and is not a joke if you are hurt.
You laugh along at someone's expense to fit in. Wise: notice how it feels to be on the other side and stop or quietly refuse. Immature: calling it just banter.

Subtopic: Friend succeeds when you are struggling
Human Learning & Development: A friend gets the offer or the marks and you feel small while smiling. Wise: admit the envy privately, congratulate honestly, and use it to clarify what you want. Immature: belittling their win.

Subtopic: Friend succeeds when you are struggling
Human Learning & Development: Your success makes a friend distant or sarcastic. Wise: stay warm without hiding your progress, and give them room. Harmful: downplaying yourself to be liked.

Subtopic: Friend succeeds when you are struggling
Human Learning & Development: You are honestly happy for them. Wise: celebrate fully, and do not hide your own hard feelings if they exist. Immature: pretending both feelings are absent.

Subtopic: Friend succeeds when you are struggling
Human Learning & Development: You measure yourself against them in ranks and packages. Wise: compare with your yesterday, and treat them as a fellow traveller. Harmful: hiding notes or sharing false tips.

Subtopic: Friend succeeds when you are struggling
Subtype: Friend × Being envied as the one who is struggling [Receiver]
Human Learning & Development: A struggling friend feels you have it easier. Wise: listen, share honestly about your own difficulties, and offer help without pity. Harmful: showing off or lecturing.
Dishes, noise and borrowed things build into fury. Wise: raise it early and calmly, with specific requests and shared rules. Immature: passive-aggressive notes or explosions after weeks of silence.
You are told you are the difficult one. Wise: listen for what is true, apologise where needed, and negotiate. Immature: defensiveness or recruiting others against them.
Your things vanish or money goes missing. Wise: gather facts, talk to them, and involve the warden or landlord if needed. Harmful: accusing without evidence.
You bring a partner over or want your space. Wise: agree beforehand on guests and quiet time. Immature: assuming they do not mind.
You become close and share meals, worries and jokes. Wise: enjoy it while keeping each other's independence. Immature: expecting them to fill all your social needs.
Their food, hygiene or religion irritate you. Wise: separate real disruptions from mere difference, and stay respectful. Harmful: mocking their culture or excluding them.
Rent and bills are unevenly paid. Wise: put the split in writing, be direct about delays, and be generous when a friend is truly stuck. Immature: silently resenting.
A roommate seems very low or unwell. Wise: check in, listen without fixing, and encourage help from family or a counsellor. Harmful: gossiping or ignoring signs of serious distress.

Subtopic: Parents pressure on career or marriage
Human Learning & Development: You love your parents and feel the weight of their sacrifice. Wise: honour the gratitude without treating it as a debt that erases your choices. Immature: obeying while resenting, or rebelling just to prove a point.

Subtopic: Parents pressure on career or marriage
Human Learning & Development: Family pushes rishtas and biodata while you want time. Wise: speak calmly about your timeline, values and what you look for, and listen to their fears. Harmful: lying or agreeing to escape the conversation.

Subtopic: Parents pressure on career or marriage
Human Learning & Development: You meet a prospective partner with family present. Wise: be honest, ask real questions about values and work, and remember you can say no. Immature: judging only on looks, salary or pressure.

Subtopic: Parents pressure on career or marriage
Human Learning & Development: Parents object over caste, religion or class. Wise: understand their fears, show consistency and respect over time, and set what you will not compromise. Harmful: ultimatums that burn bridges.

Subtopic: Parents pressure on career or marriage
Human Learning & Development: They want engineering or a government job while you want art or startups. Wise: present a thought-out plan, ask for a trial period, and hear their worry about security. Immature: hiding your plan or dropping out.

Subtopic: Parents pressure on career or marriage
Human Learning & Development: You are furious that they ignore what you want. Wise: let the anger cool, then say what you need calmly with examples. Immature: silence, shouting, or dramatic threats.

Subtopic: Parents pressure on career or marriage
Human Learning & Development: You see your parents as flawed humans, not heroes. Wise: mourn the illusion and accept them as imperfect people who did their best. Immature: contempt or dismissal of everything they say.

Subtopic: Parents pressure on career or marriage
Human Learning & Development: You feel you owe them your life. Wise: gratitude and repayment can take many forms, and you may live differently than they hoped. Harmful: sacrificing your identity to avoid guilt.

Subtopic: Parents pressure on career or marriage
Human Learning & Development: They compare your marks or salary with relatives. Wise: tell them it hurts, and remember comparison shows their anxiety more than your value. Immature: hating the cousins.

Subtopic: Parents pressure on career or marriage
Human Learning & Development: You disagree yet respect their experience. Wise: seek their reasons, differ politely, and decide as an adult who owns the outcome. Immature: dismissing them or hiding everything.

Subtopic: Parents pressure on career or marriage
Subtype: Parents × Fear for their health or ageing [Actor]
Human Learning & Development: You fear leaving them alone when you move for work. Wise: talk about a realistic plan, calls and visits, and accept you cannot control everything. Immature: giving up your path out of guilt.

You rely on them for fees and rent and feel you cannot speak freely. Wise: work toward some earning, use money wisely, and do not confuse support with control. Immature: spending carelessly and resenting them.
They track your spending or use funds as leverage. Wise: negotiate a clear budget, share information, and build your own income. Harmful: lying or manipulating them for money.
They set hostel or home timings out of worry. Wise: talk about the fear, offer check-ins, and earn more freedom by reliability. Immature: sneaking around.
You worry and want to know everything about your child. Wise: trust builds by letting them make small mistakes. Harmful: surveillance or shaming.
Family loans or sacrifices for your education weigh on you. Wise: study seriously, be honest about struggles, and work part time if needed. Immature: hiding failures to avoid disappointment.
First earnings and family expects a share. Wise: talk about what is fair while you build your own security. Immature: giving all out of guilt or keeping all in secret.

Subtype: Parents × Divorce or conflict at home [Receiver]
Human Learning & Development: Their fights or separation land on you. Wise: it is not your job to fix them, and you can love both while keeping healthy distance. Harmful: taking a side in the war.
They provide but rarely talk with you. Wise: reach out in their language, like food or small tasks, and seek other mentors too. Immature: assuming they do not care.
A sibling seems to be the favourite or more successful. Wise: talk to parents and sibling about how it feels; compare less. Immature: sabotaging them or competing for approval.
Your sibling resents your success. Wise: do not shrink, but be generous, and listen to their feelings. Harmful: boasting or fuelling old wounds.
You want to shield a younger sibling from mistakes. Wise: give guidance while letting them decide. Immature: controlling them as a substitute parent.
A younger sibling leans on you for money and decisions. Wise: support kindly, and encourage their independence. Harmful: rescuing repeatedly and feeling used.
You cover for a sibling with parents. Wise: protect their privacy but not harmful behaviour. Immature: lying that costs you your integrity.
One sibling handles ageing parents or money more than the other. Wise: have an honest conversation about fair shares. Immature: keeping score in silence until it explodes.
Distance makes you realise how much you rely on them. Wise: say it out loud and show up in small ways. Immature: assuming they know.
You respect a professor who challenges you. Wise: ask questions, accept correction, and treat their time as valuable. Immature: flattery or fear of asking.
A student looks up to you and hangs on your words. Wise: guide without creating dependence and be honest about your limits. Harmful: using their admiration for favours.
You are scared to approach a strict professor. Wise: prepare, go to office hours and see them as people. Immature: avoiding until problems become bigger.
You find a mentor is biased or petty. Wise: keep what they taught, update your view, and do not throw away the learning. Immature: cynicism toward all authority.
Grades or projects go to a favourite. Wise: gather facts, raise it through proper channels, and keep your own standards. Harmful: bitterness that damages your work.
You need a letter and worry about asking. Wise: ask early and politely, give context on your work. Immature: expecting it as a right or dropping their name falsely.
A mentor changed your direction. Wise: say thanks, pass on what you learn, and later pay it forward. Immature: forgetting them once you succeed.
You wait for a mentor to tell you what to do. Wise: bring your own ideas and grow into independent judgement. Immature: outsourcing every decision.
A senior or guide uses your work, credit or time without fairness. Wise: name the unfairness politely, set limits and involve someone neutral if needed. It is not ungrateful to protect your work.
A teacher or guide makes unwanted comments or touches. Wise: recognise it as wrong, keep records, and report to the internal committee or a trusted adult. It is never your fault.
A senior shows you the ropes and you want to be like them. Wise: learn their thinking, not just copy their choices. Immature: imitating their style while ignoring your own path.
A mentor is blunt and it stings. Wise: separate the delivery from the content and use what is true. Immature: quitting or holding a grudge.
A junior starts asking you for guidance. Wise: share what you know, admit what you do not, and encourage their own views. Immature: enjoying the status.
You respect your first manager who guides you. Wise: ask for feedback, own your work, and bring solutions. Immature: pleasing without speaking up.
You dread a moody boss and stay quiet in meetings. Wise: prepare, communicate in writing, and do not take moods personally. Immature: hiding problems until they blow up.
You are made to work late unpaid with vague promises. Wise: recognise the pattern, set boundaries, seek advice from trusted seniors, and know your rights. Harmful: silent burnout.
A boss uses praise or guilt to get extra work. Wise: check whether the reward is real, and negotiate clearly. It is not disloyal to say no.
A boss gave you a chance without a big degree. Wise: be thankful without letting it silence your fair questions. Immature: feeling forever indebted.
A manager seems to dislike you. Wise: ask for concrete feedback, document your work, and look for other mentors. Immature: assuming it is all about you or gossiping.
A colleague gets recognition you wanted. Wise: study what they did well, keep your own pace, and avoid gossip. Immature: undermining them.
A colleague becomes a close friend. Wise: enjoy it while keeping professional boundaries and confidences. Immature: sharing office secrets or forming cliques.
Groups and gossip pull you in. Wise: stay friendly to all, do good work, and avoid taking sides. Immature: passing tales for safety.
New in the team you are left out of lunches and chats. Wise: introduce yourself, join small conversations, and give it a few weeks. Immature: assuming hostility.
You are given menial work with no learning. Wise: ask for a clear role, request feedback, and decide when to move on. Harmful: silently accepting.
You are now the one showing an intern the work. Wise: teach patiently and credit their contribution. Immature: dumping your tasks on them.
A colleague or superior makes comments or advances that you dislike. Wise: say no clearly, document dates and words, and use the POSH committee or HR. It is not your fault.
Your idea or work is presented as theirs. Wise: raise it calmly with evidence, share updates in writing in future, and clarify roles early. Immature: public blowups or sulking.
You are tempted to present shared work as yours. Wise: name who did what; trust built is worth more. Harmful: taking credit and rationalising it.
A colleague blames you for their mistake. Wise: stay calm, present facts, and involve the manager if needed. Immature: retaliating.
Others do little and you carry the load. Wise: set roles early, check in, and raise it politely before deadline. Immature: doing everything silently and resenting.
You slack off because others will cover. Wise: see the unfairness and contribute honestly. Immature: claiming credit at presentation.
You disagree strongly on the approach. Wise: listen, test the ideas with data, and accept the group's decision. Immature: overriding others or sulking.
One member controls everything. Wise: speak with facts and share tasks in writing. Harmful: staying silent to avoid conflict.
You hand over a part and hope they do it well. Wise: agree on checkpoints and give feedback kindly. Immature: micromanaging.
A groupmate is better than you. Wise: learn from them and do your part well. Immature: hiding your work.
A groupmate stayed late to help you. Wise: thank them and offer help in return. Immature: taking it for granted.
The grade is poor and fingers point at you. Wise: take responsibility for your part and focus on what to change. Harmful: taking all the blame or blaming others.

Someone stopped replying without a word and you feel confused and small. Wise: accept you may never get answers, and their silence tells more about them than about you. Immature: repeated messages or chasing.
You avoid someone because a talk feels hard. Wise: a short honest message is kinder than silence. Harmful: vanishing and leaving them guessing.

Subtype: Friend × Being ghosted by a friend [Receiver]
Human Learning & Development: A close friend disappears for months. Wise: send one warm message and let go if no answer. Immature: hard accusations or public comments.
You replay what you said wrong. Wise: notice the loop, talk to a friend, and give yourself the closure they did not. Harmful: blaming yourself.
A recruiter goes silent after promising a reply. Wise: follow up once or twice politely, keep applying, and do not read it as your worth. Immature: bitterness or wasted waiting.
Someone gives just enough attention to keep you hoping. Wise: ask clearly for what you want, and if not offered, walk away. Harmful: waiting for scraps.
They twist your words and you feel confused and guilty. Wise: notice patterns, keep notes, talk to trusted people outside, and trust your perception. It is not your fault.
They deny events you clearly remember and call you oversensitive. Wise: write things down, check with a trusted friend, and see that doubt is the aim. Seek counselling.
They threaten to hurt themselves or leave if you do not comply. Wise: take real distress seriously, involve trusted adults or professionals, and do not accept being controlled through fear.
Intense adoration turns into silence when you set limits. Wise: notice the swing and judge by steady behaviour, not grand gestures.
They slowly make you distance from friends and family. Wise: keep at least one outside connection and see isolation as a warning sign. Reach out to someone you trust.
You use guilt, sulking or threats to get what you want. Wise: ask directly, accept a no, and see the fear behind it. Harmful: winning by hurting.
You control because you fear abandonment. Wise: admit this, work on it with a counsellor or friend, and let go of control. Harmful: calling it love.
You want to leave but fear them, loneliness or family reaction. Wise: plan with help from friends or a helpline, and consider safety first. Leaving is hard and it is not weakness.
A friend uses guilt and drama to keep you close. Wise: name what you will and will not do; friends respect no. Harmful: constant appeasing.

Subtype: Friend × Recognising a toxic pattern from outside [Actor]
Human Learning & Development: You see a friend in a controlling relationship. Wise: stay close, listen without judging, share what you see once, and keep the door open. Immature: ultimatums that push them away.
A relative uses guilt or sacrifice to steer your choices. Wise: acknowledge their love and still choose for yourself. Immature: complying and resenting.

Subtype: Cult or group × Love and belonging with control [Receiver]
Human Learning & Development: A friendly group offers belonging but demands secrecy, money or obedience. Wise: check whether you can question, leave and keep outside ties. Harmful: cutting off family for the group.
Juniors or friends treat you as perfect. Wise: stay honest about flaws and do not let it inflate you. Harmful: using their admiration.
You copy a senior's every move. Wise: learn their qualities, but keep your own judgement. Immature: losing yourself.
Someone openly dislikes you for no clear reason. Wise: reflect once if you did wrong, then stop chasing approval. Immature: retaliating or obsessing.
You dislike someone deeply and cannot stop thinking of them. Wise: ask what they represent for you, such as envy or old hurt, and step away from fuelling it. Harmful: spreading rumours.

Subtype: Online group × Being trolled or shamed [Receiver]
Human Learning & Development: Strangers pile on over a post. Wise: do not engage, save evidence, block, and lean on real friends. It says little about your worth.
People treat you coldly because of your looks, marks or family. Wise: stay kind and avoid flaunting. Harmful: hiding your gifts.
A classmate is a constant rival. Wise: let them push your standard while staying decent. Immature: sabotage.
False stories spread. Wise: address key people calmly, do not chase every whisper, and let your behaviour speak. Harmful: fighting fire with fire.
In a new city with no one to talk to, evenings feel heavy. Wise: create routines, join a club or gym, and accept it takes months. Immature: scrolling home lives or withdrawing.
You miss family food and language. Wise: call home, but also build small anchors in the new place. Immature: living only for the next trip home.
You want to talk to a neighbour or classmate and fear awkwardness. Wise: small repeated contact builds friendship. Immature: waiting to be invited.

Subtype: Landlord or neighbour × Feeling unsafe or cheated [Receiver]
Human Learning & Development: New city and unclear rules leave you vulnerable. Wise: get agreements in writing, keep contacts of trusted people, and ask seniors. Harmful: hiding problems from family.
You rely on gaming or online friends. Wise: value them and still seek some in-person connections. Immature: replacing all real contact.
You think everyone else has friends. Wise: many others feel the same; one honest conversation helps. Harmful: pretending to be fine.
Someone invites you to lunch or a plan. Wise: say yes even when tired; most friendships start there. Immature: declining out of shyness repeatedly.
Weeks alone drain your energy and sleep. Wise: notice the pattern, reach out to family, friends or a campus counsellor. Harmful: assuming nothing will help.

The polite "we are moving ahead with other candidates" mail stings and feels personal. Wise: it is one hiring decision, not a verdict; ask once for feedback, note one fix, apply again. Harmful: stop trying or rehearse it for weeks.

I was told "you are almost selected", then heard nothing for weeks. Hope turns to confusion and anger. Wise: do not put life on hold for one offer, keep other applications alive, follow up twice politely, then move on.

Before the panel my hands are cold and I fear being exposed as not good enough. Wise: prepare a few real stories, breathe, say "I don't know, but here is how I'd find out". Harmful: bluffing, which collapses on the next question.

My friend got the offer and I did not, and I feel warmth and a sour twist together. Wise: admit the envy privately, congratulate honestly, ask how they prepared. Harmful: quietly hoping they fail or sneering at their company.

In a group discussion I see others as obstacles and want to shout them down. Wise: contribute clearly, credit a good point, let the panel see a person who can work with others. Harmful: talking over people to look strong.

My parent sighs and says the neighbour's son already has a job. I feel small and angry at once. Wise: hear the worry under the comparison, share my plan with dates, ask for patience. Harmful: shouting or going silent for days.

A friend sits with me after the rejection and does not rush to fix it. I feel less alone and can breathe again. Wise: accept the kindness, then take one small next step. Harmful: refusing comfort because I feel undeserving.

A senior gave me a mock interview and honest feedback, even though it hurt. I feel thankful and a little embarrassed. Wise: say thank you, apply the feedback, and report back. Harmful: taking the help and vanishing.

I blame the system, quotas, connections and English accents, and there may be some truth in it. Wise: name what is unfair without letting it become the whole story, then control what I can. Harmful: bitterness that stops effort.

My boss mocks me in front of the team and calls it "directness". I feel small, hot-faced and frozen. Wise: it is his conduct, not proof I am worthless; note dates, talk to a trusted senior or HR, and start quietly building exits.

I am told to work weekends unpaid or "your growth will suffer", and to keep quiet about it. Fear and duty tangle. Wise: keep written records, know my contract and labour rights, and seek support before resigning in anger.

I dread his messages and my stomach drops at each ping. Wise: notice that this body reaction is information; separate real risk from imagined risk, plan a safety net of savings and contacts. Harmful: freezing for years.

He once helped me get in, so I keep excusing how he treats me. Gratitude and abuse mix. Wise: I can be thankful for the past and still refuse the present treatment. Harmful: treating loyalty as a debt with no limit.

I want to send a furious email to the whole company. The anger is valid. Wise: write it, do not send it, cool down, then choose one calm, documented complaint. Harmful: a burnt bridge that costs me the reference.

A coworker admits he faces the same treatment, and we quietly compare notes. I feel relief that it is not just me. Wise: share facts, not gossip; support each other without pulling anyone into a risky move.
He alternates praise and threats and says "nobody else would hire you". I feel dizzy and dependent. Wise: recognise the pattern, test his claim by applying elsewhere, and lean on people outside work.

I need this salary for the family, so I swallow everything. It is a real constraint, not weakness. Wise: stay while planning a way out, protect my health and dignity in small ways. Harmful: telling myself the abuse is normal.

My "internship" is full-time work with no pay, no learning and a vague promise of a job. I feel used but afraid to lose the line on my CV. Wise: ask about stipend and learning goals, set a time limit, walk if nothing changes.

They say they are doing me a favour by taking me on, so I feel I owe endless effort. Wise: an honest exchange is work for learning or pay; a favour does not cancel my rights. Harmful: confusing gratitude with servitude.

One manager teaches me properly and gives real tasks, and I admire her patience. Wise: ask for a reference, take feedback seriously, and keep the relationship after I leave. Harmful: idolising her and ignoring my other needs.

I watch full-time staff coast while I cover their work for free, and I seethe. Wise: name the unfairness, negotiate scope, and use the experience without letting it sour my view of all work. Harmful: sabotage or quiet spite.

We interns cover for each other and share tips on staying afloat. Wise: solidarity is powerful; together we can raise concerns about hours and pay. Harmful: competing for scraps and informing on each other.

My parent proudly tells relatives I work at a big firm, while I feel like a free helper. I feel a guilty gap. Wise: tell the truth gently and explain what I am learning and what I plan next. Harmful: keeping the pretence up.

The app cuts my per-trip rate and blocks my ID with no human to speak to. I feel powerless against an algorithm. Wise: keep screenshots, join a workers' group, track real earnings after fuel, and build other income.

A customer scolds me at the door for being three minutes late, with no eye contact. I feel invisible. Wise: stay calm, keep my dignity, use the app's report tools, and remember his rudeness is about him.

A customer offers water and says "take care on the road". A tiny kindness makes my day. Wise: accept it warmly and pass it on. Harmful: none; but do not let strangers' moods decide my self-worth either way.

I stay online eleven hours chasing incentive targets, tired and hoping the next bonus fixes things. Wise: calculate hourly earnings honestly and rest; incentives are designed to keep me hooked. Harmful: driving exhausted.
Riders at the tea stall share safe routes, warn about bad customers and help with a broken bike. I feel belonging. Wise: nurture this network and use it to ask for better terms together.

I hide from relatives that I deliver food because they see it as low status. I feel a private sting. Wise: honest work is nothing to be ashamed of; explain my plan and timeline. Harmful: lying and drifting into stagnation.

I fear that asking for more will make them withdraw the offer. Wise: research the range, state a reasoned number politely, and be ready to accept the answer. Harmful: silently accepting far less out of dread.
The recruiter says "we have many candidates, sign today". I feel rushed and pressured. Wise: real offers survive a day; ask for the terms in writing and time to read them before deciding.

I am tempted to inflate my previous salary to bargain harder. Wise: honesty is safer since verification is common, and I can anchor on the market value of my skills instead. Harmful: a lie that can void the offer later.

Asking for money makes me feel greedy, as if I was taught that good people never ask. Wise: negotiation is a normal, respectful conversation; asking is not a moral failing. Harmful: silent resentment later.

The manager is candid about the budget and offers learning and a review in six months. I feel respected. Wise: weigh the whole package, get the review promise written, and thank them. Harmful: treating a friendly tone as a guarantee.

My friend got a higher package for the same role, and I compare and stew. Wise: numbers hide bonuses and roles; use it as data for my own negotiation, not for friendship damage. Harmful: coldness or sulking.

My boss tells me to backdate a document "just this once" because everyone does. My heart races. Wise: say I am not comfortable, offer a proper alternative, and keep a record. Harmful: complying and calling it obedience.

A friendly colleague asks me to keep quiet about his shortcut. Loyalty and honesty collide. Wise: urge him to fix it first, and be clear that I cannot lie for him. Harmful: joining the silence until it becomes my problem.

I fear that refusing will cost my probation and my family's income. The fear is real. Wise: check what protection exists, refuse in a calm way, and weigh consequences honestly. Harmful: pretending I had no choice.

I copied a result to meet a deadline and cannot sleep. Guilt is a signal. Wise: correct it, admit it early to the right person, and learn from the pressure that led there. Harmful: burying it and hoping nobody checks.
A client hints at a gift if I speed up his file "quietly". I feel flattered and unsafe. Wise: refuse clearly, report per policy, and treat small favours as the start of a larger hold on me.

Colleagues call me "too sincere" and "not practical" for refusing shortcuts. It hurts to be mocked for integrity. Wise: hold my line with humour and skill, and find allies. Harmful: turning self-righteous.

Signing an education loan feels like tying a stone to my future. Wise: read the interest, moratorium and total repayment, compare the return on the course, and borrow only what I need. Harmful: signing without reading because I am anxious.

My parents mortgaged jewellery for my fees and remind me of it. I feel the weight of their sacrifice. Wise: honour it through effort and honest planning, and speak about the pressure. Harmful: hiding failures to shield them.

An instant loan app offers cash in minutes and then floods me with threats and shaming calls. I feel trapped. Wise: stop borrowing to repay borrowing, save the evidence, tell a trusted adult, and use official complaint channels.
I borrowed from a friend and dodge his calls out of embarrassment. Wise: tell him honestly what I can pay and when. Harmful: avoidance, which damages the friendship more than the debt.
I lent money to a friend, and now he avoids me. I feel used and awkward about asking. Wise: ask plainly and kindly, agree on a date, and treat future lending as a gift I can afford to lose.

I overspent on a credit card to keep up with friends and cannot tell anyone. Wise: total the figure, stop the spending, tell someone safe and make a repayment plan. Harmful: hiding it and paying only minimums until it balloons.

I refuse to ask relatives for help because I want to look self-made. Wise: pride in independence is good until it blocks a sensible short-term bridge. Harmful: paying huge interest to protect an image.
A caller posing as a bank or a job agent knew my name and urged me to act now. Fear and hope were used against me. Wise: pause, hang up, verify through official channels, never share OTPs.

I lost my savings to a fake job offer and feel stupid. Scams are professional and target hope, not stupidity. Wise: report to the cyber helpline at once, tell family, and share the story to protect others.
I keep it secret because I fear being mocked, which lets the scammer's damage grow. Wise: speaking up early can recover money and stops the loop. Harmful: silence, which scammers rely on.

A friend forwards a "guaranteed profit" scheme he believes in. He is not evil, just caught. Wise: check the source before spreading it, question calmly, and keep the friendship while refusing the scheme.

I am furious and want to trap the fraudster myself. Wise: give what I have to the police and cyber cell; do not chase him alone, as that risks more loss or danger. Harmful: revenge fantasies that lead to further scams.
My parent scolds me: "How could you fall for this?" I feel doubly hurt. Wise: hear the fear behind it, ask for help on the next steps, and offer to teach them scam signs too. Harmful: blaming back.

A finance influencer shows luxury cars and says his course changed his life. I feel drawn in. Wise: ask how he actually earns, check registration and track record. Harmful: buying a dream instead of evidence.
Countdown timers, "only 5 seats" and screenshots of profits push me to hurry. Wise: urgency is a sales tool; slow down, read the risks, and never invest money I cannot afford to lose.

My friend doubled money on a hot tip, and I feel left behind. Wise: survivor stories hide the losers; learn basics like index funds, diversification and time. Harmful: chasing his win with borrowed money.

I check the trading app every few minutes and my mood follows the chart. Wise: notice it is closer to a gambling loop than planning; set limits and turn off notifications. Harmful: doubling down to recover losses.

Friends want me to join a pooled scheme because I am the one who "understands markets". I feel flattered and burdened. Wise: be honest about my limits and do not take others' money or promise returns.
I lost most of my savings on a tip and feel foolish. Wise: accept the cost, stop trying to win it back, write the lesson, and rebuild slowly. Harmful: another risky bet to erase the loss.

After a loss I ask why God let it happen, and prayer feels empty. Wise: doubt is common in many traditions and can deepen or reshape faith; stay honest, read, ask elders. Harmful: forcing a fake certainty.

I am angry at God for suffering I did not deserve. Wise: many prayers and texts contain protest; let the anger speak, and let time and community hold me. Harmful: suppressing it until it turns to numbness.

My parents fear that my questions mean I am losing my way and my values. Wise: reassure them I still love them, share questions gently, and avoid mocking their beliefs. Harmful: open contempt for family rituals.

People in my temple, mosque or church go cold when I question things. I feel lonely. Wise: find one or two open-minded elders or peers, and value people over doctrine wins. Harmful: cutting all ties in anger.

I settle into calling myself an atheist or agnostic, and feel relieved and a little lonely. Wise: live by values I can name, respect believers, and not treat every ritual as foolish. Harmful: pride in being "rational".

Even with doubts, I still light a lamp or pray because it steadies me. Wise: practice can carry meaning beyond certainty, and it is fine not to have all the answers. Harmful: using ritual to avoid real questions.

A friend mocks belief online and I feel attacked in my identity. Wise: separate ridicule from honest questions, engage the honest ones, and leave the mockery. Harmful: matching contempt with contempt.
I feel irritated when a devout friend says "just have faith". Wise: accept that faith means different things to him, ask what it gives him, and share what I need. Harmful: calling his belief stupid.

A guru surrounded by devotees is treated as beyond question. Wise: a teacher who is genuine welcomes questions, has accountability and does not take money or obedience beyond reason. Harmful: believing the praise about himself.
I am told that doubting the teacher is my ego and that leaving will bring misfortune. Wise: fear and guilt used for control are red flags; talk to family or friends outside the group before deciding.

A teacher's kindness helped me through a dark year, and I feel deep thanks. Wise: gratitude can coexist with clear eyes; support the good, keep thinking. Harmful: feeling that thanks means never questioning.

I found out my teacher lives in luxury and keeps secrets. My heart broke. Wise: grieve the image, keep what truth I learned, and separate the practice from the person. Harmful: dropping every value out of anger.

I ask my teacher before every decision and feel lost without him. Wise: a good guide builds my judgement, not my dependence; make small choices alone and see that I can. Harmful: outsourcing my whole life.

My friend has cut off his family for the ashram and I worry about him. Wise: keep the door open, stay warm, ask curious questions, avoid attacking his teacher. Harmful: ultimatums that push him deeper.
Members shower me with attention, meals and "you belong here" in my first week. I feel warm after a lonely year. Wise: enjoy kindness but notice if love is tied to obedience or to cutting off others.
I am asked to donate, hand over my phone and stop seeing old friends "for my growth". Wise: these are control signals; keep independent contact, money and a way to leave, and talk to someone outside.

I defend the group even though private doubts are growing. Belonging is strong. Wise: notice which questions I am not allowed to ask; loyalty that forbids thinking is worth examining. Harmful: silencing my doubts.

My family begs me to leave the group, and I see them as enemies who do not understand. Wise: listen for love inside their fear, and keep one connection alive even if I disagree. Harmful: cutting them off as told.

I finally saw that the group's promises did not match its actions. I feel foolish and grieve years lost. Wise: leaving is brave, not stupid; get support, seek counselling and rebuild slowly. Harmful: self-blame.

An ex-member shares that she felt the same fears and now finds peace. I feel less alone. Wise: listen without rushing the decision and take one safe step at a time. Harmful: replacing one authority with another.

My friend joined a group I find worrying, and I want to rescue him. Wise: keep contact, ask open questions, avoid mocking, and share information gently. Harmful: pressure or secret plots that prove the group right.

I fear that the other side's victory will destroy what I value. The fear is sincere. Wise: check facts from varied sources, notice when fear is being sold to me, and act through voting and local work. Harmful: seeing all opponents as enemies.

A relative at a family dinner shouts that my views are "brainwashed". I feel insulted and want to retaliate. Wise: decline to debate while heated, say it calmly, and change the subject. Harmful: escalating until dinner is ruined.

I love my grandfather but disagree with his politics. Wise: ask what experiences shaped his views, share mine without trying to win, and treasure the person more than the position. Harmful: silent contempt behind polite words.
I unfriended everyone who disagrees and feel relieved, then oddly isolated. Wise: boundaries against abuse are fine, but an echo chamber shrinks my mind. Keep some respectful dissent in my life.
I admire a political leader and feel proud when he speaks. Wise: support policies on evidence, and stay able to criticise my own side. Harmful: treating criticism of the leader as an attack on me.
A viral clip edited to enrage me appears in my feed. I feel a jolt of fury. Wise: pause, search for the full context, and do not share until checked. Harmful: becoming a spreader of outrage.

I give time, energy and hope to a cause I believe in, and it gives my life direction. Wise: keep sleep, studies and relationships intact so the commitment lasts. Harmful: burning out or seeing all non-members as enemies.

At the march I fear arrest, batons and family reaction. Wise: know my rights, go with others, keep an ID and a contact, follow the peaceful plan and leave if it turns unsafe. Harmful: recklessness for the thrill.

The group is like family, and I hesitate to speak when it makes a bad tactical or ethical choice. Wise: dissent within a movement is loyalty too; say it early and kindly. Harmful: silence that leads to harm.
My parents call activism a waste of time that will spoil my career. I feel unseen. Wise: explain my reasons calmly, show responsibility elsewhere, and accept disagreement without breaking love.

After months of effort little changed, and I feel cynical and tired. Wise: social change is slow; rest, choose one realistic goal and find people who keep going. Harmful: mocking those who still care.

I see the other side as stupid or evil and enjoy mocking them. Wise: understand their fears, argue the issue and not the person, and keep the moral high ground by being fair. Harmful: dehumanising anyone.
A leader keeps asking for more money and says doubters are traitors. Wise: real movements welcome transparency; ask how funds are used and treat forced unity as a warning sign.

My old post went viral for the wrong reasons and strangers are abusing me. I feel sick and exposed. Wise: do not reply in heat, mute, save evidence, tell someone close, report threats. Harmful: staying up all night refreshing.
People mock a photo of me and make it a meme. Shame flares. Wise: it is their cruelty, not my failing; report, block, lean on friends, and remember the internet forgets faster than it seems.

I join a pile-on against someone who said something wrong and enjoy the group energy. Wise: pause before joining, since a mob feels righteous but rarely hears the person. Harmful: cruelty disguised as justice.

I stay up arguing with a stranger who will never change his mind. Wise: ask whether this exchange serves anyone; disengage, spend energy on offline action. Harmful: doomscrolling and hostile posts that hurt me too.
A friend is being mobbed and I want to defend him, but fear I will be targeted. Wise: reach out privately first, help him report, and speak up when it is safe. Harmful: vanishing quietly.
I follow a loud creator who says what I feel, and his attacks on others feel thrilling. Wise: enjoy his ideas, notice when he feeds on anger, and question anyone who profits from my outrage.
I realised I had shared a false claim that hurt a person, and feel ashamed. Wise: delete it, post a plain correction, apologise if she is reachable. Harmful: defending it out of pride.
I ask the AI before I even try, and my own thinking feels slower. Wise: try first, use AI to check or explore, and keep skills I want to own. Harmful: submitting what I do not understand.
The AI answers confidently and I accept it. Wise: trust but verify, especially for facts, health, law and money; ask for sources and test claims. Harmful: treating fluent text as truth.

Talking to an AI companion feels easier than people, since it never judges me. Wise: enjoy the comfort but keep human bonds growing, as real friends can hold me in ways software cannot. Harmful: replacing all relationships with it.

My professor suspects that my assignment was AI-written when partly it was. I feel exposed. Wise: be honest, show my process, and learn the rules. Harmful: lying, which turns a minor matter into a serious one.

A classmate finishes work in minutes with AI and scores well, and I feel foolish for working hard. Wise: shortcuts show in interviews and later work; build real skill, use AI as a tutor. Harmful: copying blindly to keep up.
I worry AI will take the job I am training for. The anxiety is understandable. Wise: learn the tools, build judgement and human skills, and stay adaptable. Harmful: freezing or denying the change.

My employer expects me to produce AI-level output at speed and never asks whether I understand. Wise: check accuracy myself and speak up about errors. Harmful: hiding behind the tool when mistakes occur.

What began as an occasional drink, vape or game night has become how I cope, and I keep saying I can stop anytime. Wise: honestly count the cost, tell someone safe, seek professional help early. Harmful: hiding it and calling it stress relief.

After each binge I promise myself never again, then relapse and hate myself for it. Wise: shame fuels the cycle; treat relapse as data, get support and plan for triggers. Harmful: punishing myself and drinking or scrolling again.
Friends push me to drink or use "just to fit in" and call me boring. I feel torn. Wise: a real friend accepts a no; say it simply, leave early, and find people who like me sober.
My parent finds out and shouts, and I feel cornered and defensive. Wise: hear the fear inside the anger, agree to a plan, and accept help. Harmful: lying or slamming doors to keep the habit.

I finally book an appointment for my drinking or gaming problem. Nervous and relieved. Wise: honesty with a professional is the start of recovery; go back even after a slip. Harmful: presenting only the softer half of the story.

A support group takes me in without judgement. I feel relief and belonging. Wise: return regularly, be honest and help others later. Harmful: swapping the addiction for dependence on the group's approval only.
Betting apps promise a quick win, and I chase losses at 2 am. Wise: block the apps, tell someone, and understand that the game is built to keep me playing. Harmful: borrowing to win back what I lost.

My friend says she feels hopeless and I want to help. Wise: listen without judging, take it seriously, stay with her and help her reach a counsellor, doctor or helpline. Harmful: promising to keep it secret or brushing it off.
I am scared of saying the wrong thing and making it worse. Wise: simple, warm words work best: "I am here, I care, let us get help". Harmful: avoiding him because I feel helpless.

I am exhausted from being his only support and secretly resent him. Wise: this is human; share the load with other people and professionals, and keep my own limits. Harmful: silent burnout or cold withdrawal.

My friend relies on me for everything and calls at all hours. I feel needed and drained. Wise: care includes limits; encourage professional help and other supports. Harmful: becoming her sole rescuer.

A friend confides that he is in deep pain and asks me not to tell anyone. Wise: safety matters more than the promise; gently involve a trusted adult or professional, and tell him first. Harmful: carrying it alone.

My friend lashes out at me during his lowest week. It hurts. Wise: pain often spills sideways; stay steady, do not take it personally, and address it later when calm. Harmful: retaliating or abandoning him.

I ignored his messages and then learned he was struggling. I feel guilty. Wise: reach out now, apologise briefly, and show up; guilt is useful only when it becomes care. Harmful: avoiding him out of embarrassment.
I feel like a burden and think others cope better, so I hide how bad it is. Wise: unbearable feelings need a person; tell one trusted adult or a helpline today. Harmful: waiting for it to pass alone.

My family says "it is all in your head, just be strong". I feel dismissed. Wise: try again with specifics or bring an ally like a doctor or teacher; my pain is real regardless. Harmful: giving up on asking.

I go to a counsellor and gradually let my guard down. It feels awkward and helpful. Wise: therapy takes time; be honest and try a different professional if it does not fit. Harmful: quitting after one session.

A friend notices I am off and simply sits with me. I feel seen for the first time in weeks. Wise: accept the care, say how much I can share, and let him help with practical tasks. Harmful: pushing him away to look fine.
My manager ignores my exhaustion and demands more. I feel unseen. Wise: document, use leave and support policies, and prioritise recovery over performance. Harmful: pushing through until I collapse.

I try to talk to myself as I would to a friend who is suffering. Wise: small kind acts, sleep, food and contact with people help; they do not replace professional help when needed. Harmful: forcing positivity.

The house feels wrong without him and grief comes in waves, sometimes at odd moments. Wise: let it come, keep rituals, talk about him, accept help. Harmful: stuffing feelings away or being told to move on.

I keep replaying what I should have said before my friend died. Wise: guilt is love with nowhere to go; write him a letter, share memories, talk to someone. Harmful: punishing myself for what I could not have known.
Relatives cook, visit and sit quietly with us. I feel held even though nothing fixes it. Wise: accept the presence, and say what I need. Harmful: hiding grief to make visitors comfortable.
Why did God take him? I am angry and a bit ashamed of it. Wise: anger and faith can coexist; allow the questions, seek people with wisdom and patience. Harmful: forced acceptance that hides the pain.

After my father's death, my mother leans on me as if I were the adult. I feel pride and heaviness. Wise: support her while also grieving myself and involving relatives. Harmful: taking on all the roles alone.

A week after the funeral I feel nothing and worry something is wrong with me. Wise: numbness is a common protection; be patient, keep routines, and get help if it does not lift. Harmful: judging myself for not crying.
My classmates return to normal life while I feel frozen, and it hurts that nobody asks. Wise: tell one or two people what I need; grief is invisible unless named. Harmful: assuming nobody cares.

A coworker makes a casual joke about my caste, religion, region or accent. I feel heat and shame. Wise: name it calmly, note it, use HR or a trusted senior; the fault lies in the joke, not my identity.

A landlord refuses to rent to me because of who I am. I feel angry and small. Wise: it says more about his prejudice; know the legal options, keep notes, find allies and other options. Harmful: internalising it.
People mimic my accent or food and call it banter. I laugh along and feel hurt. Wise: tell them plainly it is not fine, and look for people who respect it. Harmful: hiding my roots to fit in.
I watched someone be insulted for his background and said nothing. I feel guilty. Wise: check on him afterwards, back him up next time, or report. Harmful: excusing my silence as "not my business".

I want to hit back at someone who insulted my community. Wise: anger is valid; direct it into complaints, support and safe, organised responses. Harmful: violence or retaliatory hate towards a whole group.
A friend faces bias and I want to shield him from everything. Wise: ask what he wants, support his voice instead of speaking over it. Harmful: making him feel helpless or turning it into my story.
I catch myself assuming things about someone because of his religion or region. Wise: notice the thought without shame, test it against real individuals, and learn. Harmful: denying my own bias.
Stopped at night by police, my heart pounds. Wise: stay calm, keep hands visible, be polite, carry ID, ask for the reason, and call someone; know that rights exist. Harmful: arguing or running.

An officer asks me for money or presses me to sign a paper I have not read. Wise: do not sign what I do not understand, ask for a lawyer or a family member, and note names and numbers. Harmful: panicking and complying.
I go to the station to report a theft and hope that they will help. Wise: bring documents, stay respectful, get a copy of the complaint. Harmful: expecting everything to go wrong and not trying.

I am facing a legal notice and feel lost. Wise: consult a legitimate lawyer or a legal aid clinic, keep every paper, and ask them to explain in plain words. Harmful: ignoring the notice and hoping it disappears.
My friend asks me to lie to the police about where he was. Wise: loyalty does not mean false statements; help him find a lawyer instead. Harmful: perjury that pulls me in with him.

After an unfair fine or harassment I feel furious and helpless. Wise: record calmly, pursue complaint channels, and channel anger into action rather than confrontation. Harmful: heated words that turn a bad situation into worse.

I found evidence of fraud in my workplace and I am afraid of losing everything. Wise: keep copies safely, learn whistleblower protections, seek legal advice, and choose the safest right channel. Harmful: acting impulsively or leaking in anger.

After I reported an issue, my boss turned cold and colleagues stopped speaking to me. I feel punished for doing right. Wise: document retaliation, lean on outside support, and remember that integrity has costs and value.

The wrongdoer is a friend who helped me settle in, and I feel torn. Wise: loyalty to a person and loyalty to truth can clash; give him a chance to correct it, but do not stay silent forever. Harmful: excuses.
I noticed something wrong earlier and said nothing, and now it is bigger. Wise: speak up now, acknowledge the delay, and let the facts lead. Harmful: staying silent because I already stayed silent.

I reported and nothing happened, and I feel cynical about all systems. Wise: try another channel, connect with groups that know the process, and keep some faith in change. Harmful: deciding nobody can be trusted.

A few colleagues quietly thank me for speaking up. It gives me courage. Wise: value the support, but do not expect them to stand publicly; protect them and myself. Harmful: making them feel guilty for their silence.

In a new city or country I fear making mistakes with language, food and rules. Wise: ask, watch, be patient with a learning curve, and find a small community. Harmful: staying only in a bubble that never lets me learn.

People are polite but never invite me in, and my accent makes me feel like an outsider. Wise: keep showing up in clubs, classes and small talk; belonging is built slowly. Harmful: assuming all locals dislike me.

I adapt to new ways and feel I am betraying my parents' culture. Wise: identity can hold both; keep what I value and adopt what suits me, and explain it to family. Harmful: hiding one half to please the other.

I miss home food, language and family and cry in secret. Wise: schedule calls, cook familiar meals, find fellow migrants, and know that it eases with time. Harmful: isolating or judging myself for missing home.
Others from my home community welcome me warmly, and I feel safe. Wise: enjoy the comfort while also making friends beyond it. Harmful: treating outsiders with suspicion.

My family boasts about my life abroad and expects money and success stories. I feel a gap. Wise: share honest difficulties gently and set realistic expectations. Harmful: pretending everything is perfect.
Someone makes a snide remark about my food or dress. I feel small and angry. Wise: answer calmly or walk away, seek allies, and stay proud of my background. Harmful: withdrawing into resentment.

I did what I was supposed to do, and now I wonder what it is all for. Wise: try small experiments, meet people, help someone, and let purpose emerge from action rather than being found. Harmful: numbing with scrolling.

My parents' dream for me is not mine, and I feel like a fraud pursuing it. Wise: tell them what I actually love, propose a path with a fallback, and accept their worry. Harmful: silent compliance or dramatic rebellion.

My friends seem to know what they want, and I feel behind. Wise: most people are guessing; social media hides it. Try things and follow what holds my interest. Harmful: comparing my confusion to their highlights.

I ask an older person how she found her direction and she says she changed course three times. Wise: collect stories, not formulas; direction often forms while walking. Harmful: waiting for certainty.
I turn to a book, tradition or practice to find meaning. Wise: let it challenge and comfort me, discuss with others. Harmful: adopting a ready-made answer that spares me from thinking.

I call myself lazy and directionless and think I have wasted my youth. Wise: stagnation is often exhaustion, fear or depression; be kind, take one tiny step, seek help if it persists. Harmful: harsh labels as a way to feel in control.

After a serious mistake I hear a voice saying "you are worthless". Wise: separate what I did from who I am, own the harm, repair it, and speak to myself as I would to a friend. Harmful: hiding it or self-punishment.
I learn to say "I made a mistake, and I am still a person worth respect". Wise: self-compassion makes accountability easier, not weaker. Harmful: using kindness to excuse repeating the harm.

The person I hurt says she forgives me. I feel relief and do not feel worthy. Wise: accept it humbly, change behaviour, and do not demand more from her. Harmful: treating forgiveness as a reset with no effort.

The person I hurt refuses to speak to me. I feel the weight of it. Wise: apologise clearly without excuses, give space, and accept that repair is her choice and takes time. Harmful: pressing her for forgiveness.

My family says "we expected better" and I feel crushed. Wise: hear the honest part, share my plan to repair, and distinguish disappointment in an act from rejection of me. Harmful: swallowing it as proof I am unlovable.
Any error feels like proof that I am a fraud, so I overwork and avoid risk. Wise: aim for good, learn from the slip, and tell someone about it. Harmful: never trying anything I might fail at.
My mentor says, "I made worse mistakes at your age, now what will you do?" I feel steadied. Wise: use that grace to act, not to dwell. Harmful: hearing acceptance as permission to be careless.
I refuse to admit I was wrong because it feels like admitting I am nothing. Wise: apologising shows strength; my worth does not depend on being right. Harmful: doubling down and losing trust.

After my result a friend simply says "come, let us eat" and does not lecture. I feel held. Wise: let the kindness settle me before I plan the next step. Harmful: pushing him away because I feel undeserving.
My peers pass with ease, and I feel a bitter, jealous knot. Wise: note the feeling, congratulate them anyway, and ask what worked for them. Harmful: contempt for them or quiet sabotage.

I roll my eyes and mock my partner's habits, feeling superior and tired. Contempt is the most corrosive habit in marriage; the wise move is to name the hurt underneath and ask for what I need, not score points.

I am being sneered at or talked down to by my partner, and I feel small and unsafe to speak. It is not my fault. I calmly name the pattern, ask for respect, and seek counselling if it continues; I avoid answering contempt with contempt.

My partner is raising their voice and I feel attacked and want to shut down or flee. Wisdom is to hear the complaint under the tone, say I need a break, and return within the hour, not stonewall or counter-attack.

I am flooded with anger at my partner, heart racing, and I want to say the cruelest true thing. Mature action is to pause, cool off, and speak about my feeling and request; the harmful pattern is wounding words that cannot be taken back.

My partner is angry with me and I feel defensive and afraid of losing them. I listen without rushing to justify, ask what hurt them, and own my part; I stay firm if anger turns into threats or intimidation and seek help.

I go cold and stop speaking to punish my partner because saying I am hurt feels too exposed. Wise action is to say plainly that I am upset and need time; the immature pattern is using silence to control.

My partner has gone silent and I feel anxious, guilty, and desperate to fix it. I invite talk gently, do not grovel or guess my crime, and say that silence as punishment hurts us both and we need to talk.

After a fight my partner reaches out with a joke or a cup of tea and I feel both relief and lingering hurt. Wisdom is to accept the bid, and still return later to the real issue so peace is not just avoidance.

I decide to forgive my partner for a real wound and feel it will take time, not one sentence. Forgiving means letting go of revenge while still stating what must change; it is not pretending nothing happened.
I am being forgiven by my partner after I hurt them and feel grateful and undeserving. I do not demand quick forgiveness; I show through steady changed behaviour that I understood the harm.

When my partner names a fault I immediately explain, deny, or counter-blame because criticism feels like being unlovable. Growth is to breathe, say what is true in it, and answer the complaint before my own defence.

My partner criticises me constantly and I begin to feel I can do nothing right. I check whether some points are fair, ask for specific requests, and refuse to accept blanket attacks on my character as truth.

I discover my partner has been unfaithful and feel shock, nausea, and shaken sense of who I am. It is not my failing. I take time, avoid rash public revenge, lean on trusted people, and decide about the future when calmer.

I was unfaithful and I am torn between shame, self-justification, and fear of being found out. The honest path is to face what I did and the harm it caused; the harmful path is hiding, blaming my partner, or asking them to soothe me.

I feel jealous of my partner's friend and want to check their phone. Mature action is to voice my insecurity and ask for reassurance openly; the harmful pattern is surveillance and accusation, which erodes the trust I want.

My partner keeps suspecting me without proof and I feel watched and resentful. I offer honest reassurance once or twice, then set a boundary against constant checking and suggest counselling if it becomes controlling.
I hide messages or lie about where I was, telling myself it protects my partner from pain. Concealment slowly deadens a bond; the wise step is to end the secrecy and choose honesty, even at a cost.

My partner wants to rebuild after their affair and I feel hope tangled with anger. I can set conditions like full honesty and time, and I am free to decide the marriage cannot be saved; neither choice is weakness.

I broke my partner's trust and want the marriage to survive. I accept their anger, answer questions honestly without defensiveness, and let trust return at their pace, not mine; asking to be forgiven quickly repeats the harm.

I feel a spark toward a colleague while married and enjoy the attention. Attraction is human; wisdom is to see what the spark is answering in my life, keep distance, and bring the gap to my partner before it becomes a secret.

My partner and I fight about spending and I feel controlled or judged. Money often carries fear and values, so I ask what security means to each of us and agree on a shared budget with room for personal spending.
I quietly resent my partner over who earns more or who sends money home to parents. I say it aloud kindly, treat it as a shared decision, and avoid keeping a silent ledger of grievances.
I hide a loan, purchase, or savings from my partner, fearing their reaction. Hidden money damages trust more than the money itself; disclosing early with a plan is the mature choice.

My partner controls all the money and gives me an allowance or demands I hand over my salary. This is a warning sign of financial control. I seek shared access to accounts, talk with trusted family or a counsellor, and protect my independence.

I feel I owe my partner because they backed my career or paid for my studies. Gratitude is healthy; I show it through respect and reciprocity, not by giving up my voice or letting the debt become a leash.
My partner depends on me financially and I feel both protective and burdened. I talk openly about shared goals and their route to independence, without shaming them or using money as leverage.

I want closeness with my partner but they are tired or unsure. Real intimacy means asking, listening to a no without sulking, and understanding that willingness must be free; pressure or guilt-tripping is not love.

I am not in the mood or not ready and I fear disappointing my partner. My comfort matters equally; I can say no kindly and clearly, and a caring partner respects it. Repeated pressure is a warning sign to speak to someone trusted.

I withdraw from my partner after work stress and cannot say why. I name that I am overwhelmed, not that they did something wrong, and offer a small time to reconnect; unspoken withdrawal is felt as rejection.
