Human Learning & Development: A school-age child sweats from heat, exercise, nervousness before a test or illness. The cause cannot be told from the sweat alone, so setting and other signs matter.
A child learns idioms, hints and jokes, and asks what someone meant. Indirect speech may show politeness or humour, and asking what someone means is a good habit.
A child says cheese and smiles for a photo but looks tired in a candid moment. A posed smile shows cooperation, not necessarily feeling, and both kinds of image tell different stories.
A child begins to notice small changes such as a slight frown or lower voice in a parent. Subtle signals are easy to miss or over-read, so a short check keeps them honest.
A child keeps a straight face at a surprise, waiting for the right moment or to avoid teasing. The child still feels the excitement, and adults may enjoy the delay.
A school-age child says okay through tight lips when a rule feels unfair. Politeness shows learned self-control, yet the anger still needs a safe outlet afterwards.

Subtype: Faces shaped for peers and cameras [Regulating]
Human Learning & Development: A teenager curates a face for peers and photos, such as a practiced smirk or pout, which may show belonging or self-consciousness more than the feeling underneath. A private mood can differ from the public face.

Subtype: Snarl or scowl as a warning sign [Interpreting]
Human Learning & Development: A teenager who sees a peer's scowl or snarl aimed at them reads possible anger or threat, and may step back, stay calm and involve an adult if it escalates. Reading danger early is protection, not weakness.
A teenager reads an asymmetric smile as possible teasing, doubt or private amusement, but it may also just be habit or shyness. Context and relationship decide whether it is warm or mocking.

A teenager keeps a slight smile at school while feeling low, to avoid questions. Trusted adults can notice a smile that does not reach the eyes or fits poorly with other cues, and offer a gentle open door without pressure.

Subtype: Controlling a frown at a parent or teacher [Regulating]
Human Learning & Development: A teenager tries to smooth a frowning brow when disagreeing with an adult to avoid conflict, though the forehead may still tense. Naming the disagreement in words is clearer than relying on the face.

Subtype: Eyebrows in teasing and flirt-free banter [Expressing]
Human Learning & Development: A teenager raises the eyebrows or one eyebrow in banter to signal a joke, mock disbelief or a challenge. Friends read it through tone, and it can sting if the target is unsure it is playful.
A teenager with heavy, half-closed eyes after late screen time may look bored or rude in class, but is often simply tired. Adults can ask about sleep before assuming disrespect.

Subtype: Winking and eyelid flutter in social play [Mismatch]
Human Learning & Development: A teenager winks to share a joke or fluttering eyelids to tease, but a wink can be misread as flirting or mockery. Clear context and consent to the joke keep it kind.

Subtype: Averting gaze as avoidance or respect [Interpreting]
Human Learning & Development: A teenager reads a peer's averted gaze cautiously: it may mean shyness, guilt, social anxiety, autism-related comfort, or cultural politeness. Asking gently beats assuming dishonesty or disinterest.

A teenager who is stared at persistently by someone makes them uneasy is right to trust that discomfort, move toward other people and tell a trusted adult. Unwanted staring is not the teenager's fault.

Subtype: Sideways glance and shifting gaze in peer groups [Interpreting]
Human Learning & Development: A teenager notices sideways glances at school and reads gossip or judgement, though people also look away from shyness or thought. Assuming the worst can cause needless conflict, so checking the facts helps.
A teenager's cheeks rise in a real smile or redden from embarrassment, and either can be hard to control. Others read the state from context, and kindness spares a teenager who blushes.
A teenager wrinkles the nose at something unpleasant but learns to soften the reaction to avoid hurting a friend. Being honest in words, kindly, is better than a silent sneer.

Subtype: Lip biting when unsure or anxious [Regulating]
Human Learning & Development: A teenager bites the lip to stay quiet, hold back words or calm nerves. It signals restraint, and noticing it in a friend may open a gentle question.

Subtype: Pouting and pursing for cameras and moods [Mismatch]
Human Learning & Development: A teenager pouts or purses the lips in a selfie as a style, or in real sulking. The difference lies in context, and mocking a genuine sulk can deepen hurt.
A teenager clenches the jaw in exams or arguments to hold back words, showing tension. Slow breathing and stretching the jaw help, and adults can offer to talk without pressure.

Subtype: Moving the jaw sideways and tongue clicks [Mismatch]
Human Learning & Development: A teenager shifts the jaw sideways or clicks the tongue when thinking or being dismissive, which peers may take as attitude. The meaning depends on tone and relationship.
A teenager holds a still face to seem cool or hide nerves, while another has a resting face that looks unfriendly. Neither is proof of coldness, so asking helps.

Subtype: Tense or rigid face under threat [Interpreting]
Human Learning & Development: A teenager notices a friend's rigid, frozen face after upsetting news and understands it may mean shock or fear, not indifference. Quiet support and time are better than demanding a reaction.

A teenager meeting people in India sees the side-to-side head wobble, which can mean yes, okay, I understand or I am listening depending on the tilt and context. It is not a clear no, so ask if unsure.

Subtype: Turning away as boundary or snub [Interpreting]
Human Learning & Development: A teenager reads a peer turning away as a snub, but it may mean the person is distracted or needs space. Not taking it personally, and asking later, keeps friendships steadier.
A teenager rolls the shoulders to release tension before a match or exam, or holds them tense when anxious. Noticing and releasing them is a useful calming tool.
A teenager shrugs in response to a parent's question, which may mean I do not care, I do not know how to say it or I am upset. Patient open questions often unlock a real answer.

Subtype: Folded arms as boundary or comfort [Mismatch]
Human Learning & Development: A teenager folds the arms to signal a boundary, to feel cold or to feel secure. Interpreting it as closed-off without checking can be unfair.
A teenager opens the arms for a friend who is upset, offering comfort, and learns to ask first if a hug is welcome. Consent applies to every hug, and a refusal is respected.

Subtype: Clapping and snapping in peer groups [Expressing]
Human Learning & Development: A teenager claps or snaps as approval among friends, or slowly claps sarcastically. Tone and speed show whether it is praise or mockery.
A teenager reads open palms as honesty or welcome, but it is only one cue and is not proof someone is truthful.
A teenager uses air quotes to signal irony or doubt and a mock salute for humour or respect. The tone decides if it is friendly teasing or a put-down.

A teenager recognises thumbs-down and rude gestures, including the raised middle finger, as insults or strong disapproval, and learns to step back, stay calm and tell an adult if it comes from bullying. Using them hurts others and can bring consequences.

A teenager in an online class uses the raise-hand button, a chat emoji or a mute icon to take turns without speaking over others. The tool replaces the physical gesture, but silence in a video call is ambiguous and may mean shyness, lag or disengagement.

A teenager waves a hand to ask someone to step back or not crowd them. The same motion can mean stay away, not now, or give me air, and cultures differ on how blunt it is; a verbal follow-up clarifies without shaming the other person.

Subtype: Palm out as boundary in arguments [Regulating]
Human Learning & Development: A teenager raises a palm to stop a friend or sibling mid-rant, meaning I need a moment or I disagree. It can protect a boundary, but it can also read as dismissive; saying a few words like give me a second keeps the respect intact.

A teenager finds that pointing with a whole hand, a chin or lips, or a thumb differs by region, and some styles feel rude elsewhere. A descriptive gesture can mislead, so pairing it with words and checking understanding helps.

A teenager narrating a match or a prank sweeps hands to show speed, distance and drama. Expanded gestures usually signal excitement and involvement, while very small ones may suggest tiredness or reluctance; culture strongly shapes gesture size.

A teenager preparing for an interview or public speaking practises standing straight and taking a breath, which can help nerves. Confidence also comes from preparation; exaggerated power poses do not replace real skill.

Subtype: Slumping and crossing arms as protection [Regulating]
Human Learning & Development: A teenager slumps, hunches or crosses arms in a tense home or crowd, often to feel smaller or safer. Arms crossed may mean cold, comfort or defence, so reading it as rudeness misses the mark; a chat about how they feel may help.

A teenager dances in a group, at a wedding baraat, on a practice reel or at a school event to show joy and belonging. Styles vary by culture and gender norms; pressure to perform or teasing can turn joy into shame, so choice matters.

Subtype: Walking away as boundary or avoidance [Mismatch]
Human Learning & Development: A teenager walks away from a fight, a taunt or a hard talk. It may be wise de-escalation, embarrassment or avoidance; saying I need a break and will come back makes the meaning clear and keeps trust.

A teenager freezes, cannot speak or move when confronted, threatened or pressured. Freezing is a common involuntary stress response, not consent or agreement, and others should never read stillness as a yes.

Subtype: Shielding the body and avoiding notice [Mismatch]
Human Learning & Development: A teenager pulls sleeves over hands, hunches or covers the face when embarrassed, self-conscious or uneasy around someone. It may signal shame or fear of being seen; steady acceptance helps, and fear of a particular person merits a trusted adult.
A teenager checks hair, fixes clothes or hides behind a phone when feeling watched. It can signal self-consciousness, ordinary grooming or a wish to look good; teasing about it deepens insecurity.

Subtype: Touching the face and neck under stress [Regulating]
Human Learning & Development: A teenager rubs the neck, touches the face or bites nails before a presentation or a tough talk. These self-touches often calm nerves but are not reliable signs of hidden thoughts; slow breathing helps more.

A teenager reads a shoulder touch or squeeze as support, but the same touch from someone in power or on a private area may be unwelcome. Discomfort deserves trust; saying stop, moving away and telling a trusted adult are all right.

A teenager learns to ask or check before hugging a friend and to accept no gracefully. Stating a preference, such as I am not a hugger, is healthy; pressure or guilt over refusal is a warning sign to discuss with a trusted adult.

Subtype: Approaching and stepping back in social ties [Mismatch]
Human Learning & Development: A teenager moves closer to some peers and away from others, and the choices can be read as liking, rivalry, shyness or safety. Distance is a cue, not a verdict, and quick conclusions about popularity or hostility often go wrong.

A teenager steps back, turns away or puts an object in between when someone stands too close or follows them. Discomfort is valid, and an adult should be told if the person keeps closing in or ignores clear signals.

Subtype: Laughing to fit in or mask [Regulating]
Human Learning & Development: A teenager laughs along with a group joke that feels unkind or hides hurt behind a laugh. Fake laughter can protect belonging but leave the person uneasy; choosing safe friends and a calm boundary such as that is not funny is healthier.

A teenager laughs when embarrassed, scared, being scolded or hearing bad news. It signals stress release, not enjoyment or disrespect; reading it as mockery causes conflict, while a gentle check on feelings helps.

A teenager may cry while explaining something angry, or laugh until they cry. Mixed tears can mean overwhelmed feeling, joy, relief or tension, so labelling them from the outside can be wrong; asking helps.

A teenager cries quietly in a room or under a blanket to avoid being seen. It can signal grief, stress, loneliness or hormonal overwhelm; frequent hidden crying with withdrawal or hopelessness calls for a trusted adult or a counsellor.
A teenager yells during a quarrel with a parent or friend, driven by hurt, frustration or a wish to be heard. Taking a break, lowering the voice and returning to talk works better than escalating.

Subtype: Screams as alarm and help calls [Interpreting]
Human Learning & Development: A teenager learns that a scream or yell for help should be taken seriously, even when it might be a prank. Checking safely and calling for help beats ignoring it; false alarms erode trust, so pranks should not use it.

Subtype: Groaning, moaning and huffing at demands [Expressing]
Human Learning & Development: A teenager groans at homework or chores, meaning boredom, protest or stress. It rarely means real refusal; a light response and a clear expectation works better than a lecture, while a groan of real pain should be taken seriously.

A teenager snorts or clears the throat, and peers may read it as mockery, warning or a real need. The sound is ambiguous; a child with a cold or a tic should not be blamed, and asking calmly avoids unfair conclusions.

A teenager says huh as confusion, surprise or challenge and mm-hmm as listening, agreement or a brush-off. Tone and timing shape meaning, so a follow-up question is wiser than assuming the sound means yes.

A teenager uses ugh for irritation, fatigue or dramatic humour. Others may take it as rudeness, but often it is harmless venting; a teen can learn to add a few words such as that was a long day to avoid confusion.

Subtype: Quiet voice under stress or shyness [Mismatch]
Human Learning & Development: A teenager speaks very softly at school, which teachers may read as low confidence, respect or disinterest. Reasons vary and include culture, shyness or fear, so encouragement and a quieter setting work better than criticism.

A teenager's voice deepens or cracks during puberty, causing embarrassment or jokes. Pitch changes are physical rather than emotional, and kind peers ignore the crack; adults reassure that it settles with time.
A teenager may clip words or clear the throat to hide a choked voice when upset in front of peers. Trusted adults can offer a private moment instead of pressing for words in public.
A teenager whose voice cracks during puberty may feel embarrassed though the crack is physical, not emotional. Listeners are wise to ignore it, and the teen can laugh it off rather than go silent.
A teenager who drags out a word such as fiiine may signal reluctance, boredom or sarcasm. The rhythm can contradict the words, so a friend or parent reads both, then asks a gentle check.
A teenager whose speech races when anxious can practise measured pace by pausing at full stops and breathing out first. A steadier pace often helps the speaker feel calmer as well as sound calmer.
A teenager who waits hours for a message reply may be busy, unsure what to say or upset. Reading a delay as rejection is a common pitfall, so asking directly is wiser than spiralling.

A teenager who falls silent or stops abruptly mid-sentence may be hurt, embarrassed, angry or simply thinking. Silence is ambiguous, so a caring reply gives space and leaves the door open to talk later.
A teenager sings along with favourite songs or croons privately to express longing, pride or belonging to a group. Lyrics chosen may mirror mood, but they are not proof of what the teen feels.
A teenager may hum or sing under headphones to calm nerves before an exam or after conflict. Singing can lower tension, and it is a healthy tool alongside talking with a trusted person.

A teenager may use slang, nicknames, emojis or a nod as a greeting; changes in greeting style from a friend may signal closeness or distance. Reading too much into one missed reply is a common pitfall.
A teenager uses examples, analogies and diagrams to illustrate a point and persuade peers. Vivid examples help, though they can also be cherry-picked, so checking sources matters.
A teenager who reports something to an adult may be seeking safety or seeking revenge. Adults thank the teen, listen without assuming motives and act on safety concerns.
A teenager asks for confirmation such as so you are saying and probes for reasons. Probing can feel supportive or like interrogation, depending on tone and relationship.
A teenager who asks rhetorical questions like do you even care may be hurt, angry, sarcastic or making a point. Answering the feeling behind it works better than answering the literal words.
A teenager may sound very certain to fit in, or hedge with maybe or I guess to avoid being wrong. Tone can hide real doubt, so a friend can ask what the teen would need to be sure.
A teenager may hide surprise or confusion with a poker face or a joke in front of peers. A private check later helps sort out whether they really understood.
A teenager challenges rules and disputes ideas to build independence and identity. It is normally a sign of growth, and adults can listen for the request underneath the challenge.
In India a head wobble can mean yes, okay, I hear you or maybe, depending on context and tone. Listeners check with a clarifying question rather than assuming agreement or refusal.
A teenager who demands may be frustrated, scared, or copying a tone heard elsewhere. Adults respond to the need under the demand and restate the request politely without giving in to the tone.
A teenager invites friends or appeals to a parent for later curfew with reasons. Appeals with respectful tone and evidence more often succeed than pressure and threats.
A teenager may hear advice from a parent as a lecture or control even when meant as care. Brief, respectful suggestions and asking what help is wanted improve how it lands.
A teenager weighs recommendations from friends and influencers about trends, products and risks. Advice that carries pressure to do something unsafe or secret is a reason to consult a trusted adult.

A teenager learns that saying yes once does not authorize everything, and that consent to share a picture or location can be withdrawn. Anyone who pressures or threatens is unsafe and should be reported.

A teenager sets limits with phrases like I am not comfortable with that or I do not want to share that photo. Refusing is a right, and a true friend respects it, while pressure is a warning sign to tell a trusted adult.
A teenager may promise to keep a secret or a pledge of loyalty to a friend. Promises to keep secrets about safety, harm or abuse should not be kept, and telling a trusted adult is the caring choice.
A teenager may vow never to talk to someone again or swear to change overnight in a burst of emotion. Waiting a day before big vows allows real intention to settle.

A teenager may feel first attraction and show it with blushing, teasing, texting or avoidance, and signals can be unclear. Respect means asking and accepting a no, and telling a trusted adult if pressure or unsafe requests appear.
A teenager shows affection with emojis, streaks, memes or likes, which can be ambiguous. Meaning varies among groups, so asking directly is wiser than reading much into a like.

A teenager shows admiration with likes, comments, hearts or a shared post. Such signals are quick and low-cost, so their sincerity varies; a specific personal message usually means more than a reaction count.

A teenager may look pleased yet squirm, deflect or joke when praised in front of peers. Discomfort at recognition is often about social exposure rather than dislike of the praise; a quiet private word may suit better.

A teenager learns that praise can be genuine, strategic or teasing, and checks whether it is specific, consistent and free of a request. These are cues only; motives cannot be confirmed from words alone.

Subtype: Knowing when to involve an adult [Regulating]
Human Learning & Development: A teenager recognises that some worries, such as safety, self-harm talk or abuse, are too big to hold alone and tells a trusted adult even if a friend asked for secrecy. Care sometimes means sharing.

A teenager comforts a friend by listening, staying present and sending a supportive message. Fixing the problem or minimising it ("It's not a big deal") can feel dismissive; validation often matters most.
Words like "It will be fine" can comfort one person and feel dismissive to another, depending on tone and timing. Teenagers may hear hollow cheer as not being taken seriously.
A teenager may find it hard to apologise because it feels like losing status, so may joke, send a meme or act as if nothing happened. Repair is usually stronger with a short plain acknowledgement.
Phrases like "I'm sorry you feel that way" or "Sorry, but you also..." can sound like blame shifting. Teenagers can learn to spot conditional apologies and to give ones without excuses.

A teenager states likes and dislikes about touch, photos, sharing and closeness, and expects a "no" to be respected. Everyone has the right to refuse; adults and peers should stop and a trusted adult should be told if a refusal is ignored.

Subtype: Hiding needs to avoid burdening others [Regulating]
Human Learning & Development: A teenager may say "I'm fine" while tired, hungry, overwhelmed or unwell, fearing to seem needy. Learning to state needs plainly, and adults noticing withdrawal, helps prevent small problems becoming large.

A teenager asks for a closed door, quiet time or less questioning, sometimes bluntly. The need for space is often about autonomy and processing, not rejection; brief agreed check-ins balance respect and care.
A teenager learns to criticise the act or plan rather than the person, and to accept feedback without collapsing or attacking. "That part is unclear" is more usable than "You are useless".

A teenager objects to rules, expresses disapproval with eye-rolls, sighs, silence or arguments, or joins a peaceful protest. Underneath can be a wish for respect and voice; respectful channels are more effective than escalation.
A teenager learns to lower voice, pause, step away and say "Let's talk later" when anger rises. Cooling down is not weakness, and it prevents words or acts that cannot be taken back.

Subtype: Insults, taunts and challenges among peers [Interpreting]
Human Learning & Development: A teenager meets insults and dares in person and online, sometimes as banter and sometimes as an attack to provoke a reaction. Reading tone, history and audience helps; not answering and saving evidence are protective moves.

A teenager who receives a threat online or in person treats it seriously, avoids engaging, keeps a record and reports it to a trusted adult, school or authorities. A threat is not a challenge to be won.
A teenager builds an argument with claims and evidence in class or at home and defends a view. Debate skill includes acknowledging good points; winning by volume or ridicule is a common pitfall.
A teenager bargains for curfew, phone time or independence by offering trust-building steps. Calm proposals with a trial period tend to succeed better than arguing or sneaking around.

A teenager faces persuasion to try risky things and can say no, suggest another plan, blame a rule or leave. A good friend accepts a refusal; repeated pressure is a reason to seek an adult or new company.
A teenager tells a parent, teacher or counsellor about stress, mistakes or unsafe situations. Adults who listen first, stay calm and avoid instant punishment make later disclosure more likely.

A teenager posts personal details or feelings publicly, sometimes seeking support or attention. Pausing before posting, considering permanence and audience, and using trusted friends for heavy topics protects privacy.

Subtype: Revealing a feeling to a peer or crush [Mismatch]
Human Learning & Development: A teenager may hint at, joke about or partially reveal a feeling to test the response. Vulnerability is risky, and it is wiser to share with those who have shown care and respect.
A teenager trades quick jokes with friends and uses shared references. Banter builds belonging but can exclude, and jokes that rely on stereotypes or someone's pain can harm even when framed as fun.

A teenager shares memes, parodies and satirical clips to comment on school, politics or life. These convey shared attitudes economically, though satire may be mistaken for fact and can hurt if it mocks vulnerable people.

A teenager says "Great, just great" meaning the opposite, using tone or a flat delivery. Sarcasm can signal frustration, humour or contempt, and in text or across cultures it is easily misread, so a clarifying "Are you joking?" is fair.
A teenager uses and decodes references to shows, songs or slang that signal group membership. Outsiders may miss or misread them, and meanings change quickly.
A teenager hints "It is getting late" to suggest leaving or implies displeasure without saying it. Hints save face but are often missed, so clear requests avoid confusion.

A teenager learns that some remarks carry a suggestive or hurtful second meaning. Recognising these means noticing discomfort, the right to say "that is not okay" and telling a trusted adult if it continues.

A teenager may question rituals, adapt them or find new meaning, sometimes causing tension with family. Respectful questions can coexist with participation, and pressure from either side rarely helps.

Subtype: Reverence and respect in shared spaces [Expressing]
Human Learning & Development: A teenager shows respect by removing shoes, covering the head, standing or being quiet in a temple, mosque, church or gurdwara. Practices differ, and a visitor can watch others or politely ask.

Subtype: Hand orientation and palm direction in signs [Interpreting]
Human Learning & Development: In signed languages, the direction the palm faces and where the hand points can change a sign's meaning, like a vowel changes a word. Hearing learners must respect this grammar, not treat signs as loose gestures.

A learner watches for hand shape, movement, space and facial grammar to follow meaning, and asks for repetition instead of guessing. Signed languages vary by country and region; there is no single universal sign language.

A deaf or hard-of-hearing teenager may take pride in signing and Deaf culture, while others use spoken language or both. Language choice is personal, and signed languages are valid, complete languages.
A teenager writes essays with a thesis, evidence and counterargument to persuade or explain. Tone in writing must be carried by word choice, since no face or voice supports it.

Subtype: Personal writing and diaries as private space [Regulating]
Human Learning & Development: A teenager uses a journal or notes to sort out feelings and identity. Privacy matters, and writing something down does not mean acting on it; worries about safety should be shared with a trusted adult.
A teenager writes a slogan for a campaign, a caption for a photo or a script for a skit. Short forms compress attitude and identity, and can be read differently by different audiences.
A teenager may find that a joking message reads as rude or a serious one as a joke, since face and voice are missing. Adding an emoji, a clarifying line or a call can avoid conflict.
A teenager uses reaction buttons, hearts and thumbs-up to show quick support or agreement. These are lightweight signals, and a missing reaction should not be over-read as rejection.

Subtype: Memes and GIFs as shared language [Expressing]
Human Learning & Development: A teenager replies with a meme or GIF to convey humour, mood or belonging. Context and audience shape meaning, and an in-joke may confuse or hurt outsiders.

A teenager chooses photos, filters and captions to present a self to peers. Posts are curated, so they do not show the full picture of someone's life, and personal images should be shared only with consent and care.
A teenager reads "okay." as cold, "OKAY!!!" as shouting or excitement, and "sooooo" as emphasis or playfulness. Norms differ by group, age and platform, so such cues suggest but do not prove a mood.

Subtype: Drama and mime as emotional language [Expressing]
Human Learning & Development: A teenager uses acting, mime or improvisation to portray feelings that are hard to say aloud, such as grief or anger. Role work lets emotion be explored at a safe distance, but it is not a confession of real events.

Subtype: Playlists and dance trends as mood signals [Mismatch]
Human Learning & Development: A teenager shares a sad song or a viral dance video online, which may mean mood, humour, belonging or mere fashion. A brief kind check-in works better than assuming distress from one post.

A teenager writes verses or slam poetry about identity, injustice, love or loneliness. Lyrics use persona and exaggeration, so a listener should ask the writer before assuming the words describe their real plans.

A teenager sketches, journals visually or edits video to work through stress, anger or sadness. Making art can lower intensity, and persistent dark themes with withdrawal call for a caring conversation rather than judgement.
A teenager curates photos, edits and memes to signal humour, belonging, identity or mood. Posted images are chosen and framed, so they show a presented self rather than a full picture of life.

A teenager keeps a friendship bracelet, a ticket stub or a poster that stands for a relationship or identity. Objects hold meaning that only their owner can fully explain, so curiosity is wiser than assumption.

A teenager compares looks with filtered images and may over-control clothes or grooming. Supportive adults stress that presentation is a choice, not a measure of value, and watch for lasting distress.

A teenager balances a dupatta, a turban, a sacred thread, a bindi or a hijab with peers' fashion. The same item can be faith, family expectation, choice or style, so nobody should assume its meaning for another person.
A teenager experiments with clothing, hair colour, makeup or jewellery to explore who they are. Style changes are often trial and belonging signals, not proof of deeper trouble.

A teenager cheers, chants or wears team colours with a crowd, feeling belonging. Crowds can amplify emotion and pressure, so a teen may act differently than alone, and wise judgement includes leaving if things turn unsafe.
A teenager joins a school vigil or memorial, showing grief and solidarity with silence, flowers or lamps. Each participant may feel different things, and some may cry while others feel numb.

Subtype: Affectionate and tender among friends and family [Regulating]
Human Learning & Development: A teenager may hide affection in public while staying warm privately. Embarrassment about closeness is common, and honest words or small gestures keep bonds alive.
A teenager's banter, memes and inside jokes signal closeness, but teasing can hurt when one person is not enjoying it. Watching for the other person's response is the guide to when play should stop.

Subtype: Distressed and disappointed by exams and comparison [Expressing]
Human Learning & Development: A teenager after poor results may go silent, snap or say they are useless. Family reaction weighs heavily, and persistent hopelessness needs urgent caring attention, not lectures.

A teenager after a breakup or friend group split may withdraw, post cryptic messages or throw themselves into activity. Heartbreak can feel overwhelming, and support from friends and family helps recovery.

A teenager notices a friend who is quiet, tired or joking less and wonders about their state. A gentle question such as how are you really is better than guessing, and serious worry goes to a trusted adult.
A teenager recognises an eye-roll, curled lip or dismissive tone that says you are beneath me. Contempt is hurtful and damages trust, so the wise response is to name the effect calmly or leave.

Subtype: Defiant, irritated and frustrated with authority [Mismatch]
Human Learning & Development: A teenager's sullen silence, backtalk or refusal may mean anger, fear, wish for autonomy or exhaustion. Adults who ask before punishing learn more and keep communication open.
A teenager with intense rage may shout, slam doors or go silent and cold. Fury peaks and fades, so stepping away, breathing and returning later to talk protects relationships.
A teenager notices a peer glaring, sneering or blocking the way and feels unsafe. Hostility is a warning to disengage, stay near others and involve a trusted adult, not to retaliate.

Subtype: Apologetic and pleading in peer conflict [Interpreting]
Human Learning & Development: A teenager reads a friend's quick sorry, soft voice or begging texts and wonders if they are sincere. Sincerity shows in changed behaviour over time, and pressure to forgive should not override boundaries.
A teenager may feel I did something bad or I am bad, and the two look alike from outside. Guilt motivates repair, while shame drives hiding, so adults respond to the person with care.
A teenager blushes, avoids the spotlight or overthinks how they seem. Self-consciousness peaks in these years, and small steps into social situations build comfort.
A teenager nodding while glancing at a phone may be listening or elsewhere. Attention cannot be read from posture alone, so asking a brief question checks it.
A teenager hesitates, raises a brow or says maybe about a plan or belief. Doubt may reflect careful thinking or fear, and open discussion beats pressure.

Subtype: Reading interest and confusion in others [Interpreting]
Human Learning & Development: A teenager tries to tell whether a classmate is interested, puzzled or bored from face and voice. These cues are hints only, and asking is better than assuming.
A teenager gasps, freezes or stares at shocking news such as unexpected results. Astonishment is stronger than surprise and can lead to joy or distress, so a moment of quiet space helps.

Subtype: Excited, eager and worried mixed together [Mismatch]
Human Learning & Development: A teenager before a trip, exam or first job interview may feel eager and anxious at once, with the same racing heart. Labelling it as excitement can turn nervous energy into readiness.
A teenager cheers, pumps a fist or hugs teammates after a win. Triumph feels good and is best shared graciously, since gloating can hurt others.
A teenager delivers a joke or an insult without expression, so listeners cannot tell if it is humour. Deadpan needs shared understanding, and unclear cases are settled by asking.
A teenager who withdraws, answers in single words or stares at a screen may be tired, hurt, private or bored. Detachment has many causes, so patient check-ins over time are better than accusations.
A teenager keeps a blank face to avoid showing hurt or joy to peers. An impassive look protects privacy but can hide need, so trusted people should offer chances to talk.

Subtopic: Visible reactions with multiple possible causes
Human Learning & Development: A teenager who blushes easily may fear being noticed. Slow breathing, focusing outward and remembering that most people do not notice reduce the distress.

Subtopic: Visible reactions with multiple possible causes
Human Learning & Development: A teenager reads a friend's tears and may guess sadness, but tears also come from anger, stress, laughter and relief. Asking gently and staying present is wiser than guessing.
A teenager writes in capitals, many exclamation marks or dramatic emojis, which may be play, real intensity or performing for followers. Tone online is easy to misread, so a quick check helps.
A teenager may swing from laughing to irritable to tearful within an hour. Changing moods are common in adolescence, so patient consistency, sleep and gentle talk support balance.
A teenager plays feelings down with a shrug or fine to avoid drama. Understatement protects privacy but may hide real need, so trusted adults leave the door open.
A teenager laughs loudly after a slip in front of others, covering embarrassment. Others may read it as confidence, and the laugh may be relief or fear of rejection.
A teenager laughs off a hurtful joke to avoid looking weak. The smile is protection, and a friend may gently follow up privately, never assume, and offer support.

A young adult studying or working abroad finds that how openly faces show emotion differs across cultures and families; a restrained face may be respect or calm, not coldness. Asking directly avoids stereotypes.

A young adult reads faces through lag, small screens and frozen frames, where a frown may be a bad connection or concentration. Checking in verbally is more reliable than inferring mood from a paused face.

A young adult tells a polite, mouth-only smile from a warm, sustained smile that also involves the eyes, but treats the difference as a rough clue only, since many genuine smiles are quiet and many polite ones are convincing.

A student in a new city finds smiling at strangers is friendly in some places and odd in others; a smile can also cover embarrassment or apology, as in parts of Asia. Local norms matter more than assumptions.
A young adult in an interview raises the brows to show interest and avoids furrowing them when nervous. Interviewers should remember that a tense forehead may only signal effort or anxiety.

A person from a highly expressive culture may use big eyebrow movements while talking, while another finds them dramatic. Baseline expressiveness differs by person and culture, so compare against what is normal for them.

Subtype: Prolonged eye closure in exhaustion or calm [Mismatch]
Human Learning & Development: A young adult closing the eyes for long moments in a meeting may be tired, meditating, listening intently or overwhelmed. The same sign has several meanings, so a gentle check-in is better than guessing.

Subtype: Winking in professional or cross-cultural settings [Regulating]
Human Learning & Development: A young adult avoids winking at work or with new acquaintances because it can be misread as flirtatious or impolite in some cultures. Choosing clear words respects others.

Subtype: Direct gaze in interviews and dating [Regulating]
Human Learning & Development: A young adult adjusts gaze between direct and softer, as steady eye contact can signal confidence in one setting and intensity in another. Shy or neurodivergent people may find eye contact hard and can still listen well.
A person looks up or away while thinking or recalling, which is common and not evidence of lying or evasion. Judging honesty from gaze is unreliable, so listen to content and check facts.
A person wearing a mask shows only eyes and upper face, so smiles and nose or cheek signals are hidden. Voice, eyes and words carry more weight, and asking directly is helpful.

Subtype: Nostril flare and tension in conflict [Interpreting]
Human Learning & Development: A young adult notices flared nostrils and tight cheeks in a heated discussion and reads rising anger, but may also be seeing effort or heat. A pause and a calm check-in help.
A young adult notices a friend's downturned mouth corners and thinks they may be sad or tired, then asks instead of assuming. A resting face can look sad without being sad.

Subtype: Raised mouth corners as politeness versus joy [Mismatch]
Human Learning & Development: A young adult raises the mouth corners at work as polite friendliness even when stressed, and colleagues learn not to read every lift as happiness.
A young adult's jaw drops at surprising news, signalling astonishment or shock. The following reaction shows whether it is pleasant or upsetting.
A young adult grinds or clenches the jaw when stressed, sometimes unaware. Others may read anger, but it often reflects worry, so a kind check-in helps.
A young adult keeps the face neutral in a negotiation to avoid revealing eagerness. It is a legitimate tactic, though excessive coldness can damage trust, so warmth in words helps.

A young adult with a flat or limited facial expression may still feel strongly, including autistic people and those with certain conditions. Ask and listen to words rather than judging feeling from the face.

Subtype: Lifting the chin and lowering the head [Interpreting]
Human Learning & Development: A young adult reads a lifted chin as pride or challenge and a lowered head as deference or sadness, treating these as one clue among many.

A young adult learns that in some places nodding shows attention rather than agreement, and in some countries such as Bulgaria the meaning of nod and shake are reversed. Clarify with words in cross-cultural talks.

Subtype: Raised shoulders as fear or cold [Interpreting]
Human Learning & Development: A young adult sees a person with raised shoulders and may guess fear or worry, though it may be just cold. Context and asking come first.
A young adult finds that a shrug carries different weight across cultures, from casual not sure to rude indifference. Words prevent misunderstanding.
A young adult presenting keeps open, relaxed arms and avoids stiff crossing, making the audience feel welcome. It is a skill, not a guarantee of confidence.

Subtype: Raised arms in celebration or surrender [Mismatch]
Human Learning & Development: A young adult raises the arms in triumph at a goal, or in surrender, or in stretching. Context, such as noise and setting, shows which.

Subtype: Clenched fists and tense hands in conflict [Interpreting]
Human Learning & Development: A young adult sees clenched fists in a heated exchange and treats it as a possible warning, choosing distance, calm words and help from others. Clenched hands can also mean effort or cold.
A young adult presses fingers spread on a table to steady nerves or uses a fidget object to stay calm, a healthy regulation tool that observers should not mistake for disinterest.
A young adult reads the thumbs-up, folded-hands and wave emoji as modern equivalents of gestures, but the thumbs-up may seem curt or passive-aggressive to some. Norms differ by age and workplace.

A young adult travelling finds that the OK-sign, thumbs-up and beckoning finger carry different meanings in different countries, some offensive. When unsure, a smile, a word or a namaste-like neutral greeting is safer.

A student abroad learns that an upturned-finger beckon that is friendly in one place can be rude in another, and a palm-down scoop is common in South Asia and elsewhere. Guessing meaning from one culture is risky, so watching locals and asking is wiser.

Subtype: Signalling a turn in group discussion [Regulating]
Human Learning & Development: A young adult in a seminar lifts a finger, leans in slightly or catches the chair's eye to claim a turn. Read together, these cues show wish to contribute; interrupting anyway shows poor turn reading, while patient signalling builds influence.

A young adult in a presentation uses measured hand shapes to show a graph trend or process, but fidgety or over-large motions can distract. Purposeful gestures usually help listeners follow, and rehearsing on video can show what to trim.

A student meeting a Deaf friend learns that signed languages use shape, movement, space and facial grammar as complete languages, not mime. Treating signs as loose gestures shows misunderstanding; learning basics and asking respectfully builds connection.

A student reads a friend leaning forward as interest and leaning back as relaxed or distant. These are weak cues; a person leaning back may be comfortable, or unwell, so checking with a question is wiser than concluding disinterest.
A young adult stiffens, holds the breath or hunches in a stressful exam or confrontation. It signals threat or anxiety; slow exhaling, dropping the shoulders and grounding the feet often ease it.

Subtype: Bowing, folding hands and formal movement [Mismatch]
Human Learning & Development: A young adult uses a bow, namaste or a stand-up greeting according to custom. Meaning is politeness and respect, but the depth and manner vary by place and relationship, so watching others and following local custom avoids offence.

A young adult reads jumping, hugging or dancing in a crowd at a match or festival as shared joy. In crowds movement can turn from cheering to unsafe pushing, so watching for shifts in mood and having an exit plan is wise.

Subtype: Ducking and defensive reflex in danger [Regulating]
Human Learning & Development: A young adult drops low, covers the head or moves away in a road, crowd or fight risk. Trained safety responses, such as leaving early, protect better than bravado; de-escalating and getting help beat trying to win.

A young adult notices a friend flinching, backing off or covering up near a partner, boss or stranger. These cues suggest discomfort but are not proof; checking privately, listening and offering help or resources respects the friend's choice.

Subtype: Covering the mouth and cultural norms [Mismatch]
Human Learning & Development: A young adult covers the mouth when laughing, yawning or coughing, which shows manners in many places but shyness in others. It can also signal surprise or embarrassment, so meaning depends on the cultural setting.

A young adult clicks a pen, bounces a leg or uses stimming movements to focus or calm. For many neurodivergent people, stimming is a valid form of regulation; others should not read it as rudeness or lack of attention.

A gentle stroke of the hand or hair between partners or close family conveys tenderness. It is welcome only with clear consent and context; if the other person stiffens or pulls away, stop and check in.

A young adult uses a firm no, a raised palm or a step away to set a boundary, or a light push to get free from unwanted touch. Others must stop at once; if ignored, leaving and seeking help or reporting is appropriate.

Subtype: Touch norms across cultures and settings [Mismatch]
Human Learning & Development: A young adult finds that handshakes, shoulder pats, hugs, or touching elders' feet mean respect or warmth in one setting and intrusion in another. Watching local custom and asking how someone prefers to greet avoids discomfort.

A young adult travelling finds that comfortable conversation distance, queue spacing and seating vary across countries and communities. Stepping back may be misread as coldness, and stepping in as pushiness, so both should be read gently.

Subtype: Turning toward and away in conversation [Interpreting]
Human Learning & Development: A young adult notes that a listener turning the body toward them usually signals engagement and turning away may signal need to leave, distraction or discomfort. It is a soft cue only; asking is more reliable than guessing.
A quiet, satisfied chortle can mean genuine amusement, smug pleasure or relief. Context decides: shared humour bonds people, but the same sound aimed at someone's mistake can feel mocking.

A young adult types haha, lol, emoji or laughing reactions to show amusement or soften a message. The same lol can mean genuine humour, politeness or discomfort, so tone and history matter more than the letters.

Subtype: Types of laughter and social bonding [Expressing]
Human Learning & Development: A young adult uses chuckles, belly laughs and guffaws to show amusement and connection. Shared, spontaneous laughter builds closeness, while a cackle or guffaw may feel bold in one culture and normal in another.

A young adult cries after exams, a breakup or a hard job. Tears can release tension and are not weakness; rest, talking to a friend and seeking counselling if crying is frequent or with hopeless thoughts are wise steps.

A young adult weeps at a funeral, a farewell, a wedding or a graduation. Tears can mean grief, joy or relief, and cultures differ in how openly they are shown, so support respects the person's own meaning.

A young adult joins cheering and whooping at a concert, match or graduation. Volume and style are welcome in some settings and odd in others, so awareness of the venue and other people is a form of respect.

Subtype: Yelling at work or home and de-escalation [Regulating]
Human Learning & Development: A young adult notices a raised voice from a colleague or partner and stays calm, lowers their own tone and asks to continue later. Shouting that frightens or controls another person is not acceptable, and leaving and getting support is right.

Subtype: Sighing to hide or show stress [Regulating]
Human Learning & Development: A young adult takes a slow sigh to calm down or lets out an audible sigh in frustration. Deliberate slow breathing can steady nerves, while a loud sigh at a colleague may feel dismissive, so awareness of audience matters.

A young adult whistles or hums for calm or joy, but whistling at a person in public can be unwelcome harassment. Recognising when a sound crosses into disrespect helps, and anyone targeted may leave and report it.

A young adult uses mm-hmm as a back-channel to show they follow, and hears hmm as thinking, doubt or mild disagreement. A flat mm-hmm on a call may signal distraction, so the listener checks rather than assuming.

Subtype: Wow, ooh and ah in messages [Mismatch]
Human Learning & Development: A young adult reads wow in a text as admiration, shock or sarcasm depending on tone and emoji. Without a voice the reader can misjudge, so clear words or a follow-up call keep sarcasm from causing hurt.

Subtype: Louder, higher voice in excitement or anger [Interpreting]
Human Learning & Development: A young adult hears friends speak louder and higher when excited and sometimes the same when angry. Words, face and context decide; the wise response to a raised angry voice is to stay calm and step back if unsafe.

Subtype: Varying pitch for persuasion and presentation [Regulating]
Human Learning & Development: A young adult varies pitch and pace to keep listeners engaged in a debate or interview, and avoids sounding flat. Natural variety builds trust, while artificial theatrics can seem insincere.

A young adult in a presentation or interview who speaks with a resonant, steady voice usually signals composure, though nervous people can also sound steady. Breath and posture help build the effect honestly.
A listener hearing a trembling voice from a colleague or student may assume fear, grief, anger or excitement. The wise reading is to wait, stay warm and ask, rather than assume weakness or deception.

Subtype: Measured pace in interviews and presentations [Regulating]
Human Learning & Development: A young adult in an interview or seminar who keeps a measured pace with deliberate pauses appears organized. Slowing too much may read as disinterest, so pace should fit the room and topic.

Speech rhythm differs across Indian languages, accents and English varieties, so a fast or sing-song rhythm may be normal for the speaker. Judging intelligence or attitude from rhythm alone is a common and unfair pitfall.
A young adult in negotiation or interview may use a brief pause to think or let a point land. A long silence can feel like pressure in some cultures and respect in others, so the setting guides use.

Subtype: Chanting, devotional singing and protest songs [Mismatch]
Human Learning & Development: A young adult may chant or sing in devotion, a stadium or a protest for solidarity, faith or grief. The same rhythm can signal joy or anger, so context and respect for the group matter.

A young adult in an interview or new college introduces self with name, role and a short line about interests. Confident, clear greetings build trust, and norms differ across cultures for title use and eye contact.

A young adult reading a report or news item separates stated facts from opinion and asks about source and sample. Tone can mask bias, so double-checking claims is wiser than trusting confident delivery.
A young adult in interviews or research uses open questions and follow-ups to learn, avoiding loaded or leading questions. A wise probe stays curious rather than accusatory.
A young adult states expectations as predictions and notes the evidence, such as I expect X because of Y. Humility about limits builds credibility, while unearned certainty invites errors.
A young adult disputes a claim by focusing on evidence, using phrases such as the data suggests otherwise. Attacking the person instead of the claim is a common pitfall that escalates conflict.
In many cultures people avoid a blunt no and say maybe, we will see or yes, but. A young adult reads tone, delay and lack of follow-up and asks a clear yes or no question.

A young adult learns to spot requests that carry pressure, guilt or threats, such as if you loved me you would. A real request leaves room to say no, and unsafe pressure should be shared with a trusted person.
A young adult requests help from a mentor, friend or counselor by being specific about the need and timeframe. Vague requests such as can you help me with something invite confusion.
A young adult leading a team or lab gives clear directions with the reason and expected result. Commanding without explanation may achieve compliance but weaken trust.
A young adult reading warnings about scams, health claims or safety checks the source before acting or sharing. Panic messages that push urgency and secrecy are a warning sign in themselves.

A young adult asks someone to stop teasing, texting or touching by saying stop, clearly and without apology. If the person does not stop, leaving and seeking help from a trusted person or authority is wise.

A young adult may refuse or set limits on family expectations about career, marriage or visits, which can feel disrespectful in some families. Calm, warm explanation and time often help more than confrontation.

Subtype: Making commitments to study, work and partners [Expressing]
Human Learning & Development: A young adult makes commitments that have real cost, such as a lease, a course or a relationship. Clear terms and checking capacity before saying yes prevent broken promises.
A young adult shows care with listening, time, help and follow-through rather than only words. Loyalty is healthiest when it allows honesty, and it should not require silence about harm.

A young adult congratulates a friend on an exam result or job offer, matching enthusiasm to the friend's mood. Overdone cheer can feel performative, while a brief specific note of pride often feels sincere.

Subtype: Expressing respect to teachers and mentors [Expressing]
Human Learning & Development: A student thanks a mentor with a note, a small gift or a timely acknowledgement in a project. Norms differ; some cultures expect formal gestures such as standing or gift-giving, others value plain words.

A young adult offers condolences with a short sincere message, presence or practical help after a loss. Clichés can grate; simple words like "I am so sorry, I am here" and follow-up later usually help more.

Comfort differs across cultures: some communities bring food and visit in groups after a death, others give privacy and few words. The same gesture may read as warm or intrusive, so follow the family's lead.

Apology norms vary: some settings expect explicit words of regret, others show repair through actions, gifts or a return to routine. A bow, a folded-hands gesture or a shared meal can carry regret without saying so.
A young adult reaches out after a fallout, names their part, listens to the other side and does not demand instant forgiveness. Timing matters; some people need days before they can talk.
A young adult uses "I" statements such as "I need some time alone tonight" or "I prefer not to". Clear, calm, specific needs are easier to honour than hints, and cannot be assumed to be guessed.

Subtype: Reading a partner's or roommate's unspoken needs [Interpreting]
Human Learning & Development: A young adult notices signs such as quietness, irritability or clutter and infers a need for rest or space. These inferences can be wrong, so checking ("Do you want company or quiet?") is wiser than assuming.

A young adult gives feedback to a peer or project member with specific examples and a suggestion. A rebuke in public often produces defensiveness; private, timely and respectful feedback works better.

Subtype: Taking criticism without shrinking or bristling [Regulating]
Human Learning & Development: A young adult listens to feedback, asks clarifying questions and separates useful points from unfair ones. Immediate defence or total self-blame both make learning harder.

Subtype: Contempt and ridicule as warning signs [Interpreting]
Human Learning & Development: A young adult recognises sneering, mockery and eye-rolls in a relationship as signs of disrespect that damage trust. Naming the pattern calmly, setting a limit or seeking help is wiser than trading insults.

A young adult may face "Do this or I leave" from a friend, partner or family member. Some ultimatums state a real boundary, others are pressure or control; consider whether choices are respected and seek support if fear or coercion is present.

Subtype: Appeals to emotion, authority and logic [Interpreting]
Human Learning & Development: A young adult identifies appeals used in ads, politics and personal requests and weighs evidence. Emotional appeals are not always manipulation, but urgency, fear and flattery deserve extra scrutiny.

Subtype: Negotiating shared living or study arrangements [Expressing]
Human Learning & Development: A young adult negotiates chores, costs and schedules by stating interests, not just positions, and looking for options that serve both sides. Written agreements avoid later disagreement.

A young adult shares family stories, cultural background and personal milestones to be known. What to disclose is a personal choice, and no one is obliged to reveal private details, including identity, before feeling safe.

A young adult shares fears, history or hopes gradually with friends or partners and watches for reciprocity. Trust grows through matched, gradual sharing; sharing too much too soon can leave one feeling exposed.
A young adult says "It was slightly damp" after a flood or "Not my best day" after a disaster. Understatement conveys coping and irony, and it depends on shared understanding of the true scale.
A young adult uses jokes to ease tension or process stress. It can bond and relieve pressure, but constant joking may hide distress that deserves a serious conversation.
A young adult says "passed away", "let go" or "between jobs" to soften harsh facts. Euphemism shows tact, but it can blur meaning where clarity matters, such as health, safety or consent.
A young adult reads symbols such as a white dove, a lamp, colours or a wedding ritual. Meanings vary by culture and religion, so interpretations are informed guesses rather than fixed facts.
A young adult offers thanks through prayer, offering food, lighting a lamp, a moment of silence or a harvest festival. Thanks expressed ritually can carry deep meaning that varies by tradition.

Subtype: Touching elders' feet and seeking blessings [Mismatch]
Human Learning & Development: A young adult in many Indian families touches elders' feet on festivals or important occasions to seek blessings. The gesture signals respect but is not universal, and people may vary in comfort, so it is best done by choice.
A deaf student may use an interpreter, captions or direct signing with teachers. Hearing peers speak to the student rather than the interpreter, and wait for the interpreter's lag.

Subtype: Use of space and classifiers in sign [Interpreting]
Human Learning & Development: A signer uses space to show who did what to whom and classifier handshapes to describe objects and movement. Watching the whole signing space, not isolated signs, gives the meaning.

A young adult adjusts letters, emails and messages for a teacher, employer or friend, using greeting, courtesy and length to match the relationship. Register signals respect and understanding of norms.

A young adult writes a personal statement or profile to present goals and character. Honest, specific detail reads more convincingly than generic claims, and the text shows curated self-presentation rather than the whole self.

Subtype: Reading tone in text without voice [Interpreting]
Human Learning & Development: A young adult reads messages and emails and may misjudge tone, as brevity can seem cold or angry when it is rushed. Since cues are missing, checking with a call or a clarifying question is wise.
A young adult uses bold, lists, line breaks and quoting to make messages clear, and uses italics or capitals to add emphasis. Overuse can seem aggressive or cluttered.
A young adult reads response speed, read receipts, silence and reactions in a group chat. Slow or absent replies often reflect busyness or preference, and are not reliable evidence of feelings.
A young adult facing a heated thread pauses, avoids replying while angry, moves to a private or voice conversation and blocks or reports abuse. Screenshots can preserve evidence of harassment.

Subtype: Acting a role versus feeling it [Mismatch]
Human Learning & Development: A young adult in a drama society plays a villain or a grieving parent convincingly without feeling it. Skilled performance shows that visible emotion can be crafted, so audiences should not equate a display with the actor's own state.

Subtype: Cultural performance and shared ritual arts [Expressing]
Human Learning & Development: A young adult performs garba, qawwali, kathak or a folk song at a college fest, expressing devotion, pride or community. Meaning depends on tradition, so learners should ask about context before judging.
A young adult shapes film, graphic design or architecture to communicate a viewpoint or emotion to strangers. Audiences read work through their own experience, so intent and reception can differ.

A young adult views a painting or film and forms a view of the maker's mood. Art reflects craft, tradition and audience as well as feeling, so the maker's state cannot be safely inferred from the work alone.

Subtype: Sculpture as expression of inner states [Expressing]
Human Learning & Development: Shaping clay, stone, wood or found objects lets a person express feelings that are hard to say, such as grief, pride or tension. Meaning is layered: the maker's intent and the viewer's reading may differ, and both are valid.
A young adult chooses a tattoo, piercing or henna as a personal or cultural marker. Meaning is private and may change with time, so thinking through permanence and workplace norms is wise.

A young adult picks formal or smart clothing to fit an interview or event. Dress signals seriousness and respect in many settings, but first impressions from clothing are unreliable measures of ability.

A young adult reads a wedding baraat, a religious procession, a graduation march or a funeral cortege as marking joy, devotion or loss. Meaning is set by tradition, so an outsider observes respectfully and asks.

A young adult joins a march or rally to voice concern about a cause, using chants, slogans and processions. Peaceful protest is a form of expression, and staying aware of safety, rules and exit routes protects participants.

Subtype: Grateful, welcoming and joyful in new communities [Interpreting]
Human Learning & Development: A young adult in a hostel or new city reads invitations, sweets shared and thanks as signs of welcome. Reading them warmly builds friendships, and cultural custom shapes how gratitude is voiced.

Subtype: Loving and admiring in adult relationships [Expressing]
Human Learning & Development: A young adult shows love through time, help, messages and shared plans, and admiration by learning from mentors. Love styles differ, so asking what feels caring is better than assuming.

Subtype: Grieving and sorrowful away from home [Regulating]
Human Learning & Development: A young adult grieving a loss far from family may feel isolated and put on a brave face. Reaching out, marking the loss through ritual and talking to friends or a counsellor supports healing.

Subtype: Angry and irritated in shared living and study [Regulating]
Human Learning & Development: A young adult with a difficult roommate or group project feels irritation building. Naming the issue early, using calm words and taking breaks prevents small annoyances from becoming conflict.

Subtype: Fearful and alarmed in unsafe situations [Interpreting]
Human Learning & Development: A young adult notices a gut sense of danger, such as being followed or pressured. Feelings are cues, not proof, but moving to a public place, asking for help and leaving are all sound steps.
A young adult listens, sits with a distressed friend and avoids quick fixes or judging. Support can be more useful than advice, and serious risk means involving professional help.

Subtype: Puzzled and confused in video calls [Mismatch]
Human Learning & Development: A young adult on a video call may freeze, look away or stay muted while thinking, lagging or confused. Missing visual cues online means checking in with words.
A young adult questions sources, methods and claims in class or online. Skeptical reasoning is a strength when it is fair and curious, and stubborn cynicism is a pitfall.

Subtype: Hopeful and apprehensive about the future [Regulating]
Human Learning & Development: A young adult facing exams, placements or a move feels hope and dread. Planning, talking to mentors and small steps convert vague dread into manageable action.
A young adult celebrating a success acknowledges help and effort, and avoids putting others down. Shared pride strengthens bonds, and public boasting can create distance.

Subtype: Bored and tired in study life [Expressing]
Human Learning & Development: A young adult in a dull lecture or overloaded semester shows yawns, doodling and phone use. Boredom, tiredness and poor sleep overlap, and structure, breaks and rest help.
A young adult keeps reactions muted in interviews, family gatherings or with elders. Restraint shows respect in many cultures, yet constant suppression can be tiring.

Subtopic: Visible reactions with multiple possible causes
Subtype: Bodily signs are not lie detectors [Interpreting]
Human Learning & Development: A young adult sees someone sweat, blush or tremble in a questioning situation and wonders about guilt. These reactions occur in innocent people as well, so they must never be treated as proof.

Subtopic: Visible reactions with multiple possible causes
Subtype: Trembling and sweating before high-stakes events [Regulating]
Human Learning & Development: A young adult before viva, interview or speech feels shaky hands and damp palms from nerves. Preparation, grounding and reframing arousal as readiness help, and persistent panic deserves professional support.

Subtype: Direct versus indirect communication across cultures [Mismatch]
Human Learning & Development: A young adult meets people who state needs plainly and others who hint through politeness or silence. Neither is better, and adaptable listeners ask clarifying questions kindly.
A young adult carrying stress for weeks shows it in tired face, short answers or constant irritability. Long-lasting displays call for rest, support and sometimes professional help.

A young adult keeps a flat face on results day or during a proposal, feeling great excitement or fear inside. A blank face shows control rather than absence of feeling, so others should not assume indifference.

Subtype: Speaking politely while angry in formal settings [Regulating]
Human Learning & Development: A young adult in an interview, service dispute or family setting stays courteous while frustrated. Composure is useful, though the anger needs a healthy outlet, and a calm firm request protects boundaries.

A mature reader treats a wince, grin or scowl as one clue among tone, words and situation, holding the guess loosely and checking with the person, because the same face can come from several different states.

A young professional keeps a pleasant face with clients or a manager during a stressful day, which is useful, but long-term suppression can be tiring and is best balanced with honest outlets elsewhere.

Subtype: Broad smile as customer or leadership tool [Regulating]
Human Learning & Development: A young professional uses a broad, open-mouth smile to set clients at ease or to open a meeting. It works best when it matches honest goodwill, and habitual smiling over real worry can wear a person down.

Subtype: Sustained smile in intimacy and grief [Mismatch]
Human Learning & Development: A sustained smile can appear at reunions, weddings or even a funeral when remembering a loved one, mixing joy with sorrow. Readers should not assume a smile means only happiness.
A young adult flashes the eyebrows to acknowledge a colleague across a room, a light signal of recognition and friendliness. It is easy to overlook, so it complements rather than replaces a greeting.
A colleague's habitually drawn-together brows may reflect worry, concentration, headaches or simply how the face rests. Asking kindly about workload is wiser than reading a mood into a resting brow.

Subtype: Wet or squeezed eyes under pressure [Regulating]
Human Learning & Development: An adult blinks quickly, squeezes the eyes or looks up to hold back tears at work, a common way to regulate strong feeling. A short break to breathe often helps more.

Subtype: Widening the eyes as a listening cue [Expressing]
Human Learning & Development: A young professional widens the eyes slightly to show interest and encourage a speaker. It works when natural, and a fixed wide-eyed look may seem strained.

A young professional working across countries learns that gaze norms vary: sustained eye contact means engagement in some places and challenge in others. Adapting while staying curious avoids stereotypes.

Subtype: Looking at the phone versus at the person [Interpreting]
Human Learning & Development: A colleague glancing down at a phone during a talk may signal boredom, urgency or an actual work task. Naming the concern and asking for full attention is kinder than assuming disrespect.

Subtype: Cheek movement in fatigue and stress [Regulating]
Human Learning & Development: An adult under stress may clench the cheeks or puff out a breath, signs of tension. Noticing these in oneself can prompt a short break, and in others gentle support.
A young adult sees raised cheeks with crinkled eyes and reads warmth, but knows some people show pleasure with little cheek movement. Baseline expression differs by person.
A young professional tightens or presses the lips to hold back a comment, a sign of restraint. Naming the concern calmly later can be better than swallowing it every time.

Subtype: Trembling voice and lips at emotional moments [Regulating]
Human Learning & Development: An adult's lips tremble when speaking about something moving, a normal sign of strong feeling. Slow breathing and a pause help, and listeners can be patient.
A colleague juts the jaw in a disagreement, which may signal resolve, defensiveness or fear. Staying calm and asking questions can de-escalate, and leaving is fine if it feels unsafe.

Subtype: Tongue in cheek humour at work [Mismatch]
Human Learning & Development: A young professional pairs a tongue-in-cheek face with a dry remark, signalling a joke. With people who do not know them well the humour can be missed, so a smile clarifies.

Subtype: Blank expression in exhaustion or burnout [Interpreting]
Human Learning & Development: A colleague with a blank face for weeks may be exhausted, low or overloaded, not uninterested. A private, kind check-in and practical help matter more than judging attitude.
An adult notices a tense, rigid face before a hard talk and softens it with slow breaths and relaxing the shoulders. A calmer face often makes the conversation easier.
A young professional nods regularly to show engagement, which can be reassuring, but constant nodding may hide disagreement. Voicing a concern respectfully is better than nodding through.

Subtype: Bowing the head in respect and mourning [Expressing]
Human Learning & Development: An adult bows the head at a funeral, prayer or a formal greeting to show respect or grief. The meaning shifts with setting and tradition, and observers follow local custom.
A young professional holds tension in the shoulders during deadlines, and stretching or brief breaks help. Colleagues may read tight shoulders as irritation when it is strain.
An adult shrugs with palms up to show helplessness or an apology, but if used to dodge responsibility it can feel dismissive. Adding words shows ownership.

Subtype: Hands behind the back in respect [Expressing]
Human Learning & Development: A young professional stands with hands behind the back in a formal setting or before a senior, showing respect or attentiveness in many cultures. It can seem stiff elsewhere.
A young leader spreads the arms wide to invite the team and show openness, though the effect depends on genuine listening.

Subtype: Rubbing hands and drumming at work [Mismatch]
Human Learning & Development: A colleague rubs the hands in anticipation or drums the fingers in impatience, and it can be either. Asking about it works better than guessing.

Subtype: Wringing hands and grief or anxiety [Interpreting]
Human Learning & Development: An adult wrings the hands during a hospital wait or hard news, a sign of anxiety or grief. Quiet presence and a calm offer of help matter more than words.
A young professional chooses between a handshake, namaste or a nod based on the person and setting, respecting religious and personal preferences. Asking or following the other's lead shows care.
An adult places a hand over the heart to thank someone or show sincerity, a widely understood gesture in many places. Its warmth comes from the whole manner, not the gesture alone.

Subtype: Finger to lips and safety limits [Mismatch]
Human Learning & Development: A young adult reads finger-to-lips as a polite request for quiet in a hospital or as a coaxing secret. If someone uses it to demand secrecy about something that frightens or harms, that is a warning sign; sharing it with a trusted person is right.

A young professional uses an open palm to invite a colleague to speak, or a calm hand to slow a heated exchange. Used warmly it shares the floor; used as a sharp stop-signal at seniors it may seem controlling, so tone and status matter.

Subtype: Describing with hands to bridge language gaps [Regulating]
Human Learning & Development: A worker in a new city with limited shared language uses shapes, mime and pointing to make a request. Gestures can bridge but also mislead, since meanings vary, so checking with a confirming phrase or an image avoids mistakes.

A young professional finds hand descriptions are cropped or delayed on camera, so a shape or size may go unseen or be misread. Adding words, sharing a screen or a quick sketch reduces confusion where gestures are limited.

A young worker hunches over a laptop for hours, which reads as focus or exhaustion to others and can cause discomfort. Regular movement, an adjusted chair and breaks help body and mood, and coworkers should not assume laziness from posture.

A young professional meets bosses who lean back, sit tall or stand close, and finds that posture signals status differently across offices and cultures. Guessing attitude from body position alone is risky; behaviour over time tells more.

Subtype: Restless pacing at work or in waiting rooms [Regulating]
Human Learning & Development: A young professional paces before an interview or bad news to burn nervous energy. Others may read it as impatience or worry; stepping out, breathing and a short walk usually help more than sitting rigid.

Subtype: Walking away in conflict at work [Regulating]
Human Learning & Development: A young worker leaves the room during a heated exchange to avoid saying something regrettable. This can be sound de-escalation if followed by a return and a calm word; leaving abruptly with no explanation can read as disrespect.

A young adult steps between a friend and a threat or shields a child from a crowd. Protection can be caring but should not escalate danger; calling authorities and moving everyone away are usually the wiser choices.

A young professional pulls back, avoids eye contact or startles easily after a hard period. It may reflect stress, grief or exhaustion; supportive people offer patience and professional help rather than pushing them to open up.

A young adult picks up a phone, taps or scrolls in awkward moments as a comfort or an escape. It may show boredom, anxiety or urgent work, and others often read it as disrespect; a short explanation prevents hurt.

Subtype: Rubbing temples and neck at work [Expressing]
Human Learning & Development: A young professional rubs the neck or temples during long meetings, signalling tiredness, tension or headache. Colleagues cannot tell which from the gesture alone; offering a break or asking kindly is better than guessing.
A parent or carer strokes a child's back or an elder's hand to soothe. The receiver's comfort, not the giver's intention, decides whether it helps, so watch for relaxing breath or flinching.

Subtype: Comfort touch in grief and care [Interpreting]
Human Learning & Development: A young adult offers a hand on the shoulder or a hug to a grieving friend and watches for signs of acceptance. Touch can soothe but may not suit everyone; asking can I hug you respects choice and shows care.

Subtype: Handshake and greeting in work life [Expressing]
Human Learning & Development: A young professional shakes hands, offers a namaste or a nod according to setting, gender norms and health needs. A firm, brief handshake conveys respect, but preferences differ, so following the other person's lead is wise.

A young adult reads a delayed reply, a muted camera or a left-on-read message as distance. Such digital signals may mean busyness, tech trouble or coldness, and a direct kind question beats silent assumption.

A young professional reads who sits next to whom, who stands close to the boss and who keeps distance in meetings. Seating can reflect rank, habit or logistics; assuming a hidden meaning without evidence leads to misjudgment.

Subtype: Laughing in meetings and difficult talks [Regulating]
Human Learning & Development: A young professional uses a light laugh to ease tension, or holds one back in a solemn moment. A chuckle can build rapport, but laughing at a colleague's concern or a serious issue can seem dismissive.

Subtype: Laughing through hurt and gallows humour [Mismatch]
Human Learning & Development: A young adult laughs about stress, a mistake or a hard time as a coping tool. It can show resilience but sometimes hides pain; a friend who listens without assuming can tell which by gently asking how they really are.

Subtype: Bawling after overwhelming loss or relief [Regulating]
