An adult takes slow breaths, feels warm concern rather than merging with the pain, asks "what would help?", and looks after their own rest so care can last.
A supervisor sees a caregiver grow hard or tearful after too many hard cases and arranges rest, talk and shared load; caring people need care too.

Subtype: Adult offers words to a child [Observer]
Human Learning & Development: A parent or teacher says "your face looks cross, are you upset?" to help a child name what they feel; simple naming without pressure builds emotional vocabulary.

Subtype: Feels something but cannot name it [Actor]
Human Learning & Development: A child says "I feel weird" and points to a tight stomach when asked; the feeling is real, but finding the words for it is difficult.
A teenager answers every question about mood with "fine" or "nothing", and describes bodily aches more than feelings; they are not cold, they lack the map of words.
A person in a close relationship feels the other never says what they feel and takes it as coldness; it may be difficulty naming feelings, not a lack of caring.

Subtype: Learning words for feelings with support [Response]
Human Learning & Development: An adult builds a list of feeling words, notices bodily cues such as a tight chest, writes daily notes, and speaks to a counsellor if the difficulty causes distress in work or love.

Subtype: Hunger and sleep turn into tantrums [Actor]
Human Learning & Development: A toddler melts down over small things when hungry or tired, and a meal or nap changes the mood; body needs come before manners or reasoning.

Subtype: Teacher notices a child cannot focus before snack [Observer]
Human Learning & Development: A teacher sees a child fidgeting and tearful before break, calm after eating; unmet basic needs often look like bad behaviour.
A schoolchild who came without breakfast thinks only of food and cannot follow the lesson; the mind narrows to the pressing need and higher goals fade.

Subtype: Sleep loss changes mood and choices [Actor]
Human Learning & Development: A teenager up late every night grows irritable, impulsive and low, and takes worse decisions; steady sleep and regular meals protect mood and judgment.
A student surviving on tea and little sleep snaps at friends and makes rash choices before exams, then regrets them; rested bodies think and forgive better.

Subtype: Long scarcity leaves little room for planning [Observer]
Human Learning & Development: A person short of food, sleep or safe shelter for long has little mental room for future planning, which reflects scarcity and not laziness; support and stable basics free the mind.
A child lost for an hour in drawing or building forgets time and prizes; curiosity and joy in the task itself are early signs of a mind growing toward its own potential.
A teenager keeps learning classical music despite jokes from classmates, since it feels true to them; growth begins where inner interest outweighs the wish to fit in.
A young adult turns down a high-paying, famous job for work that fits their values, and feels both fear and calm; the path fits them better than the applause would.
A mentor notices a young person light up and stay late for their own interest, not for marks, and gives them space and tools instead of pressing them toward a set career.

Subtype: Using skills for a purpose beyond self [Actor]
Human Learning & Development: A young professional feels both content and restless, uses their skills to teach, build or serve, and sees growth as continuing, not a finish line.
An adult accepts that growth can begin amid limited means, starts with small acts of learning or creating, and does not treat comfort or wealth as a requirement for it.
A child pushes an adult's hand away from the shoelaces and insists on tying them alone, taking pride in choosing and doing; the wish for independence grows from here.

Subtype: Wants to choose own subject and friends [Actor]
Human Learning & Development: A teenager wants to choose their stream and friends on their own judgment, and clashes with parents' plans; independence feels like part of who they are.

Subtype: Forging own path despite family pressure [Actor]
Human Learning & Development: A young adult explores an unusual career, accepting risk and disapproval; freedom and curiosity matter more to them than an approved route, though they still love their family.
An adult protects their freedom of choice while honouring duties to parents and colleagues, explaining reasons and staying open to others' views rather than simply defying.

Subtype: Wants warm, sweet, soft things now [Actor]
Human Learning & Development: A toddler seeks sweets, cuddles and bubbles and cries when they stop; seeking pleasure and comfort is a simple, natural drive at this age.

Subtype: Lives for fun and good times [Actor]
Human Learning & Development: A teenager plans around films, outings and food, and finds long-term duty dull; the love of enjoyment brings vitality and friends, and can crowd out work if it rules everything.

Subtype: Pleasure versus duty in the hostel [Actor]
Human Learning & Development: A young adult skips a study session for a late-night outing and enjoys it fully while feeling a pinch of guilt; enjoyment and responsibility pull in different directions.

Subtype: Savouring without being ruled by it [Response]
Human Learning & Development: An adult treats joy as valuable, taking real time for meals, rest and play, and keeps pleasure in balance with health and commitments instead of chasing the next thrill.

Subtype: Shares a snack and comforts a friend [Actor]
Human Learning & Development: A child breaks a biscuit to share with a crying friend and pats them; early kindness comes from love for those close to them.
A child carries a classmate's bag when they are ill and keeps a secret they were trusted with; caring for people they know well is their strongest moral pull.
A homesick student is brought tea and time by a flatmate without being asked, and feels safe; dependable small kindnesses tell people they belong.
An adult helps family and friends generously, and also says no when exhausted, knowing that kindness that empties the giver cannot last.
A child objects when a classmate from another community is left out of the game and says it is unfair; concern for justice reaches beyond friends.
A teenager joins a tree-planting drive and worries about people far away who suffer from floods; wide concern grows with understanding of how the world is linked.

Subtype: Universal principle against loyalty to own circle [Actor]
Human Learning & Development: A young adult feels torn when principles of fairness for all conflict with loyalty to family or friends, and works through the tension instead of choosing carelessly.

Subtype: Turning wide concern into local action [Response]
Human Learning & Development: An adult volunteers, votes thoughtfully and treats neighbours from every background with respect, not just holding grand ideals; small consistent acts show the value at work.

Subtopic: Schwartz values: stimulation, achievement, power, security, conformity, tradition
Human Learning & Development: A child begs to try the tallest slide and every new game; excitement and challenge feel like life itself, and boredom feels worse than a little risk.

Subtopic: Schwartz values: stimulation, achievement, power, security, conformity, tradition
Subtype: Conformity: follows rules to avoid upsetting others [Actor]
Human Learning & Development: A child follows every class rule and the group's dress and speech, fearing disapproval; politeness and self-restraint help harmony but may bury their own opinion.

Subtopic: Schwartz values: stimulation, achievement, power, security, conformity, tradition
Human Learning & Development: A teenager pushes for top ranks and praise from respected people, feeling worth through results; it fuels effort and can leave little room for rest or failure.

Subtopic: Schwartz values: stimulation, achievement, power, security, conformity, tradition
Human Learning & Development: A young adult stands for student leadership to shape decisions and be respected; the wish for influence can serve a group well or slide into wanting control over others.

Subtopic: Schwartz values: stimulation, achievement, power, security, conformity, tradition
Subtype: Tradition: honours customs and family ways [Actor]
Human Learning & Development: A young adult keeps festivals, fasts and family rituals with devotion, finding belonging and meaning in them; respecting inherited ways can sit peacefully or in tension with new ideas.

Subtopic: Schwartz values: stimulation, achievement, power, security, conformity, tradition
Human Learning & Development: A young professional chooses a steady job and saves carefully, valuing certainty and safety for family over chances; calm and worry can both come with the choice.

Subtopic: Schwartz values: stimulation, achievement, power, security, conformity, tradition
Subtype: Seeing that values compete and choosing a ranking [Response]
Human Learning & Development: An adult sees that freedom, security and tradition cannot all rank first each time, names which one matters most in this choice, and respects others whose rankings differ.
A child says "I will share my pencil if you share your eraser", judging right by what gives a fair exchange for oneself; other people's needs matter mainly as part of the trade.

Subtype: Feels cheated when kindness is not returned [Receiver]
Human Learning & Development: A child who lent a toy and got nothing back declares "never again"; they read helping as an exchange and feel wronged when the balance breaks.

Subtype: Helping a child see beyond the deal [Response]
Human Learning & Development: A parent or teacher asks "how would he feel if nobody shared with him?", drawing attention from trade to feelings and shared life, without shaming the child's fair-play instinct.
A teenager offers to do chores if they can have a phone, treating duty as a price; the deal-making is practical and honest, but it is not yet care for the family.
An adult helps a colleague only if it may pay off later and keeps a mental ledger of favours; the mindset can produce fair dealing but leaves relationships thin.

Subtype: Laws as agreements that serve people [Actor]
Human Learning & Development: A student reasons that laws exist to protect everyone's rights and welfare, and that unjust ones should be changed by fair, democratic means, not simply obeyed or broken.
A professional follows the rule in ordinary cases but raises a formal objection when it would harm people, and accepts the outcome of a fair process even when it goes against them.

Subtype: Person affected by a fair process feels respected [Receiver]
Human Learning & Development: An employee whose complaint was heard, weighed openly and answered with reasons feels respected even when the result was not in their favour, and trusts the system more.
A colleague sees a peer object openly to an unfair policy through proper channels, without sneering at rules or breaking them, and learns that loyalty and principle can go together.
An adult facing a rule conflict lays out the rights and welfare at stake, invites the affected people to speak, follows agreed procedures and works to improve the rule.

Subtopic: Kohlberg stages: contrast with other stages
Human Learning & Development: A child says hitting is wrong "because you get punished", judging right by whether an adult will be angry; a rule feels like a fact of the world, not something to reason about.

Subtopic: Kohlberg stages: contrast with other stages
Human Learning & Development: A teenager acts to be seen as a good friend and son, valuing loyalty and approval from those close to them, and can find it hard to disappoint the group.

Subtopic: Kohlberg stages: contrast with other stages
Human Learning & Development: A young adult treats rules and duty as the glue of society and says "what if everyone broke the rules?", which supports order and can be hard on people who face rare exceptions.

Subtopic: Kohlberg stages: contrast with other stages
Subtype: Stages are tendencies, not labels on people [Observer]
Human Learning & Development: A teacher notices the same student reason at different levels in different situations, and treats the stage model as a way to see how reasoning grows, not a ranking of who is a better person.

Subtopic: Kohlberg stages: contrast with other stages
Human Learning & Development: A thoughtful adult acts on self-chosen principles of justice and human dignity even when laws or the group disagree, accepting the cost; this stage is rare and no age or person is fully at one stage.

Subtopic: Zone of proximal development and scaffolding
Human Learning & Development: A toddler tries to fit a shape or stack blocks and fails alone, but succeeds when an adult steadies the tower or turns the piece slightly. The child beams as if the win were entirely their own.

Subtopic: Zone of proximal development and scaffolding
Subtype: Wanting a hint, not the answer [Actor]
Human Learning & Development: A child stuck on a puzzle says "don't tell me" and accepts only a nudge, such as which corner to try. Wanting to own the win while still needing help is typical at this age.

Subtopic: Zone of proximal development and scaffolding
Subtype: Help that is too much or too little [Receiver]
Human Learning & Development: A student handed the full solution learns nothing and feels quietly small; one left alone with a task far beyond reach gives up. Growth happens where the task is hard but a guide is near.

Subtopic: Zone of proximal development and scaffolding
Human Learning & Development: A teacher or older sibling notices the learner now needs fewer prompts and steps back on purpose. Withdrawing help at the right moment builds confidence; withdrawing too early or never both stall growth.

Subtopic: Zone of proximal development and scaffolding
Subtype: Asking a mentor at the edge of competence [Response]
Human Learning & Development: A young adult facing an unfamiliar task, such as a first lab project or job, asks a senior for a framework instead of bluffing or waiting to be rescued, tries it alone, then returns with sharper questions.

Subtopic: Zone of proximal development and scaffolding
Human Learning & Development: A junior professional coaching a new hire asks what they have already tried, offers one hint, and lets them finish, resisting the urge to take over for speed. The slower route builds a capable colleague.

Subtopic: Identity foreclosure, moratorium and role confusion
Human Learning & Development: A child announces they will be a doctor or engineer because the family expects it, and repeats it with pride. It is a role handed over, not yet explored, and it feels safe because nobody questions it.

Subtopic: Identity foreclosure, moratorium and role confusion
Subtype: Foreclosure under family or community pressure [Actor]
Human Learning & Development: A teenager accepts the stream, faith practice or career path chosen for them without exploring alternatives, feeling certain on the surface and a vague flatness underneath. Certainty came from obedience, not from testing.

Subtopic: Identity foreclosure, moratorium and role confusion
Human Learning & Development: A teenager tries different friend groups, styles and opinions within months and cannot say who they really are. It is unsettling, sometimes shows as irritability or withdrawal, and is a normal part of building a self.

Subtopic: Identity foreclosure, moratorium and role confusion
Human Learning & Development: A college student changes majors, travels, tries clubs and delays big commitments while sorting out values. Done with reflection it leads to a chosen identity; done with pure drifting it can stall.

Subtopic: Identity foreclosure, moratorium and role confusion
Human Learning & Development: A young adult who questions the family career or belief is called ungrateful or lost. They feel guilt and loneliness while trying to honestly ask what is theirs and what was inherited.

Subtopic: Identity foreclosure, moratorium and role confusion
Human Learning & Development: A young professional who realises they followed someone else's script neither blames the family nor burns everything down. They test small changes, keep the parts they truly endorse, and explain their choices with respect.
A toddler who has been reliably comforted seeks hugs, shares food and shows toys to a trusted adult. This early trust is the ground on which later adult closeness is built.
A child picks one best friend, shares secrets and feels devastated by a betrayal. Learning to be vulnerable with a single peer is early practice for adult intimacy.
A teenager shows a polished self online and to peers and hides doubts, afraid closeness means rejection. They feel surrounded yet alone, and only a few real disclosures begin to change that.

A young adult in a first serious relationship drops friends and interests to be close, or keeps everyone at arm's length to stay safe. Real intimacy needs a self that can stay whole while being close.

A young adult who feels lonely despite many contacts invests in fewer people: making regular calls, being honest about struggles and tolerating awkward repair after conflict. Isolation eases through vulnerability, not numbers.

A colleague notices someone who always deflects personal questions and turns down invitations. Without forcing confidences, they keep offering low-pressure company such as tea or a walk, and let trust build at that person's pace.

Subtopic: Integrity vs despair (as foreseen by the young)
Human Learning & Development: A teenager watches a grandparent who seems content and another who is bitter, and wonders which path they will take. They do not yet grasp how choices accumulate, but the contrast plants a lasting question.

Subtopic: Integrity vs despair (as foreseen by the young)
Human Learning & Development: A student imagines being sixty with regrets: a safe job never questioned, words left unsaid to parents. The fear can push them toward paralysing perfectionism or toward acting more honestly now.

Subtopic: Integrity vs despair (as foreseen by the young)
Human Learning & Development: A young person hears a grandparent say they wish they had studied or spoken up. They take it as a warning not a burden, and think about which risks now are worth their future self's peace.

Subtopic: Integrity vs despair (as foreseen by the young)
Subtype: Living so the story is one you can accept [Response]
Human Learning & Development: A young professional considers what they want to be able to say in old age and lets it shape ordinary choices: keeping promises, repairing rifts, doing work that matters. They accept that no life is regret-free.

Subtopic: Integrity vs despair (as foreseen by the young)
Human Learning & Development: A young adult sees an older relative who dwells on old grievances and unfinished ambitions. They feel compassion and a resolve not to end up rehearsing resentments, while still listening without lecturing.
A child loves showing a younger sibling how to tie shoes or draw, feeling proud to be the one who knows. This early urge to pass something on is the seed of later generativity.
A teenager tutors younger students or helps organise a neighbourhood cleanup and feels needed. Being useful to others gives a sense of worth that grades and status do not.
A young adult volunteers, mentors school kids or builds a small project not for credit but because they want their effort to outlast them. It sits alongside ambition, not in place of it.
A young worker settles into a routine, thinks only of salary and comfort, and feels flat when asked what they are building. It is not laziness; it is a life turned entirely inward.
A young professional shares what they learned with a junior, credits them publicly and accepts being outgrown. Generativity means caring for what grows, not owning it.

A young adult in their early twenties feels neither like a child nor fully an adult: financially partly dependent, making choices alone, unsure whether to say they have grown up. The feeling is common and not a failure.
A graduate sees many possible careers, cities and partners and feels both excitement and dread of choosing wrongly. The openness is a gift, but it can freeze decisions or invite endless comparison.

A young adult is asked about a job, marriage or salary by relatives who measure life by a fixed timetable. They feel judged and rushed, and learn to answer kindly without adopting someone else's clock.

A parent sees a child in their mid-twenties still living at home or changing jobs and worries. Understanding that today's path is longer and less linear helps them ask questions instead of issuing verdicts.

A young adult builds adulthood in small acts: managing their own money, making their own appointments, keeping commitments. They accept that feeling like an adult arrives gradually, not on a birthday.
A toddler pushes away a helping hand, insists on putting on their own shoes and then clings to a parent again minutes later. Both wanting independence and needing safety are true at once.
A child settling into school waves goodbye, plays independently and runs back for a quick check-in at pickup. Knowing the parent will return makes venturing out possible.

Subtype: Wanting privacy but still needing comfort [Actor]
Human Learning & Development: A child begins closing the bedroom door and keeping small secrets, yet still wants a parent close when sick or upset. Autonomy grows alongside, not instead of, attachment.

A teenager argues over curfews, prefers friends' opinions and hides parts of their life, while quietly checking that home is still safe. The push is a way of building a self, not rejecting the family.

A parent feels hurt when a once-chatty teenager answers in single words. They can respond with steady availability, fair rules and no punishment for honesty, rather than clinging harder or withdrawing.
A student in a hostel far from family feels proud of managing alone and then aches for home cooking and familiar voices. Missing home is not weakness; it shows the bond remains.

Subtype: Becoming an adult who is also a family member [Response]
Human Learning & Development: A young adult makes their own decisions about work or partner, informs the family with warmth instead of asking permission or defiance, and keeps regular contact. The relationship shifts from obedience to mutual respect.

Subtype: Feeling watched for a group label [Actor]
Human Learning & Development: A child told that girls are poor at maths or that children from some schools are weaker feels a knot in the stomach during a test and underperforms. The fear of confirming the label uses up the mental space needed for the problem.

Subtype: Performing below ability under a label [Actor]
Human Learning & Development: A teenager from a group that is assumed to do poorly in a subject grows tense in exams, rushes and doubts known answers. The results look like low ability but come from added pressure.
A student hears a teacher's low expectations, such as surprise at a good grade, and starts believing it. They may disengage to avoid trying and failing under scrutiny.

A teacher or mentor sees a capable student freeze in situations where their group is expected to fail. They notice the pattern of strong practice work and weak high-stakes performance, and do not read it as lack of talent.

A student reminds themselves that a test measures preparation not worth, recalls their past successes and values, and seeks mentors who show belief. Instructors can help by framing tasks as ways to grow and not as verdicts on ability.

A child on a shared sports team or class project befriends a classmate from another religion, caste or region and finds the imagined differences small. Personal knowledge chips away at fear learned from others.

A teacher notices that putting rival groups in the same room, with no shared goal and unequal status, only hardens stereotypes. Contact helps when people work as equals toward a common aim with backing from authority.
Teenagers from different neighbourhoods on a school play or science team depend on each other to succeed. Shared effort turns "them" into "us" more than talks about tolerance do.

Subtype: Being the only one from your group [Receiver]
Human Learning & Development: A young adult who is the sole member of their community in a hostel or workplace feels curious eyes and carries the pressure of representing everyone. Good contact lets them be an individual instead of an example.
A young team lead arranges mixed work groups with a real common goal and equal roles, and does not tolerate mockery of any group. They see attitudes soften through shared work, not lectures.
Children given a shared bowl of sweets each grab a lot quickly, since if they wait, the others will take it. It is early experience of how each person's small gain drains what the group shares.
A child leaves the school tap running, litters the shared ground or hogs the common cricket bat, thinking one person's share does not matter. Everyone thinks the same, and the resource is spoiled.
A student sees classmates leave group-project work to the same two diligent members. He recognises that when nobody is accountable, careful people carry the load and eventually resent it.
Hostel or flat mates leave a shared kitchen dirty, each assuming someone else will clean. The mess grows and everyone suffers, and each person feels their own contribution was too small to matter.

Subtype: Setting rules everyone can live with [Response]
Human Learning & Development: A young adult proposes a fair rota, clear limits and shared monitoring for a common resource, and models the behaviour first. Communities protect shared things through trust, visible fairness and agreed consequences.

Subtopic: Prisoner's dilemma and cooperation vs defection
Subtype: Share or cheat in a game [Actor]
Human Learning & Development: A child playing a trading game can cooperate for a fair outcome or cheat for a bigger short-term prize, and worries the friend will cheat first. The fear of being the sucker often drives the cheating.

Subtopic: Prisoner's dilemma and cooperation vs defection
Human Learning & Development: Two teenagers preparing a joint presentation are tempted to shirk, thinking the other will cover for them. Each does what is best individually, so both do worse than if they had cooperated.

Subtopic: Prisoner's dilemma and cooperation vs defection
Human Learning & Development: A student who shared notes freely finds a peer who never reciprocated and used them to rank higher. They feel foolish and angry and may swear off sharing, though blanket distrust costs them future partners.

Subtopic: Prisoner's dilemma and cooperation vs defection
Subtype: Cooperation that grows over repeated rounds [Actor]
Human Learning & Development: Colleagues who work together for years learn that reliable cooperation pays and that one betrayal is remembered. Because they will meet again, keeping promises becomes the practical and the moral choice.

Subtopic: Prisoner's dilemma and cooperation vs defection
Human Learning & Development: A young professional starts by cooperating, returns kindness with kindness, calls out defection plainly and forgives when the other side corrects. This avoids both naive exploitation and endless mutual punishment.

Children given coloured bibs quickly cheer for their colour and decide their team is best, even though they were assigned at random. Belonging feels good and rapidly creates a sense of "us" and "them".

Subtype: Pride in the group and dislike of rivals [Actor]
Human Learning & Development: A child proudly supports their school house or cricket team and feels personally hurt when the rivals win. Group pride is warm but easily slips into mocking the other side.

A teenager's mood rises and falls with the fortunes of their school, region or fandom, and they defend it fiercely against criticism. Group membership is a source of esteem, and insults to the group feel like insults to them.

A student feels like a Bihari in one setting, an engineer in another and a cricket fan in a third, and different identities come forward depending on who is present. Recognising this keeps any single label from taking over.

A young adult notices the pull to favour their group, seeks a wider shared identity such as the same city, same team or fellow parents, and treats outsiders fairly. Pride in belonging need not require contempt for others.

Subtype: Feeling poor next to a friend [Actor]
Human Learning & Development: A child who has enough at home feels sad on seeing a classmate's new bicycle and phone. The hurt comes from comparison, not from actual lack.

A teenager compares their marks, clothes or family situation with peers who are a step ahead, and feels cheated even though their own situation is decent. Feeling deprived depends on who one looks at.

A graduate who expected a job like their seniors got, and did not, feels bitter and entitled to something being withheld. Frustration is sharper when a group seems to be getting what they believed they deserved.

A manager notices resentment in a team when one group gets raises or perks and another does not, even when everyone is paid fairly. Transparent criteria and honest explanation reduce the sense of being left behind.

A young adult who catches themselves fuming at a peer's promotion asks what they actually have and what they can control, and compares to their own past. They keep ambition without letting envy set the mood.
A child in a rowdy group of classmates joins in teasing they would never do alone, feeling nobody will single them out. The group masks the individual, and inhibition drops.

Subtype: Behind a screen or in a mob [Actor]
Human Learning & Development: A teenager in an anonymous group chat or comment section posts cruelty or joins a pile-on because the target feels distant and everyone is doing it. Lowered self-awareness makes actions feel less theirs.
A student mobbed by dozens of messages or a hostile gathering feels overwhelmed, since there is no single person to reason with. The sheer number and anonymity of the crowd make the harm heavier.

Subtype: Noticing the slide in a group [Observer]
Human Learning & Development: A young adult at a celebration or protest sees the mood shift from festive to reckless and realises people are acting in ways they would later regret. Seeing it early lets them leave or calm others.

Subtype: Keeping the self in the crowd [Response]
Human Learning & Development: A young adult reminds themselves that their name and conscience travel with them, uses their own words, and steps back if the group starts hurting someone. Being accountable even when unseen is a mark of character.
A teenager made class monitor or team captain starts bossing peers, enjoying being obeyed and dismissing complaints. Power narrows attention to one's own goals and reduces care about others' views.

A student leader or new intern with some authority becomes less attentive to how juniors feel and quicker to bend rules for themselves. They rarely notice it, believing they still are the same person.
A junior employee learns to read a manager's moods, hide their views and say only what pleases, and feels smaller in the process. Powerlessness makes people watchful and quiet.

A peer sees a friend become a manager and gradually stop listening, interrupt, and expect special treatment. They gently name the change instead of gossiping, while acknowledging how pressure also shapes behaviour.

A young leader invites honest feedback, keeps friends who will disagree, asks what their decision costs people below them, and shares credit. Deliberately staying curious about others limits the drift toward self-importance.

Subtype: Following a grown-up's order to hurt [Actor]
Human Learning & Development: A child told firmly by a teacher or older cousin to exclude or scold another child does it, feeling uneasy but reasoning that the adult must know best. Responsibility seems to shift onto the person giving orders.

A teenager told by a coach or senior to do something that harms another feels tension and doubt, but the calm authority, small first step and "just continue" make stopping seem harder than going on. Many comply while visibly distressed.

A student reads about experiments where most ordinary participants kept obeying an authority despite a stranger's cries of pain. They realise obedience does not need cruelty, and that they too could be the one who complies.

A junior who is targeted by a group carrying out a superior's instruction, such as ragging or a punitive policy, feels they are being treated as a thing not a person. Those doing it often insist they had no choice.

A young professional asked to do something clearly harmful stops at the first doubt, states the concern calmly, asks for it in writing or a second opinion, and declines if needed. Early refusal is easier than late; one dissenter helps others.

Subtype: Playing a role until it takes over [Actor]
Human Learning & Development: A teenager given the role of prefect or gang lookout begins to act tougher than they are, and in time the behaviour feels natural. The costume of the role slowly changes what they think is acceptable.

Seniors in a hostel or student volunteers enforce rules harshly on juniors because the role licenses it, and they come to believe the juniors deserve it. Roles, uniforms and few checks can bring out cruelty in ordinary people.

Subtype: Being cast as the lower role [Receiver]
Human Learning & Development: A person placed in a subordinate role, such as a fresher, trainee or detainee, may become passive, withdrawn or resentful and start to see themselves as they are being treated. The role shapes even self-image.

Subtype: Seeing the role, not the person [Observer]
Human Learning & Development: A peer sees a friend in a supervising job become unusually harsh and remarks that this is not how he is at home. Recognising that setting and role can distort behaviour helps them raise concern without hostility.

A young supervisor pauses to ask whether they would treat someone this way outside of work, seeks oversight and asks subordinates for honest input. Clear limits, transparency and reminders of shared humanity protect against role drift.
A child sees that everyone else picks one answer or opinion and follows though it looks wrong to them, worried about being laughed at. Even when the truth is visible, disagreeing alone feels risky.

A teenager in a group that unanimously praises a film or looks down on a classmate begins to doubt their own view and adopts the group's. Sometimes they truly change their mind and sometimes they merely stay quiet.
A student notices that when a single classmate voices doubt, others quickly dare to disagree too. Having even one supporter makes it much easier to speak honestly against the majority.

A young adult who disagrees with an entire group in a meeting or hostel discussion feels stares, pressure and self-doubt. Their stance costs something socially and takes courage even when they are right.

A young professional checks their reasoning, then states a different view politely and gives evidence, or asks a question that opens the topic. They stay open to being wrong without simply going along.
A child readily shares a treat with a sibling or grandparent and is slower to share with a visiting stranger's child. Closeness and shared belonging shape early generosity.
A child fiercely defends a sibling from a bully even after quarrelling with them that morning. Family loyalty can override personal grudges and small risks.

Subtype: Duty to family versus own wishes [Actor]
Human Learning & Development: A teenager gives up a trip or a preferred course to help with a sibling's education or family finances, feeling love and resentment together. Loyalty is real and sacrifice still has a cost.

A student sees a family friend at a workplace or election given a favour because of kinship. They understand the deep pull of loyalty to one's own, and also the harm to fairness when it displaces merit.
A young adult supports relatives in need with time and money, but declines to bend rules or hide wrongdoing for them. They say plainly that love for family and honesty toward others can both be kept.
A child shares a toy with the friend who shared last time, and refuses the one who never does. Early fairness is expressed as "you did for me, I do for you".
A child notes who helped whom, and objects loudly to unequal splits, even when they would receive the extra. A sense that fairness matters is emerging, sometimes rigidly.
A teenager who received notes or help from a friend feels a pull to return the favour, and feels resentment or guilt if it remains unpaid. Reciprocity binds friendships but can become a ledger.
A flatmate notes that one person keeps accepting help but never gives it, and the group quietly stops helping. Groups punish takers through withdrawal, gossip or pointed comment before they confront.
A young adult helps generously with no immediate return, but stops giving to someone who habitually takes, and says so calmly. Mature reciprocity is generous, alert and not afraid to set limits.
A child told "you can't play with us" cries or freezes and often says their tummy hurts. Exclusion is felt as a real physical-feeling pain, even in very young children.
A child whose friends stop speaking to them in class feels invisible, anxious and confused about what they did. Being ignored can hurt more than being openly teased.

A child who organises a group to shun a classmate feels powerful and safe from being excluded themselves, and may tell themselves the target deserves it. Excluders often act out of fear of losing their own place.
A teacher or classmate sees someone eating alone and being dropped from group chats. A small act, such as sitting with them or including them in a task, can break the cycle without drawing attention.

A young adult excluded from a friend circle admits the hurt, reaches out to other people, and does not conclude there is something wrong with them. They keep contact with those who accept them and avoid retaliating with exclusion of their own.

A teenager repeatedly asked "where are you really from?", or told they speak good English or are surprisingly smart for their background, feels singled out. Each comment is small, and the repetition adds up to feeling like an outsider.
A student makes a joke or a compliment based on a group stereotype, sincerely thinking it is friendly. They are shocked to learn it hurt, because the intent was kind but the effect was not.

A young adult hears a remark that feels demeaning and weighs the cost of speaking, wondering if they are overreacting, and whether it is worth the friction. Either choice is legitimate; carrying it silently can be tiring.

Subtype: Being told about an unintended slight [Actor]
Human Learning & Development: A person is quietly told that their comment came across badly. They feel defensive, embarrassed and misjudged, and do better by listening, apologising for the effect and adjusting without demanding comfort.

A young professional calmly says "I know you meant well, and here is how that came across", or asks what the person meant. This keeps the relationship intact while making the pattern visible, and also allows for real misunderstandings.

Subtopic: Allyship and how to help a targeted person
Human Learning & Development: A student sees a classmate being mocked and sits with them or walks them out, without lecturing the bully. A quiet act of solidarity tells the target they are not alone and often lowers the temperature.

Subtopic: Allyship and how to help a targeted person
Human Learning & Development: A peer who witnesses harassment checks privately with the target about what they want, such as reporting, confronting or just company, instead of taking over. Help should return control to the person affected.

Subtopic: Allyship and how to help a targeted person
Human Learning & Development: A person who was targeted gets a well-meaning defender who makes a scene, speaks for them or makes it about themselves. They feel grateful yet smaller, and prefer support that follows their lead.

Subtopic: Allyship and how to help a targeted person
Subtype: Speaking up in rooms the target is not in [Response]
Human Learning & Development: A colleague hears a discriminatory joke or unfair comment about someone absent and calmly challenges it, or supports them in a meeting by crediting their idea. Allyship shows in consistent small acts, not a label.

Subtopic: Allyship and how to help a targeted person
Human Learning & Development: A person announces support for a cause mainly to be seen as good and loses interest when it costs something. Real allyship listens, stays through discomfort and accepts correction.
A child sees that a classmate walks far to school while they arrive by car, or that some friends have a quiet place to study. They start to ask why, and may feel guilty, curious or defensive.
A teenager told they had it easier feels attacked, and answers "but I worked hard". Hard work and unearned advantage can both be true, and the second does not cancel the first.

Subtype: Living with a disadvantage others do not see [Receiver]
Human Learning & Development: A student from a modest or under-resourced background sees peers with tutoring, connections and safety nets, and feels the race began at different lines. They may feel resentment, and also pride in how far they have come.
A young adult recognises the head start from family, language or connections, and shares opportunities, recommends others fairly and listens to those with less. They neither wear guilt nor deny it.
A child checks classmates' marks, drawings or medals and feels proud or small accordingly. Comparing helps them learn where they stand, but constant ranking colours self-worth.

A teenager scrolls through peers' polished photos and achievements and feels dull and behind, forgetting that they see only highlights. Comparing one's ordinary days to others' best moments breeds unhappiness.

A student inspired by a friend's internship works harder, while another compares and sinks into envy and self-criticism. The same comparison can push someone on or pull them down, depending on whether the goal seems reachable.

Subtype: Feeling small at a friend's success [Receiver]
Human Learning & Development: A young adult hears a close friend has been promoted or married and feels happy and stung together. Admitting the mixed feelings honestly, rather than hiding them, leaves room for genuine congratulation.

A young professional measures progress against where they were a year ago, mutes accounts that always leave them low, and chooses a few peers to learn from. It keeps the useful side of comparison and drops the hurtful side.
A child repeatedly called lazy or slow starts to try less, and a child called clever takes on hard tasks. Others' beliefs about them become part of how they act.

A teenager who assumes classmates dislike them stays silent and looks bored at gatherings, so others leave them alone, which seems to prove their belief. Expectation changes behaviour, and behaviour changes how others respond.

A mentor notices that a junior who is trusted with challenging work rises to it, while one given only simple tasks stagnates. Expectations shape how much attention, feedback and opportunity someone receives.

Subtype: Predicting failure and drifting into it [Actor]
Human Learning & Development: A young adult who is convinced an interview will go badly prepares little, appears anxious and does poorly, taking it as confirmation. The fear helped produce the outcome.

A person notices their forecast about a situation and acts against it in small ways, such as speaking first at a gathering or preparing well. They treat the results as new evidence, and hold others to high but fair expectations.
After failing a test, one child says "I am stupid" while another says "I did not study that chapter". The way they explain setbacks, as permanent or temporary, shapes whether they try again.
A teenager who blames themselves for every setback, seeing it as permanent and affecting everything, gives up quickly. It feels like realism, but it is a learned way of interpreting events.

A student who fails an exam asks what the actual evidence is, considers other explanations and identifies one change to make. This is not forced cheerfulness; it is checking the story against the facts.

A colleague sees someone insist "everything will be fine" while ignoring real risks, and another who trusts that effort can change things and plans accordingly. Learned optimism is hope combined with preparation.

A young adult listens to a friend's despair, does not dismiss it, then helps them separate what is fixed from what can change and identify one small next step. Belief in possibility is grown, not commanded.
One toddler cries in a nursery and others begin to cry or look worried without knowing why. Emotions pass quickly between very young children.

Subtype: Catching the mood of a parent [Receiver]
Human Learning & Development: A child senses a parent's tension before a family event and becomes clingy and tearful, though nothing was said. Children pick up the mood of caregivers and can take it as their own.

Subtype: Laughter and panic in a class [Actor]
Human Learning & Development: A giggle spreads through a classroom until nobody can stop, or a rumour of an exam change spreads worry through everyone. Feelings move through groups faster than facts.

Subtype: Absorbing the crowd's excitement or fear [Actor]
Human Learning & Development: A teenager at a match, concert or rally is swept up in the crowd's energy, feeling joy or anger that is not entirely their own. Shared feeling can be warm and can make them act unusually.

Subtype: Setting the tone of a team [Response]
Human Learning & Development: A young team lead notices that their own stress and irritation spread to others, and takes a breath before meetings, speaks calmly and acknowledges pressure honestly. A steady person in the room can settle the group.

Subtype: Being known as fair or a cheat [Actor]
Human Learning & Development: A child who keeps promises in marbles or card games is invited to play again, while one who cheats is quietly dropped. Children begin to learn that a reputation forms quickly and lasts.
A teenager shares a minor secret with a new friend to see whether it stays private before sharing more. Trust is built in steps, and a single breach is remembered for a long time.
A student who lent money or shared a draft with someone who did not return or misused it feels betrayed and gullible. They learn to trust more carefully rather than to trust nobody.

A young professional hears colleagues discuss who can be relied on and who cannot, before ever working with them. They realise that reputation is gathered through small consistent actions and passed on informally.

A person who let others down admits it plainly, makes amends, and then behaves reliably over a long stretch without demanding quick forgiveness. Trust returns slowly through repeated evidence, not through apology alone.

Subtopic: Reaching a toy on a shelf
Human Learning & Development: A toddler stands under a low shelf, rises on tiptoe and stretches one arm toward a stuffed elephant, grunting, then tries the other hand when the first falls short.

Subtopic: Reaching a toy on a shelf
Human Learning & Development: A toddler tries jumping, tugging the shelf edge and pulling the rug under the toy, one after another, and keeps repeating whichever move makes the elephant shift even a little.

Subtopic: Reaching a toy on a shelf
Subtype: Approach: using the caregiver as a tool [Action]
Human Learning & Development: A toddler points at the shelf, looks at grandmother, says "uh, uh" and pats her hand. Her arm becomes the means of reaching, so the toddler does not need to work out the reaching.

Subtopic: Reaching a toy on a shelf
Human Learning & Development: After watching an older cousin drag over a small stool and climb it, a toddler pushes the same stool to the shelf and copies the climbing motion, without yet judging whether the stool is steady.

Subtopic: Reaching a toy on a shelf
Human Learning & Development: A toddler keeps stretching at the same spot for several minutes and ignores the stool close by, until tears come. Repeating one failing action leaves no room to notice other options.

Subtopic: Reaching a toy on a shelf
Human Learning & Development: Frustrated, a toddler sits down and whimpers, then looks around for mother, points at the shelf and lets her lift the toy down. The toddler switches from doing it alone to asking.
A toddler twists, pulls, bangs the lid on the floor and pokes at the edge of a snack box. Each action is tried for a few seconds and dropped if nothing gives.
Having watched father twist the lid off a tiffin box, a toddler copies the twisting wrist motion on a box of raisins, though the twist goes the wrong way and the lid does not open.

Subtype: Approach: using the caregiver as a tool [Action]
Human Learning & Development: A toddler holds the sealed box up to mother, says "open" and waits with hands out. The caregiver is treated as a tool that turns closed boxes into open ones.
Once, pressing the lid corner popped a box open. The toddler now presses the corner of every lid and box, and is puzzled when a screw-top bottle does not respond.
The lid stays stuck and a toddler grows red in the face, throws the box across the room and screams. Strong feeling ends the experimenting that might have opened it.
A toddler notices the lid lifted a tiny bit when pried at one corner with a fingernail, and keeps working that corner for a minute, guided by the small sign of progress.
A toddler sitting on the floor says "Amma" repeatedly and points at a fallen ball while mother chops vegetables. Voice and gesture are the whole plan.
A toddler tries babbling, tapping the table and carrying over a cup, and watches which one makes father look up from his phone. The one that works becomes the favourite.
Loud crying once brought mother running, so a toddler cries at full volume whenever she is busy. The method works, but it escalates and the adult starts to answer only to loudness.
A toddler copies an older sister, tugging the end of mother's sari and saying "Amma, dekho." The borrowed gesture gets mother's eyes on the toddler right away.
A toddler holds up a block, then looks at grandfather to see whether he has noticed. Seeing no reaction, the toddler shows the block again with a small squeal.
Calling from across the room brings no answer, so a toddler walks over, puts both hands on the caregiver's knee and looks up. Moving closer is the change made after the first plan failed.
A toddler picks up a star block and pushes it against the circle hole, then the square, then the triangle, testing each hole until one finally accepts it.
The block will not go in, so a toddler rotates it a quarter turn and tries again. The change in angle, rather than the hole, is what the toddler adjusts.
Mother drops the star into its slot, and a toddler copies the drop but holds the piece flat, sees it bounce off and starts again from the top.
A toddler hammers a square block on the round hole with a palm again and again. The force feels like effort, but nothing about the shape of the block changes.

Subtype: Approach: using the caregiver as a tool [Action]
Human Learning & Development: A toddler hands the stuck block to mother and looks at her. She turns it slightly, and the toddler pushes it the rest of the way, then claps.
After many failed tries a toddler drops the block, pushes the box away and crawls off to stack cups. Leaving the puzzle protects the mood and the task can be tried on another day.
A toddler tries lying belly-first on the cushion, then hooking a knee up, then rolling sideways, and stays with the version that gets the knee over the edge.
A toddler watches an older brother turn around, sit and swing legs up. The toddler copies the sequence loosely and lands halfway across the cushion, closer than before.

Subtype: Approach: using the caregiver as a tool [Action]
Human Learning & Development: A toddler stands in front of the sofa, lifts both arms and says "up." Father lifts the toddler onto the seat, so the plan needs no climbing at all.
A knee on the cushion edge helped last time, so a toddler starts every climb that way and steadily gets faster.
A toddler scrambles at the tall armrest instead of the seat, slips and is caught by a grandparent. Eagerness outruns any check of whether the spot is safe.
After slipping, a toddler cries but jumps at the same spot in the same way. Without a pause to change anything, each attempt fails as before.

Subtype: Approach: using the caregiver as a tool [Action]
Human Learning & Development: A toy car stops making its noise, so a toddler carries it to father, holds it up and says "no." The caregiver is treated as the repair service.
A toddler has seen mother call "Dadi!" when something breaks. Now a shoe strap comes loose and the toddler shouts "Dadi" toward the next room.
A toddler shakes the silent toy, bangs it on the floor and presses the button several times. Only after none of it works does the toddler set off to find mother.
A teddy is wedged behind the sofa and a toddler screams from the spot, waiting. The caregiver hears the noise but cannot tell what is wrong, so help arrives late.

Subtype: Approach: leading the caregiver by hand [Revision]
Human Learning & Development: Mother says "wait a minute," so the toddler grabs her finger and pulls her to the sofa, pointing at the teddy. Bringing the adult to the problem fixes the missing message.
The wedged teddy will not come out, so a toddler stops trying, walks away and does not tell anyone. The toy stays lost until a caregiver finds it later.

Subtype: Approach: using the caregiver as a tool [Action]
Human Learning & Development: A toddler brings an empty katori to mother and taps it, saying "aur." Handing over the bowl says more than the word does.
A toddler tugs at the kitchen cupboard where biscuits are kept, then at the fridge handle, then points at the counter. Each try shows what can be reached.
At mealtime a toddler copies the family, saying "roti" and holding out both hands. The word, learned by copying, is treated as a way to make food appear.
Rubbing the tummy and saying "num" once made grandmother bring milk. A toddler now rubs the belly whenever hungry, whether or not anyone is looking.
A toddler wanted a biscuit and gets offered a banana. The toddler pushes it away and cries, because the goal was fixed on one thing and the request was not clear.
After crying for a biscuit, a toddler sniffs, looks at the banana, and takes it. Hunger wins out, and the plan changes from getting a specific food to getting some food.
A child stacks wooden blocks into a tower, watches it fall at the sixth block, and simply builds it again with the blocks in a slightly different order.
A child tells herself, "First the big blocks, then the small ones, then the flag on top," and builds in that order. The list keeps the tower's shape in mind as it grows.
A boy sees his neighbour make a wide base with two long blocks and does the same. His tower goes higher than his earlier ones, though he cannot explain why.
A child says "stay up" to the tower and insists the red block is lucky, so it goes on top. When the tower wobbles anyway, the child blames the block rather than the narrow base.
After three collapses a child decides, "If it wobbles, make the bottom wider," and uses the rule on the next tower. A tested rule replaces the guess.
The tower falls a fourth time and a child sweeps the blocks off the mat, saying "I hate this." Feelings run ahead of thinking and the learning from the earlier tries is lost.
A child asks father to hold the bottom block while she stacks, then watches how he sets the blocks square. She copies his placement when she next builds alone.
A child of four covers both eyes in the middle of the room and believes nobody can see. The child cannot yet take the seeker's point of view.
Found in seconds behind the door, a child tries behind the curtain next round, then under the bed. Each round of being found or not found teaches which spots work.
A child hides in the almirah because an older cousin won there last time. It works this time only because the seeker does not know the cousin's trick.
A child thinks, "If the seeker goes left, I go right around the sofa," and waits to see which way he goes. It is a simple plan about another person's move.

Subtype: Approach: simple step list as seeker [Action]
Human Learning & Development: Seeking, a child checks the rooms in order: bedroom, kitchen, balcony, then the bathroom. Going in a fixed sequence stops the same place being searched twice.
A child holds her breath tightly and squeezes eyes shut, sure this will make her invisible even while standing in the open. Wishing stands in for a plan.
Found first in three rounds, a child says, "One more, then I seek and you hide." The child changes the rules of the game rather than the hiding place.
A child talks through a doctor game ahead of time, saying "You are sick, I listen to your chest, then give medicine," and acts out the first lines with a doll.
Two children assign roles, gather props such as a toy stethoscope and a bandage, and set the clinic on the mat before starting. Set-up comes before play.
Both want to be the doctor. A child says, "You be doctor first, I am doctor next game," and the play can begin without a fight.
A child asks mother for an old dupatta to use as a costume, and mother suggests it can be a nurse's cap. The adult supplies the props and one new idea.
The play stalls after the check-up, so a child announces, "Emergency! The baby has a fever!" A new problem in the story keeps the game going.
A child insists the game must go exactly as planned and corrects the friend's every line. The friend loses interest and drifts away.
A friend changes the story to a train journey, and the first child says "not fair," stops playing and sulks. The plan had no space for another child's ideas.
A child tidies in an order: books to the shelf, then toys to the box, then clothes to the basket. Doing one kind at a time keeps the mess from feeling endless.
A child follows the rule, "If it has wheels, it goes in the blue box," and sorts cars, trucks and a scooter without asking each time.
A half-built block model sits on the floor and a child asks mother whether to knock it down or keep it. The adult decides where it may stay.
Faced with toys everywhere, a child sits in the middle and starts to play with one, so nothing gets put away. The size of the job is too much to start on.
A child offers, "I do the cars, you do the books, then we read a story." Splitting the work and naming the reward gets it moving.
A child pretends to be a shopkeeper and returns each toy to its shelf, saying "Sold out!" for each one. Play turns the chore into a game.
A child pushes everything under the bed and pulls the sheet down, sure the room is now tidy. Out of sight is treated as done, until mother lifts the sheet.
A child watches another child join a group by asking, "Can I play too?" and repeats the same words the next day at the sandpit, with a smile.
A child offers a friend the first turn on the new bicycle in return for playing tag afterwards. Trading what the friend wants for what the child wants opens the play.
A child thinks, "If she says no, I ask Meera instead," and prepares a second choice. The rule keeps a refusal from ending the whole plan.
A shy child practises the question "Do you want to play?" with a doll before going out. Saying the words once makes it easier to say them to a real child.
A child tells the teacher, "Nobody wants to play with me," and the teacher helps by proposing a group game. The adult gives an entrance the child could not find.
A child says, "You have to play my game or I won't be your friend," and the other child walks away. Demanding works less well than offering.

Subtype: Approach: giving up after one no [Pitfall]
Human Learning & Development: A friend says "not now" and the child decides that nobody likes him, and sits alone. One refusal is read as the final word.
A child at the slide counts the children ahead and works out, "Three more, then me." Knowing the place in the line makes the waiting easier to bear.
Another child skips ahead on the swing, so a child says to the teacher, "He didn't wait his turn." The adult is used to settle whose turn it is.
A child agrees, "If I get twenty pushes, then I get off," and counts aloud. The rule is agreed in advance, so getting off is less of a fight.
A child says, "You push me, then I push you," and swaps places at the swing after a fair count. Both children get a turn.
A child squeezes to the front of the line for the slide, and the others shout. The turn is got for a moment and the friendship pays for it.
The line is long and a child walks off to the corner, saying "I don't want to play anyway." Pretending not to care protects feelings and gets no turn.
Shouting "my turn" got a child nowhere. Next day the child asks, "Can I go after you?" and the child on the swing agrees. Polite asking is kept as the new plan.
A child swaps the toy truck for a turn with the friend's doll. Both get something they want, so the trade feels fair to both.
A child reasons, "If I share the truck, then Aarav shares his cars." The rule ties giving to getting, and makes it less costly to hand the toy over.
Two children pull on one toy until a teacher is asked, and she proposes a sand timer for each turn. The child follows the rule the timer sets.
A child fears that the toy will be "used up" or will change once a friend touches it, and hides it. The fear has no basis but decides what the child does.
A child sees a classmate hand over a crayon and get a smile and a turn with her paints in return. The child tries the same and it works.
A child turns sharing into a shop game where the friend is a customer who borrows the toy and returns it at closing time. Play makes giving it up feel safe.
A child snatches the toy and runs to hide it behind a cushion. The toy is kept for now, and the friend cries and the game ends.
A child tries one piece after another at the same gap in a jigsaw until one fits, without thinking about the picture on it.
A child says, "Edges first, then the sky, then the house." Sorting flat-sided pieces first makes a frame to work inside.
A child watches an older sister put all the corner pieces together first and does the same, and the puzzle starts to take shape faster.
A child decides, "If a piece has one flat side, it is an edge," and uses it to sort the pile. A small rule cuts the number of pieces to check.
Stuck on the last corner, a child asks father, who shows the piece's picture and where the colour continues. The child then finds the next match unaided.
A child presses a wrong piece down hard and says, "It wants to go here." Liking the idea outweighs the evidence of the shapes not matching, and the piece bends.
The middle of the puzzle will not come together, and a child tips the pieces back in the box and says "it's broken." Blaming the puzzle ends the effort.
A child follows a picture chart on the wardrobe door: vest, shirt, shorts, socks, shoes. Each step is ticked off in order.
A child recites, "If it is Wednesday, I wear sports shoes." Attaching the action to the day means the child needn't ask every morning.
A child pretends the school uniform is a superhero costume and puts it on in "power order," starting with the cape-like tie. The story gets the child dressed.
A child says, "I will wear the sweater if I can choose my socks." Trading a small choice for a needed action moves the morning along.
Buttons are done up one hole out, and the child sees the shirt hang crooked, undoes it and starts again from the bottom button. The mistake is spotted and fixed.
A child can do everything but the shoelaces, so mother is asked to tie them. Knowing which step is too hard, and asking for only that, is a small piece of planning.
A child cannot find the second sock, climbs back into bed and says "I'm not going." One missing item ends the whole plan for the morning.
A child follows a picture list taped inside the cupboard: water bottle, lunch box, notebook, pencil box. Each item is put in and ticked.
A child asks mother, "What do I need for tomorrow?" and she reads the timetable aloud. The child then puts in the books she names.
A child follows the rule, "If it is PE day, shoes go in the bag." The rule links a fact about the day with an object to pack.
A child sees an older brother pack the night before, and lines up the bag by the door the same way. The habit is borrowed, and it works.
A child throws items in quickly and later finds the lunch box left on the table. Packing felt finished without any check against the list.
A child leaves the homework notebook out of the bag, believing the teacher will not ask for it if it isn't there. Hoping replaces doing.
After forgetting the water bottle, a child pretends to walk through the school day, saying "Now I am thirsty, I need my bottle." The rehearsal shows what is missing.
A child drags a chair to the cupboard to reach a jar of sweets, tries standing on it, and finds it still too short. Then a stool is added on top.
A child says, "Papa, can you get the jar down?" and points to the shelf. Asking is quick and safe, and the child's own plan is only needed if nobody is home.
A child sees an older brother use a long stick to hook a kite off a shelf, and tries a broom handle in the same way. The tool idea was borrowed.
A child has been told, "If it is too high, ask a grown-up," and calls out for mother. The rule from earlier stops a risky climb.
A child stretches and stretches, believing that arms can grow long enough with effort. Wanting the jar overrides a plain look at the distance.
A stacked stool starts to wobble, and the child steps down and calls for help. Feeling the danger changes the plan from climbing to asking.
A child folds the paper in half, draws a cake on the front, writes the friend's name inside, and colours it last. The order makes the card come together.
A child imagines grandmother opening the card and smiling, and decides on her favourite flowers and colours. The imagined reaction chooses the drawing.
A child copies the teacher's sample, a flower with five petals and a green stem, and adds a sun of her own. Copying supplies a starting point that can then be changed.
Glitter glue smudges the drawing, so a child tries pencil first on a fresh sheet and adds glitter only at the border. The mess teaches an order for the materials.
A child asks mother how to spell "Happy Birthday" and copies the letters one at a time from her page. The adult supplies what the child cannot yet do.
The drawing turns out crooked and a child crumples the paper and says "it's ugly," and will not make another card. The wish for a perfect result stops the effort.
Two children argue about a toy car and one runs to the teacher, who listens to both and helps them agree. The adult acts as the judge.
A child says, "You have it now, I have it after lunch." Splitting the time between them ends the shouting with each getting a turn.
A child thinks, "If he says sorry, then I forgive him," and waits. The rule is clear but rigid, and the quarrel drags on until he says it.
A child turns away and pretends the fight is not there, in the belief that it will go away. The hurt stays, and the friend is puzzled by the silence.
A third child suggests tossing a coin for the toy and both accept. The first child remembers the idea and suggests it at the next quarrel.
A child shouts, "I'm not your friend anymore," and stomps off. The fight ends for the moment and the friendship gets damaged, till the next day's play.
A child follows the sticker chart: brush teeth, finish milk, put shoes in the rack. Each finished task gets a sticker, and ten stickers means a trip to the park.
A child says, "If I eat all my vegetables, can I have two stories tonight?" Naming the price and the prize makes the deal explicit.
A child holds the rule, "If I put my toys away, I get a sticker," and does it as soon as playtime ends. The link between action and prize is understood.
A child wishes on the first star for extra stickers and expects them to show up on the chart in the morning. The wish is trusted more than the routine.
Unsure how far off the reward is, a child asks mother, "How many more stickers?" She counts three with the child, and the goal becomes something concrete.

Subtype: Approach: giving up after a miss [Pitfall]
Human Learning & Development: After missing two days, a child says the chart is finished and does not try again. One lapse feels like total failure, until a parent restarts the count.
A child looks for a lost shoe by going back through the day: the bedroom, the verandah, the gate where she played. Going in order narrows down where it could be.
A child says, "Mummy, I can't find my shoe," and mother asks, "Where did you last have it?" The adult's question gives the search a structure.
A child pretends to be the missing shoe and asks, "Where would I go?" Imagining its journey brings up the idea of looking under the sofa.
A child insists that the shoe "ran away" and that it will come home if she waits at the door. Waiting replaces searching.
A child looks in the same cupboard four times, each time hoping the shoe will be there. Without a record of what has been checked, the search goes round in circles.
A friend says, "Check the last place you played," and the child goes to the balcony where the shoe lies. The hint changes the search from random to reasoned.

Subtype: Approach: retracing the steps of the day [Thinking]
Human Learning & Development: A girl loses her water bottle and thinks back to where she had it last. She remembers drinking at PT class, goes back to the ground, and finds it on the bench.

Subtype: Approach: searching the same place again and again [Pitfall]
Human Learning & Development: A boy checks his school bag five times for a missing eraser. He feels sure it must be there, while he has not looked in his pencil case or pocket, and loses time and patience.

Subtype: Approach: searching one place at a time in order [Action]
Human Learning & Development: A child makes a plan to check the bag, then the classroom desk, then the bus and finally the lost and found box. Going in order stops him from wandering around in a panic.

Subtype: Approach: asking friends and teachers if they have seen it [Action]
Human Learning & Development: A girl who lost her geometry box asks her deskmate and the class teacher, and puts up a note by the door. Someone saw it near the library, and it was there.
A boy cannot find his pencil and quickly accuses his neighbour of taking it. Later he finds it under his notebook, and feels ashamed for having accused a friend without proof.

Subtype: Approach: staying calm and thinking where he usually puts it [Thinking]
Human Learning & Development: A child takes a deep breath and thinks about where he normally keeps his house key. He checks the hook and the shoe rack, and finds it inside his shoe.

Subtype: Approach: deciding a place for each item to avoid losing [Revision]
Human Learning & Development: After losing three pencils in a week, a girl decides her pencil case always stays in the front pocket. She notices that most losses come from putting things down casually.

Subtype: Approach: reporting to the school lost and found [Action]
Human Learning & Development: A boy loses his sweater and goes to the office to check the lost and found box. He describes it and the name written inside, and the peon returns it to him.

Subtype: Approach: letting go of a small item after a fair search [Revision]
Human Learning & Development: After searching properly and asking, a girl still cannot find her cheap sharpener. She decides it is not worth more time, borrows one and adds her name to the next one.

Subtype: Approach: listing every task and estimating time [Thinking]
Human Learning & Development: A Class 5 child lists maths sums, a Hindi paragraph and a drawing, then guesses ten, twenty and thirty minutes each. Seeing the total is one hour helps her feel the work is finite and not scary.

Subtype: Approach: doing the hardest subject first while fresh [Action]
Human Learning & Development: A boy starts with maths word problems right after his snack because his head is clear. He saves colouring the map for last, when he is tired and the task is easy.

Subtype: Approach: doing the easy fun parts first [Pitfall]
Human Learning & Development: A girl finishes the drawing and copying work first because they feel nice. By 8 pm only the hard sums remain, she is sleepy, and she rushes them with mistakes.

Subtype: Approach: pushing it off until just before bedtime [Pitfall]
Human Learning & Development: A child tells himself there is plenty of time and plays cricket and watches cartoons. At 9 pm he realises the science diagram takes an hour, and he starts crying and asking a parent to help.

Subtype: Approach: seeing the crowded evening and redoing the plan [Revision]
Human Learning & Development: Halfway through, a boy notices a cousin is visiting at 6 pm. He moves the sums to before dinner, and does the reading after the guests leave, so nothing is left undone.

Subtype: Approach: working in short blocks with small breaks [Action]
Human Learning & Development: A child sets a kitchen timer for twenty minutes of work and then five minutes of water and stretching. The breaks make the next block easier and the whole thing gets done before dinner.

Subtype: Approach: working next to a sibling doing their own homework [Action]
Human Learning & Development: A girl sits at the same table as her older brother, who is studying. Seeing him work quietly makes it easier to keep going, and she asks a question only when truly stuck.

Subtype: Approach: asking for help the moment a problem is stuck [Revision]
Human Learning & Development: A child gets stuck on a fractions question for fifteen minutes, then notices he is only getting upset. He puts a star next to it, asks his mother, and gets on with the other questions.

Subtype: Approach: rushing to finish and skipping the checking [Pitfall]
Human Learning & Development: A boy wants to go out to play so he scribbles answers fast and closes the notebook. Next day the teacher marks two sums wrong for copying errors he would have caught in a minute of checking.

Subtype: Approach: packing the finished work in the bag straight away [Action]
Human Learning & Development: Once the last page is done, a girl puts the notebooks in her school bag immediately. This avoids the morning panic of remembering that the homework is somewhere on the study table.

Subtype: Approach: counting days left and dividing the chapters [Thinking]
Human Learning & Development: A child with a Social Studies test in four days counts six chapters and plans one and a half chapters a day. Dividing the big task into daily pieces makes it feel doable.

Subtype: Approach: reading the chapter again and again [Action]
Human Learning & Development: A boy reads his science chapter three times, highlighting nothing. The words look familiar, so he feels ready, though he has only recognised the text and not tried to recall it.

Subtype: Approach: feeling ready because the page looks familiar [Pitfall]
Human Learning & Development: A girl closes the book and thinks she knows photosynthesis. When her mother asks her to explain it, she cannot say the steps, showing that familiarity is not the same as knowing.

Subtype: Approach: making questions and answering from memory [Thinking]
Human Learning & Development: A child turns each heading into a question, such as Why do we have seasons, and answers aloud with the book closed. Checking wrong answers tells him exactly what to study again.

Subtype: Approach: teaching the chapter to a younger sibling or toy [Action]
Human Learning & Development: A girl explains the water cycle to her little brother using a steel glass and steam from a kettle held safely by her mother. Where she stumbles is where she has not understood.

Subtype: Approach: practising old test papers under time [Action]
Human Learning & Development: A boy solves last year's maths paper at the dining table with a clock, then checks answers. He learns he spends too long on one question and decides to skip and return.

Subtype: Approach: skipping the boring chapter and hoping it will not come [Pitfall]
Human Learning & Development: A girl leaves out the Civics chapter because she dislikes it and thinks the teacher will not ask from it. The paper has an eight-mark question on it, and she loses easy marks.

Subtype: Approach: switching tactics after a bad practice score [Revision]
Human Learning & Development: After scoring only 5 out of 10 in her own quiz, a child notices that reading alone is not working. She switches to writing key points on cards and quizzing herself, and her next score rises.

Subtype: Approach: studying with a friend and swapping questions [Action]
Human Learning & Development: Two classmates meet after school and each writes five questions for the other. Their questions cover different parts of the chapter, and hearing each other's explanations fills small gaps.

Subtype: Approach: sleeping properly the night before and light revision [Thinking]
Human Learning & Development: A boy decides that staying up until midnight will only make him drowsy in the exam. He revises the summary points at 8 pm and sleeps by 9:30, planning to trust what he has learned.

Subtype: Approach: breaking division into smaller steps [Thinking]
Human Learning & Development: A child finds long division confusing. She notices it is really divide, multiply, subtract, bring down, and practises each step alone before joining them together.

Subtype: Approach: using an everyday example to understand fractions [Thinking]
Human Learning & Development: A boy cannot follow three-fourths until his mother cuts a roti into four parts and gives him three. The picture of real food gives the abstract number a meaning he can hold.

Subtype: Approach: memorising the rule without understanding it [Pitfall]
Human Learning & Development: A girl learns 'flip and multiply' for dividing fractions without knowing why. She gets the familiar sums right but is lost when the teacher gives a word problem in a new shape.

Subtype: Approach: drawing pictures and diagrams of the idea [Action]
Human Learning & Development: A child learning the parts of a plant draws roots, stem and leaves and labels what each does. Drawing forces him to notice details that reading skipped.

Subtype: Approach: trying easy examples first then harder ones [Action]
Human Learning & Development: A boy struggling with decimals first adds 0.5 and 0.5 with rupee and paise coins, then moves to 2.75 plus 1.5. Each success gives him confidence to try the next size.

Subtype: Approach: deciding he is just bad at the subject and giving up [Pitfall]
Human Learning & Development: After three wrong answers in a row, a girl says she is not a maths person and stops trying. This belief keeps her from practising, which is the very thing that would help.

Subtype: Approach: asking the teacher a specific question [Revision]
